In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā,
the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture," [describes] Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, and has four arms.
One should meditate on the one with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles.

Salutation to the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrin), who is the Wheel of the principles beginning with the Supreme (Para) and the Manifested (Vyūha), and whose form consists of the imperishable letters of the unmanifest triad, such as 'A' and others. 1-1.

We bow to the power of Hari, who is like Soma, Sūrya, and Anala; who is both with and without parts (sakalpa/akalpa); who has the moon as her crest-jewel; who possesses five points; and who performs the five cosmic acts. 1-2.
Then Bharadvāja questioned the sinless Durvāsas— who was seated at the supreme station after having bathed in the divine Gaṅgā— regarding the cause of the greatness of the Sudarśana.
Bharadvāja:
O venerable one, who brings joy to the heart of Anasūyā, treasury of asceticism!
I have a certain doubt; you ought to explain it to me. 1-4.
In the determination of the Atharvaṇa concerning the performance of the rites of Agni and Soma, and in the great arising of the collection of weapons that both impel and restrain. (1.5)

And in the assembly of the weapons of the world-protectors, which are endowed with their respective powers, and in the great manifestations of power belonging to the paths of fire, sun, and moon; || 1-6 ||
And within that flood of weapons, the resort of missiles created by Brahmā, Rudra, and others,
which is skilled in the acts of protecting and destroying the three worlds.
In this highly auspicious collection of mantras witnessed by hosts of great seers, belonging to Viṣṇu and beginning with the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the sword, and so forth; (1.8)
And in the *Lakṣmī*, in the *Dalagaṇḍābja* and the *Pūrva-astraugha*, as well as in the *Mahodaya*, and likewise in other various texts being proclaimed according to their power. (1–9)
However, its status as the locus of Sudarśana has been described here and there.
Is its greatness produced by itself, or even through association? (1.10)
What is that which is called Sudarśana, and what is intended by its etymological meaning?
What action is performed by it, and how does it pervade the world? (1-11)
O Sage, how many, of what kind, and what are the battle arrays (vyūhas) declared for him?
What is their purpose, and of what nature are those arrays? (1.12)
What is the relationship between him and Viṣṇu, and of what nature is it considered to be?
Is it fixed by him eternally, or is it seen elsewhere as well? (1.13)
(3) This doubt has arisen in me from the examination of various treatises; O Blessed One, sever it completely. I have approached you properly; please teach me, sir! (1-14)
Following a question and praise from Durvāsas, his reply was as follows: Durvāsas said,
"O child, this which you have thus reflected upon is indeed appropriate."
Those various austerities, O observer of noble vows, are now dawning upon you.

Only when the inner impurities have been brought to destruction by those various means does the desire to know the supreme reality arise; then, in men whose internal organs are purified, there dawns the wisdom that investigates the supreme reality. (1.16)
In this matter, even Brahmā and the others have doubts; you alone are not subject to doubt regarding the subject previously presented.
For even the wise ones, beginning with Brahmā, strive here while still possessed of uncertainty. (1.17)
The attainment of the determination of reality from Ahirbudhnya himself:
"This determination has been obtained by me here from Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, who spoke directly when questioned by the celestial sage Nārada. (1.18)
Having attained the supreme fruition of his asceticism, Nārada, who is honored by the gods,
excelled as he severed all doubts concerning Brahmā, the gods, and the great seers. (1.19)
Because he too had doubts regarding the subject of reality, he approached Ahirbudhnya;
for he himself, having encountered a profound doubt difficult for even the gods to comprehend, was an ascetic with his senses restrained, free from passion, disease, and impurity. (1.20)
One who knows the true nature of the rules governing words, sentences, and means of valid cognition;
one who is a celibate student, whose abode is self-restraint, and who understands the distinction between the higher and the lower.
Desirous of hearing, free from egoism, and intent upon the knowledge of reality as it is,
Nārada, that tiger among sages, was wandering through the three worlds.
There is no one other than the moon-crested Lord, the omniscient God, whom even the celestial sages cannot approach, who can sever this doubt so difficult to understand.
The description of Kailāsa:
With its own splendors, it seemed to mock all other mountains, like the manifestation of pure being that brings about supreme knowledge. (1.24)
Crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and frequented by gods and Gandharvas,
he went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara, in order to see Śaṅkara.
The description of Ahirbudhnya:
[He is praised] by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Siddhas, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts;
by the divine Ṛṣis and yogins, and also by various kinds of beings.
There he beheld the three-eyed, boon-granting Lord Īśāna, who bears the trident and has the moon as his crest-jewel, seated together with Umā and attended by his followers. (1.27)
To the Lord of beasts, who incessantly severs the bonds of worldly existence, who stands pervading the three worlds by means of his eight forms; 1-28.
Having seen that Lord Īśāna, Nārada, the seer of the gods,
prostrated himself and then praised him with the most excellent words out of reverence.
The hymn of praise to Ahirbudhnya composed by Nārada:
Nārada said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, whose banner bears the bull."
To the one whose vehicle is the preeminent bull, to the bull who showers down all desires.
O most bountiful one, let there be salutation to you, who are more powerful than the highest;
salutation to you, the omniscient, the independent, and the eternally satisfied.
Salutations to you, whose nature is primordial consciousness; salutations to you, the eternal power;
salutations be to you, the creator and destroyer of the worlds, who possesses the six limbs.
O Ten-fold Imperishable One, salutations to you; salutations to you who are clothed in an animal hide;
salutations to the Non-terrible, to the Terrible, and to the one more terrible than the terrible.
Salutation to you, the god Sadyojāta; salutation to you, Vāmadeva.
Salutation to Jyeṣṭha Rudra; O Bhavodbhava, let there be salutation to you. (1.34)
Homage to you, the transformation of strength, the crusher of strength!
Homage—[homage] to you! || 1.35 ||
Salutations to Kalavikara, to Kala, whose nature is calculation;
salutations to you, O Manonmana, the subduer of all beings.
Homage to Śarva, the peaceful one; homage to Śambhu, the source of bliss.
O Lord of Knowledge, homage to you; O Lord of Beings, let there be homage to you.
O Mahādeva, salutations be to you; salutations to you, the Tatpuruṣa.
O embodiment of knowledge, salutations to you; salutations to the ocean of dispassion.
Salutations to you, who are full of the quality of sovereignty; salutations to you, O treasure of asceticism! Salutations to you, O eternal truth; salutations to you, whose essence is forbearance.
Homage to you, whose essence is steadfastness; homage to you, the creator of the worlds, who presides over the three realms, perfected through self-awakening. 1.40
Salutations again and again to you, the eternal and imperishable, who possess the ten imperishables;
salutations to the Self who is earth, water, fire, air, ether, moon, and sun.
"Salutations to the one who stands over the three worlds for the benefit of all.
Thus did Durvāsas praise the best of divine sages with these foremost words.
With words sweet with grace, the bull-bannered Lord Ahirbudhnya spoke thus:
"O best of sages, I am pleased by this hymn and by your devotion. (1.43)
"Speak, what may I do today, even if it should be very difficult to obtain?
Nārada said: "What else is there to be said here, if the Lord of the World is pleased? (1.44)
For this indeed is what the wise, striving with effort, desire.
Ahirbudhnya said: "I am pleased with you today; let my appearance before you be fruitful. (1.45)
"Speak, O Nārada, according to the truth, regarding that which dwells in your mind.
[In the battle with Kālanemi, Nārada beholds the majesty of the Sudarśana.
Nārada said:
In the battle with Kālanemi, which resembled the destruction of the stars.
When the manifestation of the world-protector, the god of gods who wields the Śārṅga bow, had begun—
an event bringing fear to the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
When the armies of the lords of the gods and asuras, crowded with multitudes of weapons and missiles, had been cut down by great missiles, [he shone] like a thousand midday suns.
It was crowded with throngs of piśācas, pretas, vetālas, and bhūtas, who were overwhelmed by a mixture of fear, wonder, and agitation.
(8) While most terrible and resounding thunderbolts were falling,
and likewise as blood flowed from the bodies of the gods and the Dānavas, || 1.50 ||
While the streams were flowing with great force in every direction,
the surviving gods and asuras, terrified, fled in all directions.
While the Lord of the World was seated upon Garuḍa with the Sudarśana discus in his lotus-hand,
Kālanemi manifested the entire collection of his weapons.
Those who are the sons of Bhṛśāśva, those who have issued from your mouth,
those who were born from the mouth of Brahmā, and those who arose at the time of universal dissolution— [all these are yours].
Those who are born from the world-protectors, those who dwell in the netherworlds,
those who consist of the great elements, and those who are born from the transformative ego— [all these are present].

Those who consist of the three qualities (guṇas), those who are born from the womb of the Gandharvas, those who arise from the Rākṣasas and Yakṣas, and those known as the Vidyādharas—[all these belong to this category]. (1.55)
Those [mantras] of yours that arise from pairs of qualities, those of yours that originate from powers (śakti),
those of yours that arise from the Atharvāṅgirasa, and those of yours that originate from other mantras— || 1.56 ||
Those which perform all functions, which cause things to proceed or cease;
those which are staves or powers, and those which take the form of rods and so forth.
Possessing great strength and great heroism, they were intent on destroying the three worlds;
some resembled the king of mountains, while others resembled the king of serpents.
Some resemble the near and far shores [of an ocean], some are like the sky;
licked by hundreds of blazing flames, they abide in the midst of heaven and earth. (1.59)
Dancing, laughing, and shouting with joy, they were agile and leaping;
indescribable and incomparable, they were fair, white, reddish, and dark.
Possessing various shapes and colors, and radiant with diverse kinds of illusions,
they all assembled together, intent on battle, urged on by Kālanemi.

The defeat of all weapons by the Sudarśana, along with their applications and withdrawals, together with their secret doctrines, and by means of all those entire collections of weapons raised by the hand of Nārāyaṇa— [all this was seen]. (1.62)
Having become like moths in the great fire of the Sudarśana,
the great asura Kālanemi became the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in it.
From witnessing that most wonderful majesty, doubt arose;
having seen that great and marvelous battle, he was overcome with amazement and prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, the Teacher of the World, who had vanished in an instant.
Carrying this great mass of doubts within my heart,
I have indeed come here into your presence for the purpose of cutting through my uncertainty.
"For there exists no one who can sever this [doubt] except for the omniscient Lord.
Ahirbudhnya said: 'O divine sage, state the doubts that remain within you. (1.66)
"Even though they are indefinable, I shall now resolve them all for you.
Durvāsas: "Now, the questions were stated in sequence by the celestial sage Nārada. (1.67)
The Blessed Lord Śarva, with a mind entirely delighted, explained the introduction to the Saṃhitā;
this Saṃhitā has thus been declared, which encompasses the meaning of various mantras.
The divine Pañcarātra, beginning with the Ahirbudhnya, consists of five nights;
it is joined with meanings primarily consisting of the deeds of others and with ancient legends. (1.69)
Containing a confluence of various philosophical systems and adorned with various branches of knowledge, two hundred and forty chapters have been presented here. (1.70)
Then, during the period of the Dvāpara age, for the benefit of mankind,
it was indeed composed consisting of one hundred and twenty chapters.
Having set aside excessive prolixity, it has been refined through esoteric methods;
even from that, for the benefit of human beings whose intellects are limited, [it has been further condensed]. (1.72)
(11) During the period of the twilight of the Dvāpara age, by my own will and with the approval of Vyāsa, this Saṃhitā has been further edited by me into sixty chapters. (1-73)
The venerable Ṛṣi Nārada presented his questions as they were asked; listen to me as I relate how Śarva answered them all. 1.74.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Two, titled "The Discernment of the Sixfold Policy as Brahman," consisting of seventy-four verses;
herein is Nārada’s inquiry concerning Ahirbudhnya.
Nārada effortlessly acquired all those collections of mantras, which were like the sun and fire, as well as Hari’s Sudarśana discus. (2.1)
Is this power of his innate or acquired through association?
What indeed is that which is called "Sudarśana," and what is the meaning of the word? (2.2)
Ahirbudhnya’s account of his own attainment of knowledge from Saṃkarṣaṇa:
"Listen, Nārada, to that unsurpassed knowledge in its true essence."
In the past, after performing terrible austerities for tens of thousands of years, I [attained this].
This [knowledge] was obtained directly from Saṃkarṣaṇa, the ocean of the power of wisdom, which does not exist among others such as Brahmā or even among the great ṛṣis. (2.4)
Listen as I describe the true nature of that Sudarśana; once you have heard of this support of all things, your doubts will indeed cease to exist. (2-5)
A Summary of the Nature of the Supreme Brahman:
That which is the Supreme Brahman is without beginning or end; it is the imperishable and immutable.
It is devoid of name and form, indivisible, and beyond the reach of speech and mind. (2.6)
The definition of the term *Sudarśana* is the sixfold power (*ṣāḍguṇya*) which is all-powerful, named as "all-encompassing," undecaying, and eternal;
it is the resolve, whether through existence or non-existence, that "I shall become that. (2.7)
That which transforms in a form that cannot be questioned due to its autonomy is called "prekṣaṇa" (contemplation); that is celebrated as "darśana" (vision). || 2-8 ||
In reality, that which is his unimpeded state throughout time and space is what constitutes worship here; this is the meaning of the word "su," and thus it is called "Sudarśana."
That which is the cause of everything, being dependent upon the Sudarśana [discus], that which is the support of the world,
that which is the means of valid cognition for the world, and that which is the entire object of those means of valid cognition— [all these belong to Him]. (2.10)

In this regard, those who are the qualified practitioners, the various divisions that pertain to them, the method of their protection, and for whom that [protection] is proclaimed—[all these shall be explained]. (2.11)
"Everything depends upon Sudarśana and consists of Sudarśana;
thus his innate form transcends all. (2.12)
(14) Whatever sovereign power exists in the entirety of the collection of weapons, all of that belongs to him; thus it is obtained by himself, for it is his own. (2-13)
Furthermore, the questions posed by Nārada:
Nārada said—
"O God of gods, O Lord of the world, O benefactor of the three worlds!"
My mind seems to be utterly bewildered; my doubt has been greatly increased. || 2.14 ||
What is the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya), what is the supreme Brahman, and of what nature is it?
What is its resolve like, and how does its state of being perceived come about? (2.15)
And how is his range unimpeded throughout all regions? What is the cause of the world, and what is its nature and what kind is it? (2-16)
What is the support of the world? Of what nature and how many kinds is it?
What is said to be its measure? And of what nature and how many kinds is that [measure]? (2-17)

What indeed is the object of valid cognition? Of what nature is it, and how many kinds does it have? Who are those qualified [to receive this teaching]? Of what character are they, and of what sort are they? (2.18)
And what is the protection for all this? What is its procedure and of what kind? Who is the qualified person for that purpose, and what qualities are required of him? (2-19)
O Blessed One, tell me this collection of questions in their entirety;
having clasped your feet, I have approached you as a disciple—teach me, sir! (2.20)
p. 15) Durvāsas:
Then Śaṅkara, having prostrated before the sage who was purified by the mere sight [of him], explained everything to that ascetic who had approached him with devotion. (2.21)
An extensive description of the nature of the Supreme Brahman by Ahirbudhnya:
"It is one, characterized by the experience of infinite bliss free from suffering."
The supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end and free from all affliction.
It is the dwelling place created by all beings, pervading and abiding as everything;
it is irreproachable, undistracted, and like an ocean without waves. (2.23)

The Supreme Brahman is the adversary of all that is to be abandoned and possesses a form composed of auspicious qualities; it is untouched by material attributes, the abode of non-material qualities, the further shore beyond the ocean of worldly existence, stainless, and untainted. (2.24)
Because it is not limited by form, place, or time, it is full, eternally manifest, all-pervasive, and free from that which is to be rejected or accepted. (2.25)
This [reality] cannot be immediately delimited by such qualities as "this" or "so much";

it is the state of being denotable by all terms such as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and so forth, [which characterizes] each successive level of reality as it arises from the preceding one. (2.26)
Because he has cultivated the supreme state within himself, he is proclaimed as the Supreme Self (Paramātman);
because of his entry into all principles through the yoga of attaining "Om. (2.27)
The Blessed One is celebrated by virtue of his possession of the sixfold qualities;
he is proclaimed as Vāsudeva because he dwells within all beings. (2.28)
He is described as having the nature of the world because he pervades it;
he is celebrated as the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) because his form and mode are unmanifest. (2.29)

Because it possesses the power of all primordial natures (*prakṛti*), it is called "all-nature" (*sarvaprakṛti*); because it is that in which effects are deposited, it is celebrated as "the primary" (*pradhāna*). (2.30)
Because he leads and because he does not lead, he is also recited as "the Eternal" (nitya);
and because he eats and because he does not eat, he is indeed recited as "the Infinite" (ananta). || 2-31 ||
Because it is non-existent on all sides, it is called "unlimited" (aparimita) by the wise;
because it is imperishable, it is called "indestructible" (akṣara); and because it is free from misfortune (riṣṭa), it is called "secure" (ariṣṭa).
Because its nature is unchangeable, because it is non-pervasive, and likewise because it is unfallen;
because it is free from defects such as passion and because it is the object of equanimous cognition. (2-33)

It is proclaimed as "equal" because it shares the commonality of being the basis for all appropriation; it is so called because it lies outside the path of meditative absorption and because it does not conform to intrinsic nature. (2-34)
Because it cannot be conceived even by such a measure, it is proclaimed as "inconceivable" (acintya).
From this all worlds arise, and it also prevails everywhere. (2-35)
And because existence (*bhava*) is preeminent within him, he is celebrated as the Source (*prabhava*);
he is imperishable (*avyaya*) because he is the ground of all dissolution, and because he is devoid of decay (*vyaya*). (2.36)
In the depths of the Vedas, he is called Brahman because of his vastness and because he nourishes;
Kapila is so called because of his preeminent knowledge and because of his supreme brilliance. (2.37)
Beneficial and delightful, the embryo named Hṛdaya is thus proclaimed by the yogis as Hiraṇyagarbha. (2.38)
He is known as Apāntaratapas because of his connection with penance that destroys the self;
he is proclaimed as Śiva by those established in the Pāśupata [tradition] due to his nature as the bringer of auspiciousness. (2.39)
Reality is characterized by such terms as "not situated at a great distance," "not non-penetrating in its actual nature," and so forth. (2.40)

When the obstruction is removed— upon the exhaustion of merit and demerit accumulated over many births, and when the web of latent impressions has been cut away by the weapon of perfect knowledge— the experience of Brahman becomes possible. (2.41)
When the three guṇas have ceased, that [state] is capable of being experienced by itself;
we cannot describe it clearly in words as "this is directly perceived. (2.42)
Even if one were as swift as thought, like the king of birds swooping through the air for thousands of years, one would never reach the end of Brahman, which is not to be attained by effort. (2.43)
Advancing higher and higher while training in such and such a manner, they did not attain greater manifestation during the stage of the exertion of knowledge. (2-44)
Therein, all principles (tattvas) rest within the Supreme Self;
both existence and non-existence are woven together by means of the nature of the thread of knowledge. (2.45)
Brahman is devoid of the threefold limitations;
because it perceives everything directly, it is the Self of all, that supreme state.
In the past and future times, as well as in the interval between them, [it remains] withdrawn. (2.46)
That Brahman is not present in the present, nor is it past, nor indeed is it yet to be;
it is not in front, nor behind, nor above, nor on either side. (2.47)
Neither spotted, nor defective, nor black, nor tawny;
neither dappled, nor yellowish-brown, nor reddish-brown, nor crimson. (2.48)
It is neither brown nor a mongoose, neither dark nor red;
neither long nor short, neither thick nor minute.
It is neither turned forward nor turned back; it is not supported, yet it is not unsupported.
It is neither existence nor non-existence, nor is it for the sake of worshipping that state. (2.50)
It is neither cold nor indeed hot, nor even neither-hot-nor-cold;
it is neither suffering nor happiness, and it is neither free from suffering nor a happiness devoid of wounds. (2.51)
O Sage, it has no root, nor its middle, nor indeed its end;
it neither lies down, nor does it sit, nor does it stand, nor does it go. (2.52)
Completely free from all dualities and devoid of all limiting adjuncts, that Supreme Brahman possesses the six qualities and is the cause of all causes. (2.53)

Nārada said: (p. 19) "O God of gods, O Lord of the world, what is that which is called the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*)? And how is it that this sixfold policy is proclaimed to be devoid of qualities (*guṇa*)? (2.54)
Ahirbudhnya’s exposition of the sixfold qualities of Brahman:
"He is celebrated as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), untouched by the qualities of material nature."
Listen, O sinless Nārada, as the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is being described by me.
Those who contemplate the qualities declare that the first quality is what is called knowledge (jñāna): it is non-inert, self-awareness, eternal, and all-pervasive. (2.56)
The nature of Brahman consists both in its being of the essence of knowledge and in its having knowledge as a quality; thus, both the essential form of Brahman and that quality are proclaimed.
[Now follows] the determination of the nature of power (*śakti*).
That which is the state of being the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the world is proclaimed to be Śakti. || 2.57 ||
Regarding the definition of the nature of sovereignty:
that which is called agency, when it is augmented by autonomy, is declared as "sovereignty" (aiśvarya) by those who contemplate the meaning of the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva). (2.58)
The definition of the nature of power (*bala*):
"The constant exhaustion-free state of one who perpetually sustains the world is called the quality (*guṇa*) known as power (*bala*) by those who contemplate the qualities. (2.59)
The definition of the nature of *vīrya*:
That which is indeed free from modification even while existing as its material cause—that quality is called *vīrya*, which has another name, "imperishability" (*acyutatva*). (2.60)
The definition of the nature of *tejas* (luminosity):
that which does not depend upon auxiliary causes is declared to be *tejas*.
It is the mode of the quality of knowledge within the pentad of qualities beginning with power (*śakti*).
These five qualities, beginning with power (śakti), are proclaimed to belong to knowledge. (2.61)
Knowledge alone is the supreme form of Brahman, the Supreme Self.
That Supreme Brahman, augmented by its own power, possesses the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya).
It is that Sudarśana which assumes the volition, "May I become manifold. (2.62)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Discernment of the Brahman of the Six Attributes," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī-Pāñcarātra*.
From the beginning, 136 verses.
The third chapter, titled "The Summary of the Cosmic Form.
Nārada said:
How is that sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) Brahman when augmented by its own power? And what indeed is that power by which it is said to be augmented? (3.1)
The power (*śakti*) of all things is an inseparable attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*); as stated by Ahirbudhnya:
"The powers of all entities are inconceivable and reside non-separately [from them]."
They are not perceived at all in their own nature; rather, they are perceived through their effects.
For that [nature] of theirs exists in a subtle state, pervading all things; it cannot be established as "this" nor can it be negated. (3-3)
The powers are not subject to questioning,
for the powers residing within entities are indeed beyond the questioning of all;
even the power of the Supreme Brahman is an inseparable attribute.
Thus [was it said] by that Blessed One, the supreme Brahman, the Sage.
The power that follows all existents is like the moonlight of the cool-rayed moon;
following both existence and non-existence, it brings about every effect of that omnipresent Lord. (3.5)

That radiance of Viṣṇu, which consists of sovereignty and is identical with the universe, has arisen in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and takes the nature of closing and opening [the eyes]. (3.6)

The power of the Blessed One is denoted by such words as "Bliss" (Ānanda) because it is independent; it is blissful and autonomous due to its eternal fullness. It is the state of the higher and lower worlds manifesting upon the wall of its own self. (3.7)

She is eternal because she is not delimited by time; she is full because she is never separated from her perfect form; she is all-pervasive because she is not restricted by space; and she is both empty and full at all times.
When she is perceived as the world itself, she is celebrated as Lakṣmī;
when she assumes the state of Viṣṇu, she is called Śrī. (3.9)

Because she is unmanifest, because she is time, and because she is the state of the Puruṣa, she is Padmā; because she wears a garland of lotuses, she is Padmamālinī; because she grants desires, she is Kamalā; and because of her union with perfect bliss, she is [Kamalā].
Because she is of the nature of Viṣṇu’s own power (*sāmarthya*), she is celebrated as the power of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇuśakti*);
protecting the being of Hari, she is proclaimed as the consort of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇupatnī*). (3-11)
Because she contracts the form of the universe, Kuṇḍalinī is so called by the wise;
because the mind, speech, and other faculties are unstruck [therein], she is declared "Unstruck" (Anāhatā) by the wise. (3.12)

Through the awakening to supreme bliss and also by means of the subtlety of mantra, Gaurī is indeed Aditi, due to her being the locus of pure being and because there is no distinction between them. (3.13)
Because it is the source of all merit, that earth is truly great;
likewise, its prosperity is unassailable, for its sovereignty remains unchallenged.
Because she animates the world through her own self-awareness, she is called the "Life-force of the World" (jagatprāṇā);
because she has struck down the form of the Asuras, she is proclaimed as the "Mother of Mantras" (mantramātā). (3.15)
Because she protects all who sing, she is called Gāyatrī; because she creates the world by her own nature, she is celebrated as Prakṛti. (3-16)
She is celebrated as Mātṛ because she measures (mimīte) and expands (tatā);
she is Śivā because she brings about auspiciousness (śivaṃkaratayā) by ensuring that all things are free from error (aviparyāsāt).
She is *tārā* because she is desirable as a young woman and because she carries one across the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
She is *satyā* because her nature is free from error and because she conforms to the two truths. (3-18)

Because all modifications have been stilled, she is considered "Peaceful" (Śāntā) by the wise; because she removes delusion even from that which is more delusive than delusion itself, she is "Deluding" (Mohinī). (3.19)
Iḍā is so called because she is the substratum of the oblation (havis) and because she is desired; furthermore, since she causes delight, she is proclaimed as Rantī and Rati. (3-20)
The Sarasvatī, renowned by the wise as "the far-famed," is called the "Great Radiance" (Mahābhāsā) because its manifestation is uninterrupted. (3.21)

By various names derived from different scriptures, this supreme Vaiṣṇava power, whose entire majesty has been revealed through those names that accord with their meanings, [is thus described]. (3.22)
It was like the stability of the ocean, like the vastness of the sky, like the radiance of the sun, and like the moonlight of the cool-rayed moon. (3.23)
The divine power of Nārāyaṇa, belonging to Viṣṇu, is complete in all her limbs, follows both existence and non-existence, and is approved by all established doctrines. (3.24)
The power is distinct from the possessor of power;
it is distinct from the God who possesses power, from Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Both he and she are described in the scriptures according to the nature of attribute and substratum. (3.25)
By way of the nature of both existence and non-existence, these two have arisen as if they were a single reality;
yet by her own independent nature, she is this wondrous consort of Viṣṇu.
Since the world is about to come into being, it attains a certain manifestation from power;
there is a twofold nature of power, a threefold nature of the power of manifestation (bhūti-śakti), and portions consisting of thousands, tens of thousands, crores, koṭis, and arbudas. (3.27)
That manifestation, consisting of Lakṣmī, is established in two ways through the distinction between action (kriyā) and power (bhūti); and that power is considered to be threefold. (3.28)
Because their state as male and time is unmanifest, their form will now be explained.
(p. 25) The power of action is that which sets in motion the power of manifestation: "This unfolding known as action is the transformer of manifestation. (3-29)

Consisting of Lakṣmī and having the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), it is called the volition (saṃkalpa) of Viṣṇu; it has independence as its root, consists of will, has discernment as its form, and results in action. (3.30)

That which is the unfolding [of consciousness], characterized by excellent volition and unimpeded in all its actions, consists of both the sentient and the insentient, appearing in the forms of the Unmanifest, Time, and the Person (puṃs). || 3.31 ||
He contemplates Bhūti, the power of Viṣṇu consisting of Lakṣmī,
as the unmanifest through its transformation, and Time through the act of reckoning.
In the process of creation, this [Prakṛti] joins the Puruṣa with efforts toward enjoyment;
in the process of transmigration, she disjoins him from the bestowal of the threefold capacity.
Whatever capacity belongs to that which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa) for an uneven transformation,
it bestows that upon creation, and its opposite upon withdrawal.
At the beginning of creation, it brings about the sequence of the conjunction of the unmanifest and the Puruṣa through their activity;
and at the time of dissolution, it effects the reverse.
And the capacity and incapacity of a person regarding food—[all] this is brought about by the will of Viṣṇu in the processes of creation and re-absorption. (3.36)
He maintains these three, joined together during creation and separated at the time of reabsorption, by means of his own form, just as a quality [colors] a collection of gems. (3.37)
And he provides protection for those established [in his service] by overseeing their affairs;
that which consists in being unimpeded everywhere is the characteristic of the Sudarśana. (3-38)
Due to the manifold nature of the power of action (kriyāśakti), its pervasion of all entities is as follows:
"This very resolve named Sudarśana, whose essence is vibration, assumes many forms through division and abides within every single entity. (3-39)
Listen as I proclaim this manifold expansion and the all-pervasiveness of the Sudarśana;
by knowing which, a person in this world attains the state of having accomplished all that was to be done. (3–40)

That which is the sixfold policy, that which is the supreme Brahman, and that which is the ultimate goal of yogis—he is Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe; this world is his existence and non-existence. (3.41)
When, by means of its partless essential nature, it attains and restrains [the world], that which is its eternal existence is indeed the power for the creation of the universe. (3.42)
The Goddess Lakṣmī, who is the self-nature of all beings and the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) of the Supreme Self, having become the possessor of those attributes, [pervades] this entire world. (3-43)
In her partless essential nature, she likewise exercises control;
a single power (kalā) belonging to her is manifestation, known as the coming into being of the world.
The real activity therein consists of the governance of the universe;
it is the partless power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the *saudarśanī* aspect of Lakṣmī. (3-45)
When those two Lords of the worlds assume a form that delights the mind and eyes, then the activity of the discus and the lotus is for the protection of the worlds. (3.46)
For as long as those two gods desire protective equipment,
for that long the Sudarśana [discus] appears in the form of the conch, the Śārṅga bow, and so forth.
Then, that Sudarśana-cakra, which desires to benefit the universe through showers of light, bliss, and destruction, exists in the form of the sun, the moon, and fire. (3.48)
Whenever those two themselves assume the forms of beings such as gods or daityas, the divine power consisting of the Sudarśana weapon then becomes the action of the Goddess.
When they compose a scripture based on various fruits for the benefit of the world, that action therein is the teaching residing in the heart. (3.50)
When those two become your scripture for the benefit of the entire world, O All-pervading One,
then that essence of the scripture is the ritual action of the Sudarśana-kalā.
When those two parents are indeed established as the authorities of the scripture,
then their authority consists of the power of action, which is the Sudarśana.
When those two, being the very meaning of the treatise, resort to the means for attaining the fruit, then the capacity to produce that fruit is clearly seen as "action" (kriyā). (3.53)
When those two themselves become the four aims of human life, then the Sudarśana discus possesses the power to satisfy the Self. (3.54)
When one devoted to the protection consisting of mantra for the welfare of the worlds, then this Goddess, who consists of mantra and yantra, is indeed the power of action (kriyāśakti). (3.55)
The summary of the manifold nature of your power of action, which consists of the Sudarśana, has been demonstrated; what more do you wish to hear? (3.56)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Universal Form of the Power of Action," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 192.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "Description of the Reabsorption" (Pratisaṃcara-varṇana).
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Omniscient One whose banner bears the bull, what is that cause which has been described as proceeding for the sake of creation? (4.1)
Tell me in detail about that which is pervaded by Sudarśana in terms of form, function, and purpose— the supreme cause of the universe.
Ahirbudhnya describes the dissolution of the primary elements:
"Listen attentively to the reality of the cause as it is being declared by me."
In that regard, first understand this natural process of reabsorption.
At that time, that primordial Vidyā, known as Mūla-prakṛti,
became a cow in the form of clouds for the purpose of producing crops and other vegetation.
In that duration of time, during the process of reabsorption,
she— no longer a cow, sapless, dried up, and bearing the name "the unmanifest"— becomes so.
Nārada said:
"In how much time will that cow, who can assume any form at will, cease to be a cow and become that goddess [the Earth] during the period of re-absorption? (4.6)
Regarding the measurement of time during the period of dissolution,
Ahirbudhnya states:
"Eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those [constitute] a *kalā*."
Thirty of those [tatkṣaṇas] constitute a kṣaṇa; twelve of those are traditionally held to be a muhūrta.
Fifteen of those [days] constitute a day; that many [such days] are held to be a night.
Fifteen of those [days and nights] constitute a fortnight (pakṣa); two fortnights are held to be a month.
O Sage, a human year is reckoned by those [days] as twelve;
likewise, a year of the Kāmyas is reckoned by sixteen of those [years], O Sage.
Knowledge may become a cow or a non-cow within that much time; for when the dissolution occurs, I intend to act toward that which has become a non-cow.
There was the dissolution of everything upon the earth; this entire world, both moving and unmoving, became sapless and utterly parched.
It was completely dried up by a great wind and scorched by a great fire.
When everything on the earth, from the mountains down to the blades of grass, has become level,
then human beings go to their dissolution among other human beings.
(31) Those four hundred humans go to dissolution among humans themselves. Thus, when the entire class of sentient beings has gone to dissolution among humans alone, [the world is destroyed]. (4-13)
O Sage, exactly four pairs of Manus alone remain upon the earth, which is level like the back of a tortoise.
O Sage, through the unimpeded will of Nārāyaṇa and his Sudarśana discus, the earth dissolves into the waters;
at that time, the waters swallow the essence of the earth, which consists of its fragrance.
When the earth has absorbed its fragrance through the agency of water, then the Manus, having transcended the earth, are established in the waters. (4.16)
But the earth, by its own inherent power, constantly abandons both its specific forms and its names;
now it is water that brings forth this world of moving and unmoving beings. (4.17)
The dissolution of water into fire occurs simply by the will of Hari from his previous form consisting of the Sudarśana;
the causal light swallows even the essence and sapidity of the waters. (4.18)
Then, having transcended those waters, the Manas abide in light;
thereafter, the waters, being devoid of taste, eternally abandon their individual names and forms.
O Sage, this world is now nothing but a brilliantly shining light;
the dissolution of that light into the wind is impelled by the will of Viṣṇu, and the wind is designated as the cause. (4.20)
O Sage, at that time even the Manus, impelled by their own volitions, surely swallowed the very essence and internal form of the luminaries. (4.21)
When all light has become exceedingly subtle, they take refuge in the wind alone;
then that light, having assumed its [subtle] form, abandons both its manifest appearance and its name.
The wind, violently shaking this entire world of moving and non-moving beings,
dissolves into space;
thereafter, space, the cause, impelled by the will of Viṣṇu, [dissolves].
It seizes the essence of touch, which is indeed the cause of the wind;
even the Manus, O great sage, were impelled by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana.
Like ashes, they do not remain, having merged with the wind;
then the wind, having taken up touch, abandons its specific individuality and name.
That entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, resounded intensely;
this is described as the dissolution of space into the ego (ahaṃkāra),
which is the power of action (kriyāśakti) belonging to Viṣṇu, the ego endowed with self-consciousness (abhimānavān).
O Sage, it swallows the essence called sound, which is the cause of space;
impelled by that very [essence], it far surpasses the state of the sky belonging to Viṣṇu.
(33) The Manus, who consist of the Blessed One, abide in the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra).
Space (viyat), having assumed sound, then abandons its individuality and name. (4.28)
"O Sage, this entire universe is of the nature of 'I', consisting of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The dissolution of the ego-sense occurs within the intellect (buddhi);
the essence of the ego-sense, which consists of self-conceit (abhimāna), is its cause. (4-29)
O Sage, impelled by the Sudarśana, Viṣṇu’s intellect indeed devours [the elements], and further impelled by the Sudarśana, it likewise devours his ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).
O great sage, the eight Manus remain as Buddhas alone;
their ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), having abandoned its self-conceit, relinquishes both its manifest form and its name. (4.31)
O Sage, this entire universe is indeed the intellect (buddhi) endowed with volition; the dissolution of the intellect into darkness is its essence,
and that which is called non-volition (adhyavasāya) is the imperishable cause of the intellect.
O great sage, the primordial cause, impelled by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana, devours the darkness;
even the Manus, O great sage, are impelled by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana.
Then, having excessively resorted to their intellect while remaining in darkness itself, this world became shrouded in gloom—unperceived and devoid of defining characteristics. (4.34)
Inconceivable, unknowable, motionless, heavy, and delusive—
there is the dissolution of the sense organs along with the elements into their respective causes:
the nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear as the fifth.
The anus, the generative organ, as well as the two feet, the two hands, and speech as the fifth;
the pairing of these two groups of five begins respectively with the nose and the anus. (4.36)

When the causes—earth, water, and so forth—dissolve each into their own respective [subsequent] elements, [the sense of smell and the others] undergo simultaneous dissolution along with the functions of the olfactory and other senses. (4.37)
The mind and the ego—these two instruments, along with their functions, merge into the ego; and the faculty of cognition [merges] into the intellect. (4.38)
All this now remains as darkness alone;
for there is the dissolution of darkness into passion (rajas), and that which is the power of stability belonging to this darkness consists of heaviness.
Passion constantly devours her when she is impelled by the will of the Lord;
even the Manus of Viṣṇu, O great sage, are driven by His will. (4.40)
Having transcended the course of darkness, they remain established in rajas alone;
that darkness, having extracted its essence, then abandons the names "manifest" and "unmanifest."
At that time, the world is indeed *rajas* alone, consisting of the suffering of constant activity;
the dissolution of *rajas* into *sattva* is that power (*śakti*) consisting of vibration, whose nature is movement and which is composed of *rajas*. (4-42)
The causal principle indeed devours that being who has been impelled by Sudarśana;
likewise, the Manus, abiding in rajas, are impelled by the resolve of Viṣṇu.
O Sage, having completely transcended *rajas*, they enter the stainless *sattva*; then, having extracted its essence, that *rajas* abandons both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the name. (4-44)
This world of moving and non-moving beings was then merely light and of the nature of *sattva*.
At the time of the dissolution of *sattva*,
there arose that which is called Time (*kāla*), a quality of Viṣṇu impelled by the Sudarśana [discus].
From that sattva, which consists of wisdom and is the cause of knowledge, they extract the essence;
then, having transcended that sattva, men become dependent upon time.
At that time, O sage, this entire world was Time alone;
and when that Being has extracted its essence, it abandons both its manifest form and its name.
The dissolution of Time (kāla) occurs within Niyati;
Kālī is the power that has entered into Time, she who manifests everything without exception.
That which is called Niyati swallows that [Kālī] as it is impelled by Īśvara.
And those eight Manus, O great sage, impelled by Sudarśana,
having passed beyond the principle of time, attained that destiny.
Then that time, having extracted its essence, abandoned both individuality and names;
that which is called Necessity (niyati) was this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
O great sage, when there is the dissolution of Niyati into Śakti— that power consisting of Mahāvidyā which belongs to Niyati—
then, impelled by Īśvara, that power indeed swallows her.
Even the Manus, commanded by the Lord, having indeed transcended that very destiny, enter the vast power of Viṣṇu consisting of Māyā. (4.52)
That Niyati, having extracted its essence, abandons the names "Manifest" (vyakti) and "Name" (nāman);
then this power was the universe, the world of moving and non-moving beings.

The dissolution of power (śakti) occurs within the immutable person (kūṭasthapuruṣa), until the emergence of consciousness; for power is eternal. Yet, impelled by the Sudarśana [discus], the person himself swallows that power. (4-54)
Having transcended their power, those men, impelled by the Lord, enter that [state];
then, its essence having been taken up, the power abandons both its manifestation and its name.
The Person is the self of all, possessing power everywhere, facing in all directions;
he is omniscient, omnipresent, and everything itself, standing pervading all. (4.56)
This Puruṣa, who is the immutable foundation of the Manus and consists of two and four parts,
indeed possesses full authority over all ritual actions belonging to Hari, the God of gods.
O Great Sage, for these thirteen [principles], beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti,
once their respective functions have dissolved, their duration is one hundred desired years.

The dissolution of the Puruṣa into the immutable Puruṣa occurs after three hundred [cycles]; thereafter, the Puruṣa consisting of Manu divides himself fourfold according to the states of Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and so forth. (4.59)
In its own respective place—the mouth, arms, and so forth of the Sage Aniruddha—it dissolves in an instant, like water on a heated iron ball. (4.60)
Then that Blessed One, alone, with his consciousness and unconsciousness dissolved, remains for sixteen hundred years. (4.61)
The dissolution of Aniruddha occurs within Pradyumna;
having remained there, he then enters the undecaying and all-pervading Pradyumna.
Having restrained all activities, he remains in his own state for that duration of time. (4.62)
The dissolution of Pradyumna occurs in Saṃkarṣaṇa;
thereafter, that Blessed One named Pradyumna, the lotus-eyed,
dissolves into that Blessed One, the flawless Saṃkarṣaṇa.
For that duration of time, Acyuta, who embodies all the gods, remains;
he is the entire universe, interwoven with consciousness and the unconscious, in its entirety, both pure and impure.
Bearing upon his own body, which consists of pure knowledge, the marks of a *tilaka* and a *alaka*,
this Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is Balarāma, is the mountain of sunrise and the mountain of sunset.
For those who pursue the digits of the moon of consciousness— which is devoid of the mark of insentience—
this supreme [reality] consisting of Saṃkarṣaṇa is indeed not inferior to the day.
Wherein various states of being are manifested by their respective names—
this Acyuta, having remained for sixteen hundred years as Saṃkarṣaṇa within Vāsudeva, [attains dissolution]. (4.67)
He departs unto that blessed, eternal Vāsudeva.
At that time, O Sage, there was neither non-existence nor existence. (4.68)
Having dissolved within himself both existence and non-existence, which arise as various manifestations of power,
Vāsudeva abides as the supreme Brahman, which is indefinable.
That night is that supreme Brahman; it is declared to be the unmanifest (avyakta).
It is the totality of the six [qualities], such as the power of discernment (vijñāna) and the rest. (4.70)
That in which the three dissolve is called Night, because from it the coloring [of the world], beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Bhūmi, has vanished. (4.71)
That is to be known as the unmanifest; because of its equanimity, it is called "the Equal.
That power of the Blessed One which is the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) pervading all states of being—|| 4.72 ||
Existence that does not move apart [from consciousness], consisting of supreme great bliss, is the Supreme (Parā).
From Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the earth, it is said that [the entire manifest world] is but a ten-millionth part of that.

When that [reality], in which the universe shines forth through forms both existent and non-existent, conscious and unconscious, has forever ceased—the source of the world's clamor—[then all is stilled]. (4.74)
The power, which is unperceivable through its effects and which, by divine will, abandons all differentiation,
is his own Sudarśana power, the action that brings about the dissolution of the universe.
Having withdrawn that state which consists of volitional construction (saṃkalpa), she maintains it;
just as a flame, due to the absence of fuel, returns to the nature of fire.
In this way, that supreme Vaiṣṇava power indeed attains the state of Brahman;
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, and she is that Nārāyaṇī power. (4.77)
Due to their pervasive and extreme union, they remain as if they were a single reality. As long as the day of Saṃkarṣaṇa is held to last, which is the duration of a human day,
so long does the night of Puruṣa last, during which all things are withdrawn.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Reabsorption," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 270.
Chapter Five, titled "The Description of Pure Creation. Ahirbudhnya said:
This dissolution of the category of cause and effect has been demonstrated;
O Sage, I shall now describe to you his creation consisting of the Sudarśana.
The nature of Brahman in the state of dissolution,
in which all effects are dormant and which has attained a state of perfect equanimity on all sides—
Nārāyaṇa is that supreme Brahman, the abode of all, the unstruck (anāhata). || 5-2 ||
He is full and steady, possessing the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), resembling a windless sky;
there is at times the unfolding (unmeṣa) of Lakṣmī in the form of power (śakti)—that power which is of the nature of stillness and whose form is emptiness. || 5-3 ||
Precisely because of its autonomy, that power—which is indeed the very self of the supreme Brahman Hari—attains its unfolding (unmeṣa) from something toward something else. (5.4)
That goddess shines forth in some places like lightning in the sky;
that power, shining in the firmament, is called Śakti.
[The text] reveals that power (śakti) manifests various states (bhāva):
"It manifests various states—pure, impure, and embodied—[which arise] from its own freedom as it attains its unfolding. (5–6) p. 41)
That volition, whose nature is perception, is called Sudarśana;
it is that action, that vigor of Hari, and that splendor and strength.
And those entities which are manifested, revolving within their own foundation—that is the manifestation (bhūti), the power of Viṣṇu; it is fashioned from a ten-millionth part of that power.
That power, consisting of the elements, exists through many states of duality, distinguished by purity and impurity, and by the forms of the cognizable and the unconscious. (5.9)

Through the distinction between morning and time, through the division of the manifest and the unmanifest, through the form of the indicated and the indicator, and through the differentiation of the signified and the signifier. || 5-10 ||
It is divided by the distinction between the enjoyed and the enjoyer, by the distinction between the body and the embodied, and by other such dualistic divisions. (5.11)
O divine sage, know that power which has become the cause through such various distinctions—that divine portion belonging to the Sudarśana. (5.12)
Just as fire is fanned by the wind, or even as a cloud is driven by the wind,
so too is the power (vibhūti) impelled by a portion (kalā) through the Sudarśana alone.
In the process of emanation it proceeds in direct order, while in the process of reabsorption it proceeds in reverse order;
just as that [power], abiding in the space of the Sudarśana [cakra], is impelled.
Listen as I speak of how He brings forth various states of being.
Among those, first hear of the pure creation—the manifestation of the expansion of pure existence—arising from the Lord's power. (5.15)
That which is called the sixfold quality— consisting of knowledge, sovereignty, power, and so forth—
through three cycles of these, the pure creation of the elements proceeds.
From the three pairs of qualities, the manifestation of the three Vyūhas occurs; therein, from the union of knowledge (jñāna) and power (bala), the form of Hari is Sāṃkarṣaṇa;
from the blending of sovereignty (aiśvarya) and heroism (vīrya), the form is called Pradyumna. (5.17)
Due to the preeminence of the power and splendor [of the Lord], the body of Hari becomes Aniruddha;
these are the manifestations consisting of Śakti, characterized by the unfolding of the Guṇas. (5.18)
In all three arrays as well, there is the persistence of the sixfold policy;
the gods, who are the embodiments of the sixfold policy, are lotus-eyed Puruṣas.
In each of those, O Sage, there remains a pair of qualities among the [remaining] virtues.
It indeed follows its course accordingly in each respective case.
The state of the three-fold Caturātman is threefold: mere pervasion, the emergence of the qualities (guṇas), and the formation of a physical form. (5.20)
The fourfold state of Viṣṇu arises from the intermingling of his qualities.
In that [state], the powerful Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa consists of the nature of knowledge. (5.21)
He reveals the exclusive path that is the means for attaining the Blessed One;
the god Pradyumna, who consists of valor and sovereignty, is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) whose function is that of Pradyumna. (5-22)
Established in the nature of the meaning of the scripture by way of the path to attaining the Blessed One,
the task of Aniruddha is that which is the fruit of the meaning of the scripture, characterized by the attainment of the Blessed One. (5.23)
Being unobstructed, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) leads the practitioners to their goal;
these [four] are the means of carrying out the scriptures, the meaning of the scriptures, that which is to be accomplished by them, and the resulting fruit. 5-24.
The persons with lotus-like eyes are the manifestations consisting of power belonging to Hari;
together with the supreme Vāsudeva, there is the fourfold nature of the manifestation.
O sage, these three are the Lord Vāsudeva and the other manifestations.
Know this fourfold self to be characterized by the manifest and the unmanifest;
it is the manifestation of the nature of the unfolding of the *guṇas*.
Those *guṇas* which consist of power are knowledge, sovereignty, strength, and so forth. (5.26)
The simultaneous manifestation of these [powers], characterized by the absence of stillness, is that which is fashioned by Viṣṇu’s volition; it is defined as their manifestation. (5.27)
The Blessed One Vāsudeva is that supreme primordial nature (prakṛti);
she is the power (śakti) of the all-pervading Viṣṇu, the transcendent source of the universe. (5.28)
Because of the distinction between power and the possessor of power, he is called Vāsudeva. From Vāsudeva, who desires to create, there is the manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the god Vāsudeva, who consists of all powers, [appears] through the desire to create. (5.29)
He who divides himself by means of himself is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
regarding this, there is an illustration:
just as when the sun is situated on the mountain of sunrise, its radiance expands forth. (5.30)
Likewise, when the Lord is situated at the point of rising, his radiance consists of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
his power remains unengaged for sixteen hundred years, and these sixteen hundred powers abide [within him]. (5.31)
He is directly the essence of Saṃkarṣaṇa; through the waters of the power of consciousness, he is the Lord Ananta Viṣṇu, the possessor of power, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
With the sixfold qualities fully stabilized, he is like a waveless ocean, due to the simultaneous manifestation of the six qualities impelled by his own nature. (5.33)
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is indeed infinite and eternal;
therein, through the manifestation of the power of knowledge impelled by his own volition, [he acts].
The Lord, the god Ananta himself, is Saṃkarṣaṇa, the infallible (Acyuta).
Having manifested as Pradyumna and remained so for sixteen years, the god, consisting of power, is the infallible (Acyuta). (5.35)
The Blessed One Pradyumna, the Supreme Person, is indeed infinite;
the power of Pradyumna, the radiance of the Blessed One, has arisen as a portion of a portion.
This [power] remains silent for sixteen hundred years without being active;
from that arises the unobstructed manifestation, the god Pradyumna, the Supreme Person, who consists of power (śakti). || 5.37 ||
Having remained for sixteen hundred [years], impelled by his own resolve,
the Blessed One Ananta indeed becomes Aniruddha.
The power of Hari, known as Āniruddha, arises as a fraction of a fraction;
this radiance, though inactive, remains silent for sixteen hundred [years].

O Nārada, after sixteen hundred years of the Vyūha, Aniruddha, possessing power, remains active for sixteen hundred years in the work of creation; at that time, he engages in creation together with the two preceding ones.

These four, the wide-eyed and supreme among men, are the manifestations (vyūhas). They are the adversaries of all that is to be abandoned among manifestations; they are beginningless, faultless, free from suffering, irreproachable, and eternal. (5.41)
O Great Sage, this fourfold nature is infinite and imperishable;
in the state free from waves, they are devoid of objective existence and consist solely of consciousness. (5.42)
In their state as power (*śakti*), they abide during the phase of the unfolding of the qualities (*guṇa*);
therein, in their gross state, they have attained the condition of manifestation (*vyakti*). (5.43)
For the benefit of the worlds, they are characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
this fourfold nature is established as an object of the mind for the sake of providing a support for the mind. (5.44)
Those who know the secret tradition have taught that from one manifestation (vyūha) another manifestation appears;
and they [teach] the various distinctions, such as the manifestation of other manifestations, which are fashioned by volition. (5.45)
There are twelve intermediate manifestations (vyūhāntara), and ten plus two intermediate manifestations are proclaimed as Keśava and the others;
from Vāsudeva arise the triad beginning with Keśava.
Therein, the triad beginning with Keśava is manifested from Vāsudeva.
From Saṃkarṣaṇa, the manifestation of the triad beginning with Govinda occurs;
from Saṃkarṣaṇa, the wondrous triad preceded by Govinda appears.
From Pradyumna, the manifestation of the triad beginning with Trivikrama occurs.
O Sage, the triad beginning with Trivikrama arose from Pradyumna.
The manifestation of the triad beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa from Aniruddha:
"O great sage, the reality consisting of Hṛṣīkeśa and the others arises from Aniruddha.
(p. 47) The threefold nature of the other vyūha.
The subtle ones, residing within their own causes, are remembered as having two arms.
Those who are the lords of the three worlds, being gross, are to be known as having four arms;
the arrangement of their weapons, such as the discus and others, will be described in the Yantra-tantra.
There are thirty-nine manifestations (vibhavas):
the thirty-nine beginning with Padmanābha are indeed [as follows]:
Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātmā, and Madhusūdana. (5.50)
Kapila, the presiding deity of knowledge; Viśvarūpa; Vihangama;
Kroḍātman; Baḍabāmukha; Dharma; and likewise Vāgīśvara.
The Lord who reclines upon the single ocean, the Lord of the Tortoise,
Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and likewise the Stealer of the Nectar (Pīyūṣaharaṇa).
The Lord of Śrī, the Blessed One, the God whose nature is light, the bearer of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, and likewise the taker of the Pārijāta tree.
The Lord of the World, whose nature is peace, the great master Dattātreya,
the Blessed One who reclines beneath the banyan tree, and likewise he whose body has a single horn.
The god who possesses a dwarf body, the all-pervading Trivikrama,
as well as Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa.
Rāma is the wielder of the flaming axe, and the other Rāma is the archer;
the Lord Kalki is the knower of the Vedas, and he is remembered as the one who reclines upon Pātāla.

(48) These thirty-nine [deities], beginning with Padmanābha, are thus considered; their birth and other details should be known from the *Sāttvata* and other sources, since it is there that their origin, their activity, and their weapons are described. (5-57)
Whatever their form may be, how they appear, and where they are situated— along with their various ornaments and diverse garments.

O great sage, in the Sāttvata doctrine, it is stated that there are three groups of external and internal organs along with their functions; and that power which is fashioned by volition and operates within the sphere of its respective effects— everything regarding these has been declared therein.
Summary of the Chapter's Meaning:
Thus, this pure creation of Viṣṇu, fashioned by his volition, has been described as a mere fraction of his power; now hear of the other kind of creation. (5–60)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Pure Creation," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the illustrious Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 330.
The sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Creation of the Impure," concerning the establishment of both the difference and the non-difference between Śakti and its Possessor (Śaktimat).
Ahirbudhnya:
That Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is the eternal Supreme Self—his power consists of the nature of the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva), and it possesses the same attributes as he. (6.1)
These two are spoken of as one in terms of the relationship between the differentiated and the differentiator;
yet in the scriptures, they are described as distinct causes of the world.
The power and its possessor exist inseparably;
there is no causal possessor of power without power, nor does power alone exist independently of the possessor of power. (6.3)
The statement that both the Blessed Lord and Lakṣmī are each individually the cause of the world is made by those who have mastered the Tantras and Vedānta on account of their respective greatness;
thus, the two deities are shown as if they were each alone the cause of the universe. (6.4)
The promise to describe the creation of both the pure and the impure having been established, listen now to this remaining portion concerning creation:
that the power of manifestation (*bhūti-śakti*) is set in motion by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists of its own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*).
This manifestation consisting of prosperity, which was previously described as the power of Viṣṇu, || 6-5 ||
(p. 50) By its very manifestation consisting of volition (*saṃkalpa*), she causes that [universe] to dance manifoldly.
That manifestation of the pure nature of the array (*vyūha*) and the expansion (*vibhava*) which serve as the support for yoga is the manifestation consisting of purity;
that manifestation of purity has the form of the *vyūha* and *vibhava*. (6-6)
Relying upon which, yogins cross this ocean of existence; now, the manifestation of both the pure and the impure proceeds as being rooted in the *vyūha* and *vibhava* [forms]. (6–7)
Its threefold nature is declared as the Person (puruṣa), Time (kāla), and the Quality (guṇa).
The manifestation of Viṣṇu is both pure and otherwise; the Person consists of two and four parts.
That is the collective assembly of the Manus, distinguished as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth.
From Pradyumna arises the production of four pairs;
the Brāhmaṇa and the Brāhmaṇī constitute one such pair of Manus. (6.9)
From the mouth of Pradyumna was born the [Brahmin] caste, impelled by his own volition;
from his chest arose the pair of Kṣatriyas, and from his thighs the pair of Vaiśyas.
From his two feet, a pair of Śūdras likewise emerged from Pradyumna;
he who is the aggregate of the Manus is the Puruṣa consisting of twice four [parts].
The creation of time and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of the subtle states of time and the qualities (*guṇa*), was impelled by Sudarśana;
it was uttered from the forehead, the eyebrows, and the ears of Pradyumna. (6.12)
The command to protect is given to Aniruddha;
"the Person is power"—this consists of both the conscious and the unconscious.
"May you cause [it] to increase" is thus presented to Aniruddha by means of Pradyumna. (6.13)
By means of that, Aniruddha, having taken up that power residing within the Inner Person which is present in his own form, causes it to increase through yoga by means of his own splendor.
The emergence of *niyati* and *kāla*: this power, impelled by *saṃkalpa*, arises in two ways from the unobstructed [source] as that which consists of the nature of *kāla*. (6.15)
That threefold nature of the *prakṛti* consisting of the *guṇas*,
which is the form of that *śakti* proclaimed as being composed of *guṇas*, arises in sequence as the triad of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. (6.16)
From *sattva* and the other [guṇas], *rajas* and the others arise; from *sattva* come *rajas* and *tamas*, and from that *tamas* the intellect (*buddhi*) emerges.
From the intellect comes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*), and from that, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the [five] gross elements. (6.17)
The eleven faculties from the [subtle] matrices, the five elements from the elements, and all derivative matter from the elements—this is the summary of creation. (6.18)
Furthermore, Nārada asked in detail about the elaboration of creation:
"O Blessed One, destroyer of the eyes of Bhaga, ocean of the knowledge of reality!"
Tell me today in detail about this wonderful manifestation of Bhūti.
Ahirbudhnya elaborates upon that:
"Listen, O Nārada, to the truth regarding Viṣṇu’s power of volition."
The manifold transformation of existence, crowded with the multitude of sentient and insentient beings.
The demonstration of the Supreme Vāsudeva’s possession of eternal glory:
That pure creation previously described, which is differentiated into the Vyūhas and so forth, is the radiant manifestation of that very Lord arising from His resolve known as Sudarśana. (6.21)
Consisting of knowledge and bliss, it becomes solidified and indeed assumes the state of space;
that space is the supreme void, stainless and beyond the Puruṣa.
There, the continuity of bliss is inexhaustible, faultless, and undisturbed;
the enjoyments there consist of bliss, and the worlds are characterized by bliss. (6.23)
(53) The bodies of the liberated ones whose selves are purified consist of knowledge and bliss.
Those gods always behold the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, the lotus-eyed Puruṣa, who is eternally to be experienced by the liberated. (6.24)
The god who embodies the sixfold policy, endowed with such splendor,
and who has accomplished through mere will the entire expansion of bodies and bodily requirements.
To the Lord of all this moving and unmoving world,
the abode of all, yet himself without abode, to the flawless Nārāyaṇa— 6.26.
Having attained that state which is the true nature of the liberated, those who know reality are freed, their impurities gone;
they are as numerous as motes of dust and adorned by millions of rays of light. (6.27)
Devoid of the distinctions of the properties of manifestation and disappearance,
they do not return;
having taken refuge in that supreme Vaiṣṇava station, the further shore of the path.
They enter this path, which is turbulent with the waves of time;
according to their mode of worship, they attain the fruit, for those devotees abide in the state of saṃsāra in whatever form they possess. (6.29)
Those who dwell in the supreme ether behold you as such,
having sported for a very long time amidst the movement of millions of floods.
Then they enter that divine, Vaiṣṇava glory consisting of the six attributes. That supreme sky is impossible to describe; this very supreme sky has been shown to you only in brief. (6.31)
Even in ten thousand years, its full extent cannot be described.

It has been stated that the Person who is the aggregate of individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭipuruṣa) occupies a position within the lower realms; he is the person entitled to perform ritual action (karmādhikāra), and he consists of four yugas.
Therefore, he remains within this intermediate state from that supreme ether;
he is the collective totality of all individual selves, like the hive of honey-bees.
That state consisting of purity and impurity is known as the Puruṣa; it is accumulated by selves that are obscured by the dust of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). (6.34)
Even though the selves are inherently pure, their essential nature is concealed by the power of the Lord;
these manifestations of the self are omniscient and face in every direction.
Thus, consisting of the power of the Blessed One, it exists in states ranging from weak to intense.
With their very selves imitating the opening and closing of those various Sudarśanas,
they are pierced on all sides by ignorance and brought under control by that which consists of affliction.
For those whose true nature is concealed, there is a fourfold form;
they assume a fourfold state as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, distinguished as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (6.37)
(55) Those selves known as *jīvas* undergo bondage and liberation;
due to their subjection to *karma*, they descend to the earth.
Those called *manus* are the immutable ones (*kūṭastha*), described as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of them. (6.38)

Untouched by the latent tendencies of the afflictions, omniscient, and facing in all directions, these portions of the primordial prosperity are eternally perfected; they are declared by me to be identical with the Blessed One.
O Nārada, those who cause their own selves to appear and disappear within their own self are indeed the authoritative Vaiṣṇavas.
Abiding in this state of Puruṣa in the form of Viṣṇu’s volition,
they descend by means of yoga through their portions from station to station, down as far as the earth.
Having descended, these [sages] possess the power of creating progeny;
once the land of action has been created, they couple and produce four hundred more human beings from Manu and Mānavī.
And all of them are immeasurable; their extent will be described there.
From Aniruddha arises Śakti, from that Puruṣa in the subsequent stage, after four yugas.

From the Unmanifest, Śakti was created; from that [Unmanifest] impelled by Sudarśana, the descent of the Manūs occurred within Śakti. Then, O great sage, when Śakti had been created, the eight Manūs appeared.
Having descended from their own abodes, impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, they remain as embryonic masses (kalala) within that state consisting of power (śakti). (6.45)
Time and quality—these two reside within its womb.
The origin of time arises from power and necessity; necessity is subtle and the universal regulator. (6.46)
Impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, Śakti first arises;
there the Manus reside, and they descend here impelled by the Sudarśana [discus]. (6.47)
Whatever form, whatever function, and whatever intrinsic nature one may have,
that remains established through the power of Sudarśana, being cultivated by its specific discipline.
The arising of time occurs through necessity;
that which is the purifying form of time consists of its own creative activity (kalanā). Then, impelled by volition, that time arises from necessity. (6.49)
In that regard, the duration of the Manus is fixed by destiny; for even the Manus descend here at this time.
That Time alone, impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, measures everything. (6.50)
Just as the current of a river erodes its entire bank over time, so too does Time gradually bring about the manifestation of forms composed of the *guṇas*.
That form consisting of the *guṇas* has been previously described as belonging to Śakti. (6.51)
Through the sequence of stages over time, that secondary form is manifested.
Therein, first there is the arising of *sattva*; *sattva* is light, clear, consisting of qualities (*guṇa*), and free from affliction. (6.52)
First, at the appropriate time, the Manus descend from this [source];
therefore, through the Vaiṣṇava form of Āniruddha, his locus is Āniruddha; thus, that form is impelled by its own volition.
That *sattva* presides over that [being] and bears the name "Viṣṇu" alone;
from that very [cause], its nature consists of happiness and clarity. From *sattva*, *rajas* arises; all this was at first clear, happy, and undisturbed. (6.54)
O Sage, the sattva-guṇa that exists within is the internal conscious quality;
it is presided over by Viṣṇu, and therefore [the world arises] impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu.
The quality known as rajas emerges fully from that [sattva];
therein resides the station of the Manus, and the Manus descend there, impelled by their resolve, from sattva. (6.56)
Its nature as the form of Brahmā presided over by Aniruddha is the "Brahmic form" (*brāhmī mūrti*); and that quality (*guṇa*) in turn presides over Aniruddha.
Therefore, it possesses the nature of suffering (*duḥkharūpatva*).
This very suffering is restless; passion (rajas) is characterized by constant activity.
O Sage, when this entire universe had become dissolved and remained within that [Prakṛti],
then from that [Prakṛti] presided over by Brahmā, the production of *rajas* and *tamas* occurred from that which was situated within.
Impelled by the will of Viṣṇu, the quality named Tamas came into being;
therein resides the stability of the Manus,
and there those Manus descend, impelled by the Sudarśana.
Its nature as Rudra presided over by Aniruddha is as follows:
the quality named Rudra is also presided over by Aniruddha;
therefore, it possesses the nature of delusion and so forth.
The heavy state is constant obstruction and delusion, characterized by a lack of activity.
That is called *tamas* by those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of qualities;
it is the partial attainment of equilibrium among the three *guṇas* here [in this state],
brought about indeed by Hari’s resolve consisting of the *sudarśana*.
Then, even as it is impelled for the purpose of creation, that pair of complete qualities attains partial equilibrium, urged by the resolve of Viṣṇu.
p. 59) That very [state] is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
it is called "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*) and is celebrated by the knowers of reality as *tamas*.
These are synonyms for *prakṛti*.

The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya), ignorance (avidyā), inherent nature (svabhāva), the womb (yoni), the imperishable (akṣara), the non-womb (ayoni), and the womb of the qualities (guṇayoni)—these and others are designations for that which possesses the three qualities (traiguṇya). || 6.63 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Creation of the Impure," in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pañcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 393:
The seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Creation of the Pure and the Impure," concerning the aggregate of Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Kāla.
Ahirbudhnya:
That equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), consisting of darkness (tamas), which is neither deficient nor excessive, is called by the Sāṃkhyas the root of the world and "Prakṛti. (7.1)

The person who has descended there in succession through the four ages of Manu, who is the collective totality (samaṣṭi), the Puruṣa, and the source (yoni), is called the Immutable (kūṭastha). || 7.2 ||
That reality which consists of time and brings about the evolution of the world,
having assumed the role of their effect, acts as the uniter and the divider of those two.
O Sage, from this triad impelled by the will of the Blessed One, the evolution of Mahat and the other principles occurs;
this triad, beginning with Time, has become like a lump of clay, yet it is set toward its respective functions by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana alone. (7.4)
Prakṛti is that which brings about the group of principles beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth;
by its very nature and essence, it is transformative, like water, clay, and so forth. In this regard, Prakṛti is the transformative [cause]. (7.5)
The person (*puruṣa*), being by nature immutable, is the cause through mere proximity. Time possesses the quality of ripening both *prakṛti* and the person.
Time indeed ripens both principles: primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
