O great sage, from Prakṛti— presided over by Puruṣa, impelled by the will of Viṣṇu, and conditioned by Time— the Mahat-tattva arises from the state of equilibrium of the Guṇas.
O Sage, that which is called Mahat is the principle of Greatness (mahattattva) arisen from the Unmanifest.
The synonyms for the principle of Greatness are Vidyā, Gaurī, Ayanī, Brāhmī, Vadhū, Vṛddhi, Mati, and Madhu.
O Sage, Akhyāti, Īśvara, and Prājña are the names that denote it;
the Great One (Mahat) is proclaimed as threefold—as Time, Intellect (Buddhi), and likewise as Vital Breath (Prāṇa). || 7-9 ||

Due to the differentiation of *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas*, time—consisting of moments (*truṭi*), instants (*lava*), and so forth—is designated by the respective names of their manifestation; the intellect (*buddhi*) is that which performs determination (*adhyavasāyinī*). (7.10)
Prāṇa is the form of effort; these are the great divisions.
Among them, the fourfold nature of the sāttvika is designated by the names dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya. (7.11)
The Sāttvika form of the Great One (mahat) is divided into four kinds. (p.
62) Likewise, the Tāmasa [form] is also fourfold: unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery—these are the Tāmasa qualities. (7.12)
The eight Manus reside within the principle of Mahat, in the womb of Vidyā; they are impelled by Sudarśana, and these all-knowing, all-seeing Manus enter into the state of being embryos. (7–13)
In that regard, the arising of cognition— that is, what is called "awakening"— is produced as a faculty with respect to those [objects],
by which they may determine objects as being distinguished into the existent and the non-existent. (7.14)

The emergence of the great ego (mahat-ahaṃkāra) occurs within the womb of Vidyā; therein, that which is called the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is born, impelled by the will of Viṣṇu and further urged by his Sudarśana discus. (7.15)
Synonyms for the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra):
Ahaṃkāra, abhimāna, Prajāpati, ahaṃkṛti, abhimantṛ, and boddhṛ—these are its synonymous designations. (7.16)
The threefold nature of the ego (ahaṃkāra):
its form known as vaikārika is said to be sāttvika;
its form known as taijasa is rājasa; and that named bhūtādi is tāmasa. (7.17)
(63) Desire, anger, greed, pride, contempt, and thirst— these varieties of the form of egoism have been shown to you, O Sage. (7.18)
When the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) of the Manus has arisen, endowed with various manifestations,
that cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*) of the Manus enters into its interior womb.
From the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises the mind (manas).
That which is impelled by Sudarśana is the sense organ derived from the ego of Viṣṇu;
it is called the mind, and it is born as the essence of thought among the Manus. (7.20)
The embryo is likewise possessed of mind and intellect, consisting of the essence of Manu. From Bhūtādi arises the subtle element of sound;
thus, from the tamasic Bhūtādi, the subtle element of sound is born. (7.21)
Therefore, there is the origination of space; and from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), space is born, characterized by sound.
These are the quality and function of space.
Space has sound as its sole quality and primarily provides room.

O one of great intelligence, impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, the eight Manus then enter into a state of embryonic development within that space; from that, they emerge once again through the vaikārika [ego]. (7.23)
O Sage, the pair consisting of the ear and speech— the sense organ of hearing and the organ of action, speech—
arises among human beings solely through the contemplation of the Divine. (7.24)
That indeed is the distinction of the Manus; moreover, he is possessed of hearing and eloquent, and the embryo is composed of Manu. Now follows the production of the subtle element of touch.
From Viṣṇu, impelled by the Sudarśana [discus], there is merely the contact with the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
From that, the arising of wind occurs;
from that, wind possessing touch is born, and from that also arise the various types of motion of wind.
Drying up, impelling, movement, expansion, and contraction. || 7-26 ||
O Sage, these various functions arise from that wind;
the origin of the skin and the hands is from the *vaikārika* ego-consciousness, O Sage, as are the pair consisting of the skin and the hands.
From his volition, the pair of the organs of knowledge and action arises;
the Manus abide in the wind, and then the Person consisting of the Manus enters into the state of being an embryo within it. (7.28)
(65) At that time, as the embryo was striving, impelled by the resolve of Viṣṇu,
it came to possess both skin and hands for the sake of accomplishing touch, grasping, and so forth. (7.29)
From the *bhūtādi* characterized by *tamas*, impelled by *sudarśana*, there arises the production of fire from the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*).
From that [subtle element] alone, light is born; and from that [light], that which possesses form [is produced]. (7.30)
The various functions of fire—
such as form, manifestation, cooking, luster, and radiance—
arise as these fiery distinctions from the Vaikārika [sattvic] source. (7.31)
The origin of the eyes and feet:
O Sage, the pair of eyes and feet was born from that which was impelled by Sudarśana;
the sustenance of the Manus occurs within the radiant energy.
Impelled by the Sudarśana, they enter into the state of being its internal embryo.
Regarding their excellence of eyes and feet:
those Manus are possessed of form, endowed with beauty, luster, and so forth;
they possess eyes and feet, being capable of seeing and walking. (7.33)
From the *bhūtādi* [elemental source] of Viṣṇu, impelled by his glance and characterized by *tamas*, the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) arises,
and from that, indeed, the waters are produced. (7.34)
From the differentiation of those activities,
their qualities— taste, moisture, fluidity, and so forth— are produced;
[and from them] the sense organs of taste and generation arise.
Then, from that Vaikārika [ego], impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, [the following arose].
The sense of taste and the organ of generation arise from this [water], consisting of the nature of perception and action.
Within the waters, the Manus abide; impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, they enter into a state of embryonic gestation therein. (7.36)

O one of great intelligence, those humans are presiding over the activities of Viṣṇu; they possess a preeminence of the tongue and the generative organ, and they are full of flavor, possessed of affection, and endowed with fluids such as blood. (7.37)

Beings possessing the sense of taste are born, distinguished by the sexual characteristics of male and female; from that *bhūtādi*, impelled by *sudarśana*, there arises the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*). (7.38)
From that arises the subtle element of smell, and from it the earth, which possesses smell.
The specific qualities of the earth-element are hardness, weight, stability, and so forth; these are the qualities belonging to the earth. (7.39)
(67) O Sage, the nose and the anus arise from the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*) as impelled by Sudarśana;
this pair, consisting of the nose and the anus, is of the nature of both knowledge and action.
On earth, the Manus abide; impelled by the resolve of Viṣṇu, they enter into the state of embryos within your womb.
Among them, there is a distinction regarding the nose and the anus.
The heavy elements consist of stable aggregations, such as the union of bones, teeth, and so forth.
O Sage, they possess a sense of smell and an anus, with all their limbs complete;
there is the arising of volition and so forth,
as well as volition itself, agitation, and the fivefold vital breaths.
From the mind, the ego-sense, and the intellect, they are born first;
thus the Manus possess the fullness of all their limbs.
Thus, with all their members complete, they are endowed with the vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna. (7.43)
O Sage, the embodied beings there possess all their sense organs;
and the measure of time during the periods of creation and dissolution is equal to that which was previously described regarding the duration of the pratisaṃcara (the period of reabsorption).
In the process of emanation, this very transformation of Vidyā should be understood by the Vaiṣṇavas who contemplate the principles as being sevenfold through the glance of Hari. (7.45)
O Sage, they say those great elements (mahābhūtas) are divided sevenfold;
the divisions of Manu, and even the Manus themselves, are further divided as impelled by Sudarśana. (7.46)
In each successive age, first and then later, distinguished by gender as male and female,
they were all-knowing and all-seeing, having attained wisdom spontaneously.
Then, they perceive within themselves the Lord Aniruddha as the presiding overseer;
subsequently, impelled by his volition, those [sages] who possess such an overseer perform the production of the embryo through the sacred mantras.
Those Manus deposit hundreds upon hundreds of embryos in women;
they are designated by the names Brāhmaṇa and so forth, and are of four kinds: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (7.49)
From Manu and Manu’s wife were born humans characterized by pairs; those born from them received the designations "Mānava" and "Mānavī" and so forth.
Having been consecrated by the Manus, they [the progenitors] produced Mānavas through their own wives. (7.50)
They procreate many sons; they shall be human beings among men. (p.
69) Their performance of service to the Blessed One, their numerous lineages by which this entire world is pervaded—[these are described in verses 7.51].

These people belonging to the four castes are performers of the Lord's work; for those virtuous ones who perform the service of the devotees for a hundred years, there is the attainment of liberation. (7.52)
Having attained the knowledge born of discernment, they enter the supreme Hari;
for others, there is the attainment of saṃsāra, as they perform various other actions during the beginning and decline of the yugas.
Those who covet fruits go to the state produced by those very fruits.
O Sage, that creation of gods and others which has karma as its cause was previously described by you as "Vidyā," which contains the human embryo.
While still pregnant, she [beheld] the gods distinguished by various qualities,
as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kiṃnaras.
Thus, impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu, these various kinds of wombs are created by his own volition; they create others, and those too create yet others. (7.56)
But during the period of Manu’s gestation, the ancestors, gods, seers, and humans were thus created by Brahmā himself through that eternal Vidyā. (7.57)

(70) The fact that the Manus and the gods, etc., are individual manifestations of the immutable person (kūṭasthapuruṣa) is stated as follows: "The immutable person who was previously described as being below the supreme ether— The Manus, the deities, and so forth, are said to be his individual manifestations. (7.58)
O Sage, all individual souls are manifestations of the Lord; all distinctions among living beings are fashioned from portions of Viṣṇu’s glory,
just as the transformation of a great cloud into various forms.
Then, when manifest human beings had been born again and again, || 7.59 ||
Knowledge itself, through some particular aspect, becomes the eternal cow;
knowledge that has attained the state of a cloud is called the cow. (7.60)
The milk known as "the rain" flows forth like the transformation of food and other substances;
this is the explanation of the cause for the loss of knowledge among living beings.
Having consumed that medicinal milk, all men and women [shall be restored]. (7.61)
Those who were omniscient fall away from knowledge by their very own nature;
thereafter the scriptures come into being, and then the scriptures are set in motion by the ancient Manus.
Proceeding by the path thus indicated, they attain the supreme goal.
O Sage, this creation of the elements—both pure and otherwise—has been described by you in brief.

"That which is thus contemplated by Viṣṇu through the Sudarśana [form]—this is the summary of the meaning of the two chapters. Furthermore, O Nārada, hear this summary again according to the truth. (7.64)
The single power of Hari-Viṣṇu follows all states of being;
that Goddess is full of the six divine attributes and consists of knowledge, bliss, and action. (7.65)
Through the distinction between the object of meditation and the meditator, that [discipline] attains a twofold nature.
Therein, the meditator is the volition (saṃkalpa) consisting of the Sudarśana [weapon] of Hari.
O Sage, that which is its non-obstruction is its "Sudarśanatā" (the state of being well-seen);
it consists of action rooted in knowledge, and is transparent, consisting of independent consciousness. (7.67)
That which is called the "object of cultivation" (bhāvya) is the supreme aspect; it is celebrated as "manifestation" (bhūti).
Extending from Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the Earth, it is divided into pure and impure portions.
O Sage, that which begins with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ends with the divine manifestations (vyūha) consists of pure creation; that which begins with Śakti and ends with the earth consists of impure creation.
O great sage, know that the person situated between the two portions is the four-yuga one; he is the immutable (kūṭastha) who consists of both the pure and the impure.
Thus, O Sage, this manifold manifestation, consisting of various principles,
is driven in many directions by Sudarśana, the wind, like a flame.

In accordance with the process of emanation (*sarga*) by way of conformity (*ānulomyena*), and likewise in the process of dissolution (*apyaya*) by way of reversal (*prātilomyena*), it is established in the intermediate state; thus, it is made to function in various ways accordingly.

(72) O Great Sage, there is not even the slightest trace of the insignificance of an entity that is independent of being perceived; for that which does not come under the control of perception at its very birth and so forth, has no existence at all. (7-73)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Impure," in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 466:
The eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Support of the World.
Regarding creation, there are many diverse disagreements among disputants.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O God of gods, O Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes!
All of this that has issued from the lotus of your mouth has been heard by me.
But my inner self is agitated and deluded by various forms of ignorance;
some proponents of the truth speak of a creation consisting of the three worlds. (8.2)
Some consider her to consist of the four elements, others of the five elements;
some consider her to consist of six constituents, and others of seven constituents.
Some say it consists of eight constituent natures, others of nine;
some say it is composed of ten principles, and others that it is elevenfold.
Thus do the sages, the perfected ones, the gods, and likewise the Vedas, declare this manifold enumeration concerning the scope of the principles and primordial nature.
Some say the creation was born from an egg, others that it was born from a lotus; some say the creation was born from fire, and some that it arose from within the body.
(p. 74) Some [describe her] as consisting of the womb of knowledge (*vidyā*), while others [describe her] as being of the nature of emptiness (*śūnya*).
Among these, the question arises from a desire to know the reality (*tattva*).
Thus are those various high and low subjects within the great ocean of the diverse scriptures. (8.7)
Today my intellect, lacking a boat, is utterly bewildered by this formidable clamor arising from the waves of various philosophical systems. (8.8)
O Śaṅkara, ferry her across by providing a raft of definitive resolution.
[The beginning of the narration of that answer: Ahirbudhnya said:
O divine sage, it is fitting that this question has been raised by you.
Even the great are deluded in this matter; hear from me the determination of the truth:
the Supreme Self is the one supreme deity, resplendent with the six divine attributes.
Even the words of the Vedas lack the capacity to fathom reality in its entirety;
though beginningless and infinite, speech does not penetrate that reality,
remaining as if ignorant, situated merely at its periphery by means of various attributes.
O Sage, when there is disagreement regarding the names of the qualities, those who are weary of them are the knowers of reality;
for by those very qualities of Manu, they are the best among the knowers of reality. (8.12)
O Great Sage, they point to the cause of the world through their own established [doctrines], by means of those various signs of qualities uttered by various speakers. (8.13)
People who do not understand synonyms maintain distinctions by means of words; yet even for the single Lakṣmī, there is the state of being the domain of various words.
Thus, she who is the beloved light of Viṣṇu is Śakti, whose very form is the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
Though she is but one, she is worshipped by the knowers of reality under various names;
for those who know reality speak of the object as they have perceived it when she proceeds with creation according to their own volition. (8.15)

Likewise, O Sage, as she was returning and withdrawing [the elements] by her own volition, those who were knowers of reality—due to the disparity in their power of discernment—[perceived her differently]. (8.16)
According to the various distinctions of deficiency and excess that they perceived, so many and so many different doctrines did those teachers proclaim when urged by their disciples. (8.17)

Therefore, one whose intellect does not perceive everything becomes deluded regarding numbers, as well as those such as the Grandfather (Brahmā) who hold authority over the affairs of the world. (8.18)
Even their state of deficiency or superiority is imagined due to the difference among speakers;
however, the sovereignty of Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of the six divine attributes, is beyond being directed by others.
The manifestation of the cosmic egg, the lotus, and so forth arises from the diversity of the Supreme Soul’s intellect and will;
as such, these activities of the Supreme Self do not admit of questioning. (8.20)
The infinity of the Lord’s modes:
however He acts in creation, maintenance, or even dissolution, those modes are indeed infinite due to the power of Time. (8-21)
Among the various disputants who each maintain their own particular position regarding this manifold diversity of modes, some assert one mode,
another asserts a different one, and yet another asserts yet another, [all] concerning the Lord Harimedhas.
Having understood this through his own intellect, he spoke out of a desire for the welfare of his disciple.
Therefore, there is a diversity of scriptures; thus proceeds the manifold activity of the various treatises on creation and so forth.
Just as in the present day, for human beings, there is an established order of pleasure and pain according to the divisions of days and nights, arising from the diversity of their karma. (8.24)
Likewise, O best of sages, the arrangement of pleasure and pain is established during the days of Brahmā;
some of these Brahmā-kalpas are of various forms,
while others are days of Brahmā agitated by wind.
Likewise, some are troubled by rain, some are beset by heat;
some have many enemies, while others are very pleasant and charming.
Relying upon this very certainty with a steadfast mind, steady your inner self; let your delusion perish.
"O Sage, the cause has been described as having various forms, distinguished by its activity and manifestation, and characterized by the production of signs. (8.28)
Nārada, restating the meaning of what was heard, said:
"O God, O omniscient one whose banner is the bull, the cause has been explained."
That power of the Creator of the world which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) [is this]. || 8-29 ||
That which is called Lakṣmī is twofold, distinguished as action (kriyā) and manifestation (bhūti). That which is called action is volition (saṃkalpa), and it bears the name Sudarśana.
That which is called Bhūti has the form of the world and consists of Time, the Unmanifest, and the Person;
it is both impure and pure in nature, consisting of the Vyūha and Vibhava forms.
"Action is the initiator of existence, and it takes the form of the Sudarśana;
this reality has been shown to me by the God of gods, as I have heard it. (8.32)
A reminder of the second question:
"Now, O Lord, I wish to hear the second question, O Bull-bannered One, regarding that which is called the support of the worlds. (8.33)
Regarding the status of Sudarśana as the support of the world,
Ahirbudhnya says: "Listen, O Nārada, to the truth concerning that which is proclaimed as the support."
By which this universe is sustained, like beads by a thread. || 8.34 ||
O great sage, that primordial power of Hari known by the name Lakṣmī, she who follows the existence and non-existence of Viṣṇu, the soul of all; (8.35)
It has been described that even a ten-thousandth part of that [power], manifesting as its own autonomy, arises through the differentiation of action (kriyā) and being (bhūti). (8.36)
O Sage, just as a leaf is held by a thorn through its very structure, that prosperity is perpetually sustained by the Sudarśana through its activity; hear from me the details thereof.
In that regard, the wheel of the sustaining power of the Great Night is the expansion of that very stillness of Brahman from which all beings have been withdrawn;
its dissolution is the Great Night itself, which is sustained by His volition.
That which was formerly known as Mahārātridhara is indeed now called Sudarśana;
that great discus, whose essence is the syllable E, is meditated upon by the gods even today.
The second wheel is that of Uṣas (Dawn), which is the form of Brahman arising from Śakti, characterized by the desire to emanate;
it is impelled by volition, just as the flame of fire is by the wind. (8.40)
That wheel of Uṣas, adorned with two spokes, is designated as such;
it is constantly maintained by Brahmā and by those who desire prosperity.
The third is the Wheel of Arising (*udayacakra*);
he who always sustains that which is the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of Saṃkarṣaṇa—that is the Wheel of Arising itself, consisting of the triad of cognitions. (8.42)
That resolve of Saṃkarṣaṇa is cultivated by those desiring knowledge;
it is the fourth wheel of sovereignty, which is the unfolding of Pradyumna, consisting of sovereignty and full of vigor.
He is sustained by that very Vaiṣṇava resolve which pertains to Lakṣmī;
for that is indeed the resolve of Pradyumna, consisting of sovereignty and full of vigor.
Those established in sovereignty properly worship the four-spoked wheel;
the fifth is the Great Wheel of Power (Śaktimahācakra),
which is the unfolding (unmeṣa) of Aniruddha, illuminated by the splendor of power.
Volition (saṃkalpa), arising from the power of Brahman, always sustains that [universe];
that great wheel of power (śakti-mahācakra) is conceived as having five spokes.

For the sake of increasing power and splendor, all the gods worship the six-spoked wheel, which is designated as the sixth manifestation and consists of the group of twelve beginning with Keśava. (8.47)
That great six-spoked wheel, which manifests the internal array of emanations, is held by Sudarśana, who takes the form of volition.

(80) That is declared to be the Ṛtvara; those desiring vows worship it as the Great Sudarśana-cakra. It is the seventh [manifestation], which was previously described as Vibhava, the powerful one beginning with Padmanābha. || 8-49 ||
O great sage, that which sustains him by the will of Viṣṇu is called the Mahāsudarśana, and it is said to have twelve spokes.
That which is known as the "intermediate state of existence" (vibhavāntara), arising from the penetration of power,
was sustained by the Wheel-bearer through his twelve-spoked wheel and his corresponding resolve.
That which is the eighth, the thousand-spoked wheel, is the supreme ether, the mighty abode of Viṣṇu;
it is sustained by the thousand-spoked wheel through its volition.
These arrays of the Sudarśana have been proclaimed in brief;
O Sage, they exist by themselves through the relationship of the container and the contained. (8.53)
Volition is but a ten-millionth part of Śakti, and manifestation likewise is twofold;
that Vaiṣṇava existence, which is Śakti, thus shines forth in many ways. (8.54)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Support of the Universe," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
From the beginning, verse 520.
The Ninth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Support of the Impure World," the First Wheel of Puruṣa.
Ahirbudhnya:
The pure support has been described as that by which she is sustained;
she who exists as manifestation in the form of the emanations and so forth is the Goddess who proceeds [therein]. (9.1)
Just as everything from the primordial Puruṣa down to the earth consists of both pure and impure natures, hear now that wheel by which it is sustained, which is composed of volition. (9.2)
That wheel of the Person has three spokes, by which the Person is sustained;
the wheels of Śakti and the others are said to be a wheel of thirty spokes, by which that Śakti is sustained.
Such is that fixed wheel by which destiny is sustained;
it is the six-spoked Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), and he by whom that is sustained is Time itself.
O great sage, those by which sattva, rajas, and tamas are sustained are known by the wise as the three-spoked foundational wheels (ādhāracakras). || 9-5 ||
The wheel with eleven spokes is that by which the intellect (buddhi) is sustained;
the great wheel with eight spokes is the sustainer of the ego (ahaṃkāra). (9.6)
The single-spoked wheel is indeed ethereal (vaiyata); the two-spoked wheel is that which sustains the wind;
the three-spoked is called fiery (taijasa); and the four-spoked, O Sage, is watery (āpya).
The earthly wheel has five spokes by which the earth is supported;
all the wheels of the qualities are marked with three spokes each.
The elevenfold wheel consisting of the sense organs, along with the two pairs and the fire (Ara),
is called your individual foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), O Sage.
Listen to the great wheel of vast manifestation, the single-spoked great wheel that brings about great power—
just as a great banner-cloth is held stretched out in the sky. 9–10.
O Sage, by means of the purifying Pavamāna hymn,
that [energy] consisting of Viṣṇu’s power likewise extends from Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the earth without ceasing.
On a supportless canvas, manifestation is sustained by intention alone;
that wheel consisting of intention has infinite spokes, O great sage. (9.12)
It is divine, known as the Great Splendor, transcending speech and mind,
immeasurable, without beginning or end, and characterized by both existence and non-existence.
It is infinite and boundless, crowded with endless lineages,
and manifested as a mass of millions upon millions of cosmic eggs.
(83) The manifestation of thousands upon thousands of floods of great elements, by means of sense-faculties whose brilliance is like that of fireflies, numbering in the tens of millions. 9-15.
It was marked by world-eggs as terrifying as small clouds, yet it was not adorned by them;
rather, in some places, it was spread out as if by the waters consisting of the great elements.
Like droplets from the rains, the vast domain of Viṣṇu was spread out,
shining in some places with the great elements and in others with tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of lights.
In some places, it was fanned by the winds of the elements as if by fans raised;
in others, it was filled with millions upon millions of spaces that appeared like small openings.
It is pierced by various forms of egoism (ahaṃkāra), characterized by the sense of "I," consisting of both small and great [elements], and divided into millions upon millions of parts.
It was marked with various forms of darkness made dense,
and in some places filled with tens of thousands of fluctuations of diverse torments.
In some places it is colored by base, bright, and light dust; in others it is marked by many pure beings, numbering in the tens of millions upon tens of millions. || 9.21 ||
By means of the threefold and sixfold divisions, further divided into twelve, with twenty-four variations, and shining with thirty-two and a half [verses]. (9.22)
[He was surrounded] by many thousands of Kālas, crowded with tens of thousands, divided into millions upon millions, and filled with sixty-six [units].
It is strewn with the form of necessity (*niyati*), consisting of various constraints, and possessing millions upon millions of trillions of qualities. (9.24)
By means of its power, which has the nature of a honeycomb of various forms,
it [bestows] drops of honey that are the very essence of the flowing stream of reality.
With a form possessing thousands of millions, billions, trillions, and quadrillions of aspects,
it appears in some places exceedingly smooth, as if by a man, and in other places as if stationary.
[The body] has a form fashioned by white, red, and black karma,
and its nature is like an udumbara fruit swarming with many gnats.
Distinguished by the diversity of various living beings, partaking in the manifestation of various fruits,
and having a nature entangled with latent impressions (vāsanā) of both auspicious and inauspicious forms.
It is situated nowhere by a person who is a treasury of manifold afflictions, yet it consists of the great being that is stainless bliss and perfect awakening. (9.29)
By those who are eternal, liberated, unassailable, and characterized by stainless bliss,
who directly behold the Lord Īśāna, the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
Seated with the Goddess Lakṣmī, whose body is the embodiment of the six perfections,
he is eternally risen, eternally satisfied, and has transcended great darkness.

Thus adorned by their own selves with excellent marks, it was marked by the constant presence of lotus-eyed men who were the personified embodiments of the six political expedients (ṣāḍguṇya) in their various military arrays.
(85) Thus, he beheld this supreme Vaiṣṇava majesty pervading all, which is presided over by those who effect the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world. 9.33.
Wearing the variegated garment properly by means of the self upon the self—this Vaiṣṇava resolve indeed stands like a thread upon jewels. (9.34)
Immediately following that is the unmanifest, the great Sudarśana-cakra;
when cultivated through mere recollection, it brings about all states of being.
The wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhṛticakra*) is that which consists of the desire to withdraw; it is the eternal, supreme Vaiṣṇava resolve.
That Sudarśana of withdrawal is infinite and boundless. (9.36)
But that single resolve alone is praised in manifold forms—as infinite, undifferentiated, immeasurable, and incomparable. (9.37)
That one Great Supreme Brahman is like a waveless ocean and resembles a cloudless sky; it is motionless in its sixfold attributes.
His single, inseparable power consists of both existence and non-existence;
it is the divine attribute-bearer of that possessor of attributes, like the celestial moonlight of the cold-rayed moon.
The volition of that [mind] is the state of being occupied with form;
the volition of remaining in stillness is that which is stilled—this is the Sudarśana.
O Great Sage, whether in manifestation, withdrawal, or even in persistence, the wheel of movement exists; therein, volition (saṃkalpa) abides as the prior form of that movement. (9.41)
That great wheel called Calana consists of the Sudarśana;
its threefold nature and its three divisions should be understood by those who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of the tantras. (9.42)
Therein, that which consists of the Great Emanation (mahāsṛṣṭi), characterized by both summary and detailed exposition,
and filled with various powers, has been described to you previously.
And the wheel of great withdrawal (mahāsaṃhāracakra), characterized by both summary and detail, should be understood here to be exactly like that; and it has been shown to you previously. (9.44)
Now I shall explain in detail the extent of that wheel of stability which stands in the center, characterized by both concise and expanded forms, and which exists according to its specific measure.
For just as a single actor is divided into various forms through his roles, so too is volition alone divided by those various distinctions. (9.46)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Support of the Impure World," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 566:
The tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Means of Valid Cognition Consisting of Objects.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Lord of the life of Bhavānī, Protector of the world, Lord of the universe, Bestower of fearlessness upon the gods! 10.1
Salutations to you, the destroyer of Tripura, the ocean of the knowledge of reality;
salutations again and again to you who are eternally the ten imperishables and possess the six limbs.
That which has been described as the eternal, imperishable cause of the universe,
and that which is declared to be the support known as Saṃkalpa, the Sudarśana— [these two are one].
O Lord, all this has been understood by me in its true essence, both in its concise and detailed forms, as the manifestation of Viṣṇu’s volition.
Now, O Destroyer of Death, I wish to hear in detail:
what is that which is called "measure" (pramāṇa), of what kind is it, and of what nature is it? || 10-5 ||
"For what purpose and of what nature is it, O Lord? Tell me that in detail;
for there is no one other than you who can speak of all that is secret. (10.6)
(p. 88) The Promise to Define the Means of Valid Cognition (pramāṇa): Ahirbudhnya said:
"Listen, Nārada, to the unchanging status of the means of valid cognition according to its true nature."
In which alone the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, finds its rest.
The definition of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
That which is the intermediate resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of Viṣṇu, who has created the universe, remains manifest as the eternal path of the world; such is its nature. (10.8)
O great sage, that is declared to be the Wheel of Abiding (sthiticakra), which is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Its division into means of valid cognition is conceived as being of two forms, by way of the collective totality (samaṣṭi) and the individual parts (vyaṣṭi). || 10-9 ||
O Sage, that volition which exists regarding all objects with a uniform nature, having the totality as its measure and essence,
is celebrated as this wheel consisting of the Great Abiding.
O Soul of all, that individual magnitude and essential nature— in which all the specific arrangements of every being, however they may be, are contained— is the reality. (10–11)

(89) Having as its object the place, form, and so forth, which are to be accomplished through the activity of transformation, that [power] is established as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) within the wheel consisting of individual manifestations. 10–12.

O Sage, that object which consists of a single activity and so forth, that which is characterized by creation and so on, and that which consists of the systematic arrangement of the scripture, the meaning of the scripture, and what is to be accomplished through it; || 10-13 ||
In the manifestation beginning with Vāsudeva, each arises from its own respective volition.
That by which all this is measured as having a finite extent,
and that which is its detailed exposition— the supreme void characterized by divine enjoyment. (10–15)
By means of that resolve of Hari, it remains established in the form of its own duration and measure—
unrestricted, uncontracted, and infinite.
O Sage, that which is the supreme source (yoni) of insentient principles is the power consisting of Kāla and Kālī; such is that supreme [power] in its threefold aspect.
In matters such as intrinsic nature, causal efficiency, and existence, that necessity is based upon valid cognition;
these two, namely Niyati (Necessity) and Kāla (Time), are considered the two divisions of Time.
In the midst of that which consists of both pure and impure, there is a Person who stands like a peak;
his imperishable state is the great womb of manifold living beings.
That which is "this-muchness" (iyattā) is established as the measure within the Wheel;
and that which is the differentiation of this-muchness pertains to the domains of the *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and so forth. (10.20)
O Sage, that entire wheel consisting of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) extends throughout the nature of the constituents such as sattva, as well as their activity and their fruit. (10.21)
In all those cases, the limit [of the object] is determined through the clear perception of the means of valid cognition;
such is the threefold nature of the intellect, as well as the modifications beginning with dharma.

Whatever determination of activity and vibration there may be, and whatever entire state consisting of the closing of the eyes, that state here consists of this muchness [finitude] due to the perception of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 10-23 ||
Whatever pride there is, whether it be the agitation of the mind or the ego-sense;
whatever state there is, such as desire and the like; and whatever stability there is in those very things—[all these constitute the nature of the ego]. (10.24)
By means of that Sudarśana [discus] within this wheel consisting of the instruments of valid cognition,
he [perceives] that group of five which exists among the five types of mental constructions.
And such is this pair of conceptual constructions, O Sage;
that which constitutes their limit exists pervasively through the clear perception of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Lightness and dexterity, as well as the fivefold faculty of perception, and the form characterized by the peaceful, the terrible, and so forth, which resides in the fivefold faculty of intellect; || 10-27 ||
And that which consists of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation, as well as the forms that are peaceful, terrible, and so forth, reside in the five organs of action. (10.28)
In that regard, whatever form consists of limitation and whatever body consists of persistence—all that resides within the Sudarśana of Viṣṇu’s will, which is the very measure of all things. (10.29)
Arrangement, providing space, lightness, impelling activity, and drying;
as well as arrangement, providing space, manifestation, moisture, oiliness, and even minuteness. (10.30)
Stability, earthiness, and hardness—this is the elemental body;
its state consists of an arrangement of one, two, three, four, or five qualities.
By means of which [faculties] it remains pervading that [object], its extent is known through the clear perception of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
and in each respective reality, whatever specific limit is eternally established [is likewise perceived]. (10.32)
Such is the course of Hari’s wheel of authority and his resolve;
thus has this established limit and extent been proclaimed regarding the wheel.
O Sage, hear now of another state of existence born from Viṣṇu’s resolve;
O Sage, it is that natural course which arises through the removal of all obstructions.
O Sage, that state of the principles (tattvas) and their essential qualities (tāttvikas) is now described:
it is the powerful manifestation of *sattva* through the favoring influence of other *guṇas*. (10.35)
Consisting of the knowledge of dharma and so forth, impelled by Sudarśana, that specific magnitude should be understood as the sustainer of the three worlds. (10.36)
Gradually being guided by those whose intellects are radiant with the spirit of awakening, he perpetually sustains heaven and earth through the giving of rain, food, and other gifts. (10.37)
That exertion of *tamas* which occurs through the assistance of other qualities is of the nature of *adharma* and so forth; it is impelled by the volition of Viṣṇu. (10.38)
Being practiced slowly by those whose intellects are clouded by darkness, it destroys both heaven and earth through the destruction of rain, food, and other necessities. (10.39)
Therefore, the affliction of beings constantly arises from another source due to two qualities [of the age]:
the deployment of weapons and military arrays, and the establishment of dharma by intending to eliminate the unrighteous. (10.40)
When Viṣṇu, the Lord, assumes the state of Janārdana,
then the resolve of that deity is known by the name Sudarśana.
He assumes a formal manifestation in the nature of weapons and other implements, in the form of the discus, plow, Saunanda mace, conch, Śārṅga bow, and arrows. (10.42)
In the form of a sword and shield, with noose, goad, and battle-axe; in the form of staff and spear, and with the nature of thunderbolt and mace.
In the form of fire with a hundred mouths, consisting of spears and javelins, likewise in the nature of tridents, and in the form of weapons such as the short-handled spear; || 10.44 ||
Thus, assuming various forms fashioned by his own volition and resting within the hand of Nārāyaṇa, he arises for the growth of the world. (10.45)
Thus, the array consisting of weapons has been shown to you in brief;
now another array consisting of missiles, the Saudarśana, is described.
Having assumed a divine form consisting of an array of weapons, adorned with its various limbs and members,
he [manifests] through the nature of the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and so forth, from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. (10.47)

He creates the military array composed of the Brahmāstra and other weapons, which both initiates and withdraws them for the sake of complete protection, and which is approved by the two groups of sixty.
In various ways, for Prajāpati, the ancestors, Brahmā, and the gods,
there arises a divine [power] of manifold forms, possessing the nature of a weapon.
Even among the Brahman-sages, celestial sages, and royal sages whose very selves consist of mantra,
it persists in the form of verbal discourse, curses, and the like.
O best of sages, there is nothing on earth or in heaven where this [mantra] is not an effective means for either restraint or favor. (10.51)
This much has been shown as the array of the means of valid cognition in the form of objects;
now hear the form of sound belonging to the god Sudarśana.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Array of Means of Knowledge Consisting of Objects," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 618:
The eleventh chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Array of Means of Valid Cognition Consisting of Words."
Nārada:
Salutations to Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Mountains, the beloved of Gaurī; salutations to you, the bestower of happiness and auspicious fortune upon all the gods. 11.1.

O Lord of the Gods, I have heard the inquiry concerning the means of knowledge consisting of sound; now tell me that entire manifestation of the meaning of the means of knowledge which has been described as having the form of sound.
As an introductory statement intended to explain that [matter],
Ahirbudhnya says:
"In the primordial creation, as it occurred in the past, adorned with various states of being..."
This thought, which brings about happiness, occurred to the powerful Viṣṇu. || 11.3 ||
At the beginning of creation, the manner of the Blessed One’s reflection was as follows:
"This vast creation has been fashioned by me, preeminent in the quality of goodness (sattva);
its objects and purposes are directly perceived, it is free from obstruction, and it is characterized by supreme happiness. (11.4)
This world has come into being, crowded with gods, sages, and Brahmās;

through the increase of sentient beings, there occurs the manifestation of one's true nature preceded by the attainment of the Supreme Person, by means of the conjunction with the knowledge of reality and also through the practice of the True Dharma. (11.5) p. 95)
"Having obtained me before long, he will surely resort to his own true nature.
Through the increase of rajas and tamas, there will be a decline of sattva; the predominance of the qualities of rajas and tamas will come about in due time. (11.6)
By the power of that very unfolding, even the quality of goodness (sattva) is consumed;
then the manifestation of Daityas and others occurs,
and then the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas will appear.
By them, the boundaries of the Vedic tradition will be destroyed; by them, this divine and sattvic boundary will be shaken. Through the loss of knowledge, dharma will be obscured.
When right knowledge has been destroyed by the manifestation of the qualities of rajas and tamas, [the self remains obscured]. || 11-8 ||
That Dharma, which is the cause of knowledge, will also disappear;
from that comes the agitation of the people, and then these pure people, being without support, will perish. (11.9)
Then, when the incarnations of the Blessed One have found their opportunity, my purpose there shall be eternal through manifold forms;
in those [incarnations], there will be various requirements for instruments. (11.10)
The resolve to establish the Dharma:
having repeatedly entered into living beings by means of his own form through his illusory power (*māyā*),
he dispels those who hate righteous deeds by employing various diverse means.
In various instances, the boundaries of the Dharma will be easy to maintain.
There are two means for the purpose of eliminating unrighteousness (adharma), and the means for the rejection of those who hate the Dharma must be carried out in two ways. (11–12)
"Indeed, by the will of the Blessed One, the manifestation of both [the weapons and the scriptures] occurs in the form of an array of missiles and weapons, as well as in the form of the scriptures.
Having said this, [he described] that which consists of the essence of meaning, crowded with a flood of missiles and weapons. (11–13)
Having formed a mental resolve, he created a military array by the power of his own will;
and that Sudarśana array was capable of maintaining the established boundaries.
The nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been indicated and will be explained accordingly;
for the meaning of the scripture concerning the nature of the means of valid cognition is indeed the Vaiṣṇava resolve. || 11-15 ||
Therefore, understand how that [knowledge] arose from Brahmā:
it is the description of the nature of the primordial scripture, consisting solely of volition, which dispels all internal darkness. (11.16)

At that time, there arose from the void a single scripture, like the sound of a thunderclap, composed of phonemes and meanings, and of syllables that were great waves of consciousness and bliss. (11.17)
The form of Viṣṇu known as Sudarśana is strung together with jewels arising from the ocean of Viṣṇu’s power, like pearls, fashioned by his mere will.
That treatise, consisting of consciousness and expounding the true Dharma,
was proclaimed as an eternal work of one million chapters by Kāmapāla.

It contains the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, is endowed with the four aims of human life, and is filled with logical reasoning; it is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Aṅgiras, and Atharva Vedas. || 11-20 ||

It is filled with numerous conceptual distinctions regarding words, sentences, and the objects of valid cognition, and it is adorned with various auspicious conventions, both divine and human. || 11-21 ||
It is encompassed by various meters constructed from those conceptualized kalpas,
along with the numbers of temporal divisions, grammatical bases, suffixes, and vowels.

It is adorned with case endings, grammatical relations, gender, its own [proper] bases and euphonic combinations, technical names together with their governing rules, and by means of metarules (paribhāṣā). || 11-23 ||
By means of substitutes, augments, elisions, and modifications, as well as by grammatical conditions, various suffixes, sentences, and even prefixes. (11.24)
(98) By means of indeclinables, prefixes, nouns, verbs, and particles;
by the measures of meter, the strength of vowels, the *abhiniṣṭāna* sounds, and the *sāman* chants. (11.25)
It is adorned with the distinctions of poetic sentiments and the various arrangements of words,
as well as by the variations of syllable-insertion and the transposition of syllables.
And by means of light conceptualizations regarding both the transformation and the primordial matter,
as well as through various etymological explanations and diverse scriptural conclusions.
By means of the various calculations arising from the positions of the planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs,
and by means of the various divisions of the horā-skandha and the prescriptions devised for their results.

Through investigations arising from injunctions, explanatory passages, and mantras, through the conceptualization of ritual acts, and through the application of auxiliary elements, logical reasoning, sequential order, and the extension of rules by analogy; || 11-29 ||
By means of numerous topics, investigations within the scope of sentences, principles established by valid cognition, and the points of defeat, quibbles, and futile rejoinders; || 11-30 ||
Through conceptualizations of substances and actions, and through the postulations of qualities and universals;
through the variations of the fourfold sacrificial offices, and through the expansions of the four Vedas. || 11-31 ||

Through the ritual procedures of the four stages of life, through the various distinctions of the four social classes, through the diverse rites of purification, and through the sequences of obligatory and optional actions; || 11-32 ||
It is endowed with various Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
as well as with various enumerations conceived according to their own inherent natures and so forth.

It is variegated by the conceptual constructions of a soul (puruṣa) and a Lord (īśvara), as well as by the imagined notions of transformation, and by the diverse fabrications of the explanation of states, characteristics, and dharmas. (11.34)
It is endowed with various conceptualizations regarding the combinations of the means of valid cognition,
as well as through investigations into defilement and non-defilement, and the spheres of the person and the unmanifest.

Through various conceptualizations of reality and unreality, through reflections on the manifold courses of rebirth, through investigations into the sequence of liberation, and through numerous conceptualizations of fame; 11.36.

Through investigations into the merits and defects designated as knowledge and ignorance, through the conceptualizations of the three qualities (guṇas), and through reflections on the conjunctions of creation; || 11-37 ||
It is endowed with various Sāṃkhya enumerations arranged in systematic order,
as well as with the methods and systems of Yoga, and even with the conceptualizations of mental states.
Through various types of repeated practice and diverse conceptualizations of detachment, as well as through contemplations on the limbs of yoga, both internal and external. || 11-39 ||

Through descriptions of afflictions, karma, and its maturation, as well as of latent dispositions; through reflections on ascetic practices and mental formations, and through contemplations on the various types of suffering. || 11-40 ||

By means of those various conceptualizations of the four bases, there is a separate conceptualization of that which is to be accepted, that which is to be rejected, and also of the rejection and acceptance themselves. (11.41)

Through various contemplations on one's own true nature, through conceptualizations desiring enjoyments, and through numerous practices of *kriyā-yoga* that serve as means for purifying the mind. (11.42)

It is adorned with various supernatural powers (siddhis) established in the mind, and with conceptual constructions consisting of explanations of the Lord (pati), the bonds (pāśa), and the bound souls (paśu), variegated by their respective causes. || 11-43 ||
It is further adorned with manifold contemplations on the five categories of reality, distinguished by the divisions of ritual action and knowledge, and by the conceptualizations of the pure path.

Through reflections on the five powers, through investigations into the three impurities, through accounts of the instruments of enjoyment, and through the conceptualization of the forms of individual souls. (11.45)
And by means of the *dīkṣā* and *pratiṣṭhā* rituals, as well as the *pāśupata* dharmas—
thus, through the manifold variety of conceptual constructions of the intellect.
He is constantly engaged in conceptualization, which constructs various offices;
he explains the true dharmas in many ways according to those offices. (11.47)
Formerly, there was a recitation of a million chapters spoken by Saṃkarṣaṇa;
it consisted of the creative resolve of the primordial Viṣṇu, for it was indeed born from his will.
Regarding that scripture being the cause of the Lord’s pleasure, [it is said]:
"By means of that scripture, those divine Manus and those humans who were mentioned at the beginning of creation—those Manus and humans likewise [attained it]. (11.49)

Having gratified Nārāyaṇa with manifold acts of veneration, [the sage composed] that scripture; yet, due to the reversal of time and the emergence of the distinctions between the ages (yugas), the circulation of that scripture became sluggish.

(p. 101) At the beginning of the Tretā age, due to the contraction of the quality of goodness (sattva) and the expansion of passion (rajas), while the high-souled Brāhmaṇas were freely indulging in their desires, || 11-51 ||

That teaching of his, which was so beautiful to behold, became slow in its dissemination; thereafter, when the world was confounded by delusion, Vātsyāyana and others divided those scriptures for the sake of establishing the governance of the world.
Having assembled, the creators of the world deliberated upon what ought to be done;
there was a sage named Apāntaratapas, who was born from the speech of Hari.
And I am Kapila, the ancient seer born from the Primordial God;
I am Hiraṇyagarbha, the source of the worlds, and Paśupati, Śiva. (11.54)
Having performed intense austerity for ten million years,
and being impelled by the God of gods, they obtained the permission of the Primordial God.
Endowed with even a fraction of Sudarśana’s power and joined with his resolve,
they attained the strength of higher knowledge through dharma born from divine grace.
Once that scripture had appeared, we fashioned it for you in part.
In that regard, the venerable sage Apāntaratapas first performed the division of the Veda; therein, Vātsyāyana carried out the division.
From Hari, the son Vācyāyana received [the Vedas], and from him,
there arose that which was taken up— the form of wisdom consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
This [work], born from the resolve of Viṣṇu and proclaimed by Vātsyāyana,
was carved out by the noble-minded Kapila from the original scripture, according to the extent of the Sāṃkhya system he discerned. (11.59)
That became the Sāṃkhya scripture, devoted to thorough discernment.
Hiraṇyagarbha performed the classification of the Yoga scripture, for he, the origin of the worlds, fashioned it according to the primordial instruction. (11.60)
This divine instruction on yoga, which constitutes the limb of Yama,
was carved out by me from Śiva’s *Pāśupata-vibhajana*— that portion [of the teaching] extracted from the scripture crowded with various vows. (11.61)
That which is called Pāśupata, which effects the liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu),
arose from that divine teaching consisting solely of the eternal Āgama, through the division of the Pañcarātra by the Blessed One. (11.62)

Viṣṇu himself, having extracted the essence from that which is free from confusion, fashioned this work which defines the nature of the supreme manifestation (paravyūha), the manifest expansion (vibhava), and so forth. (11.63)
The Tantra known as Pañcarātra has liberation as its sole defining fruit;
it is that supreme Vaiṣṇava resolve called Sudarśana.
He himself split [himself] into five parts by means of that [power], abiding in five faces;
this manifestation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇavyūha*), which consists of the determination of Viṣṇu, is declared to be the conclusion of the meaning of the chapter.
(103) What more do you wish to hear regarding the distinction between the Śāstra and the Śastra? || 11-65 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Array of Means of Knowledge Consisting of Sound," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī-Pāñcarātra*. 11.
Chapter Twelve, titled "The Determination of the Specific Nature of the Array of Means of Knowledge Consisting of Words," from the beginning: Verse 683.
Nārada, recounting the events: Homage to you, O beloved of Pārvatī, who are worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras!
O Lord, by your grace, I have heard that divine glory of Viṣṇu.
Regarding that primordial and great scripture consisting of the Sudarśana of Hari,
Vātsyāyana and others say that from it various separate scriptures arose.
The inquiry into the essential nature of the Triad and the others:
"O Lord, I desire to hear the nature of that which consists of the Triad, as well as Sāṃkhya, the Yoga-śāstra, Pāśupata, and Sāttvata. (12.3)
The promise to provide that reply was made by Ahirbudhnya:
"Listen, Nārada, to their forms individually according to the truth."
To the extent that volition persists as distinct from Viṣṇu. || 12-4 ||
(p. 105) The Definition of the Nature of the Threefold Veda:
Among these, the first form consists of the three Vedas and is the seer of all objects.
Because it takes the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas], it is celebrated as the "Trayī" (the Threefold Veda). || 12-5 ||
Although it is threefold due to the difference in its functions, it is proclaimed as fourfold:
namely, the Ṛks, the Yajus, the Sāmans, and likewise the Atharvāṅgirases.
Because the Cāturhotra is primary, the triad beginning with the Ṛk constitutes the Trayī;
this is the reason for the separate treatment of the Atharvaṇas.
The form of the Atharvāṅgirases consists entirely of Ṛk and Yajus. (12.7)
Nevertheless, because of the predominance of pacification (śānti) and malevolent rites (abhicāra), they are treated separately.
Regarding the number of branches (śākhā) of the Ṛgveda and the others, it is proclaimed that the Ṛgveda consists of twenty-one branches.
There are one hundred and one branches of the Yajus, which follow a single path;
there are a thousand branches of the Sāmans, and five branches of the Atharvans.
Only these many Vedas possess direct perceptibility.
Only these many are recorded as directly perceived by the great seers;
they are constantly remembered by the sages who have received permission from Maheśvara.
The obligatory duties of these [Vedas] concern the study of their own essential forms;
they have six ancillaries (aṅgas), beginning with Kalpa:
Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Śikṣā, Nirukta, and Jyotiṣāṃ Gati. || 12-11 ||
The wise know that the six limbs [of the Veda] are phonology, ritual, grammar, etymology, metrics, and prosody;
Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya are the two subsidiary limbs, and these two consist of the Mīmāṃsā and the expansion of Nyāya. (12.12)
The conventions of those who know the Dharma and the purposes arising from Vedic declarations, as well as the continuous succession of refined conduct, whether codified or uncodified. (12–13)
The Dharmaśāstra is that which has been compiled from the inner hearts of the great sages;
the Upavedas and so forth, known as Itihāsa and Purāṇa, are proclaimed as the Upavedas. (12–14)
O Sage, the Vāstuveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Āyurveda—these five are proclaimed as the Upavedas. (12–15)
The science of government (daṇḍanīti) and the science of livelihood (vārtā)—these two are the supreme branches of knowledge;
they are proclaimed to have twenty-one divisions along with their various sub-classifications.
Prior to the seer Vācyāyana and before the emergence of Viṣṇu’s speech, this much variety of differentiation was manifested through the creative resolve in the form of the three Vedas.
A Description of the Nature of Sāṃkhya: Listen to me in its entirety regarding that very form of Sāṃkhya which was previously proclaimed by the Vaiṣṇava sage Kapila as his own resolve. (12.18)
O Great Sage, the Tantra known as Sāṃkhya is traditionally said to have sixty divisions;
in brief, there are two mandalas, namely the Prākṛta and the Vaikṛta. (12-19)
Description of the Prākṛta Maṇḍala:
Therein, the Prākṛta Maṇḍala is held to have thirty-two divisions;
among them, the first is the Brahmatantra, while the second is marked by Puruṣa.
Then there are three other tantras: those of Power (śakti), Necessity (niyati), and Time (kāla).
Next are the three tantras of the Qualities (guṇa), and then the tantra preceded by the Imperishable (akṣara). || 12-21 ||
Then there is another, the Prāṇatantra, and yet another, the Kartṛtantra;
then another, the Sāmitantra, and the five Jñānatantras. (12.22)
There are five Kriyātantras, five Mātrātantras, and five Bhūtatantras; these are the thirty-two divisions.
The natural (*prākṛta*) maṇḍala has been described; now hear of the modified (*vaikṛta*) maṇḍala.
That modified maṇḍala is known to have twenty-eight divisions; such is the description of the modified maṇḍala. (12.24)
First, there are five sections on duties (kṛtyakāṇḍa), followed by another section on enjoyments (bhogakāṇḍa);
likewise, there is one section on conduct (vṛttakāṇḍa), and five sections on afflictions (kleśakāṇḍa).
There are three sections on the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), followed by the section on manifestation (khyāti);
then there is the single section on dharma, preceded by that on dispassion (vairāgya). || 12-26 ||
p. 108) Now follows the section on sovereignty (aiśvarya-kāṇḍa), and after that the section on qualities (guṇa-kāṇḍa);
then there is the single section on the marks (liṅga-kāṇḍa), and after that the section on vision (dṛṣṭi-kāṇḍa). || 12-27 ||

The section on what is heard (ānuśravika), the section on suffering (duḥkha) following that, then the single section on accomplishment (siddhi), and the section designated as "the dyed robe" (kāṣāya). || 12-28 ||
Likewise, there is the Samayakāṇḍa and, after that, the Mokṣakāṇḍa;
thus, that Vikṛtimaṇḍala consists of twenty-eight divisions.
O Sage, there are sixty systems, and each of these is of various kinds;
this Sāṃkhya system of sixty topics is the beautiful vision of Hari.
From the omniscient great sage, the supreme rishi, there emerged the great instruction on yoga, which is the very nature of the science of yoga and the embodiment of Viṣṇu’s resolve. (12.31)
Listen now to these divisions that have arisen from Hiraṇyagarbha:
at the beginning, two Yoga-saṃhitās were spoken by Hiraṇyagarbha; thus there are two Yoga-saṃhitās. (12.32)
One is called Nirodhayoga, and the other is named Karmayoga;
thus the Saṃhitā known as Nirodha is remembered there as being twelvefold. (12.33)
First is the *aṅgatantra*, then the *doṣatantra*;
next is the tantra called *upasarga*, and finally the *adhiṣṭhānaka*. (12.34)
The foundational tantra and the yoga [tantra], which possess the authority over external principles;
the tantra known as the "Empty Yoga" and that very one known as the "Full Yoga. (12.35)
The three known as Siddhi and Yoga, and beyond that the Mokṣatantra;
thus, these twelve divisions are proclaimed to belong to the Nirodha [Tantra]. (12.36)
Regarding the fourfold nature of the *karmasaṃhitās*, Brahmā declared therein: "There are four *karmasaṃhitās*;
one consists of various rites, while another consists of ritual actions. (12.37)
Both are considered to be of two kinds, according to their external and internal forms;
thus the treatise on the instruction of yoga has sixteen divisions.
That which consists of the Sudarśana was proclaimed by Viṣṇu to Prajāpati;
it is the Tantra named Pāśupata, which describes the true nature of Paśupati and effects the liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu). || 12-39 ||
This unsurpassed tantra, which has issued from my mouth and is the manifestation of Viṣṇu’s resolve,
is proclaimed by me as the *Aṣṭakāṇḍa*, the eight-sectioned [treatise] of the Pāśupata.
Now, the first section is that of the husband (patikāṇḍa), followed by the section of the animal (paśukāṇḍa);
the third is declared to be the section of the noose (pāśakāṇḍa), according to its fivefold division. || 12-41 ||
The *Śuddhacaryā* and the *Miśra* are proclaimed as two sections (*kāṇḍa*). Then follows the sixth section, the *Devakāṇḍa*, and after that, the *Dīkṣākāṇḍa*. (12.42)
The eighth is declared to be the great Pāśupata section concerning union (sāyujya).
This scripture of eight sections consists of the Sudarśana of Hari.
O great sage, the divine Pāśupata scripture was spoken by me alone;
that which describes the nature of the Pañcarātra is the expansion of Viṣṇu’s Sāttvata doctrine known as Saudarśana. (12.44)
Its division is proclaimed in brief as being tenfold:
the Bhagavat-saṃhitā is the first, and likewise there is another, the Karma-saṃhitā.
The third is that consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya), and the fourth is the Kālasaṃhitā;
another is the Kartavyasaṃhitā, and the sixth is indeed the Vaiśeṣikī-kriyā.
In that context, the seventh is declared to be worshipful when conjoined with self-restraint;
the eighth is concerned with reflection, and the ninth is conjoined with the path.
The pure tenth [chapter], the Sāttvatī, which is connected with liberation, is sung;
thus far has this eternal Sāttvata scripture appeared from the Sanātana.
O Sage, these five treatises are indeed the fundamental sources;
in age after age, they are divided by those impelled by the will of Viṣṇu.
Those various Saṃhitās of the three Vedas and others, which are designated after their respective authors, become localized and cease to exist in accordance with the period of decline. (12.50)
Indeed, the cause for the emergence of pseudo-scriptures is solely the intention of the malevolent to delude others;
these pseudo-scriptures proceed from the mouths of gods and Brahmanical sages. (12.51)

This conclusion of the matter has been stated by me, O Sage: this supreme and divine array of the two means of knowledge, according to the distinction between word and meaning, is that of Sudarśana. (12.52)
Prāṇa, Māyā, Kriyā, Śakti, Bhāva, Unmeṣa, Udyama, Sudarśana, and Saṃkalpa— these are the synonymous terms that denote [the same reality]. (12.53)
The culmination of all five scriptures lies in the Blessed One;
indeed, the culmination of these five paths of scripture is one alone:
the scripture named Sudarśana, and its meaning is the imperishable Viṣṇu.
O Great Sage, this manifestation of Viṣṇu in the form of Sudarśana has been briefly described according to the authoritative scriptures. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Specific Nature of the Array of Means of Knowledge Consisting of Sound," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the glorious *Pāñcarātra*. 12.
From the beginning, verse 738:
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Object of Valid Cognition" (*pramāṇārthanirūpaṇa*).
A question concerning the object of valid cognition.
Nārada said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Lord of the Maruts;
salutations to you, the husband of Bhavānī; salutations to you, whose banner bears the bull. 13.1
I have comprehended the meanings arising from the lotus of your mouth, as well as the reason why you are the support of the worlds and that which constitutes the very essence of the worlds. (13.2)
O Śaṅkara, that which is the threefold authority for the worlds has been determined; you should now tell me the purpose of that authority.
And whatever, of what kind, and to what extent this object of valid cognition is held to be—
Ahirbudhnya declares his promise to provide an answer to that:
Listen, Nārada, to the supreme meaning of the authoritative means according to its true nature.
That which has its root in the resolve of Viṣṇu expands in many ways.
The virtuous have declared that *mā* is the act of measuring, and *pramā* is defined as excellent *mā*. (13.5)

(113) Furthermore, this excellence of cognition consists in its being a determination that accords with reality. That which is the most effective means for establishing a cognition is designated as "pramāṇa" (valid means of knowledge). 13-6.

The nature of the object of valid cognition is that which is sought by means of valid cognition; it is called the "object of valid cognition" because it is that which is ultimately beneficial for a person in all places and at all times. (13.7)

In this context, that which is intended as the object of valid cognition is established as being twofold: it consists of the beneficial and the means [to achieve it]. Listen now to the true nature of these two. (13.8)
The nature of welfare is that eternal happiness characterized by the absolute cessation of a person's succession of suffering; that is remembered as welfare. (13.9)
That which attains the status of a means by being invariably related to it is called "the means to welfare" (hitasādhana) by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta. (13.10)
The true nature of what is beneficial consists in that which is one's own essential nature; that which is beneficial for the person is declared to be happiness.
That state of being identical with the Blessed One is his "Bhagavattā," which is also known by another name.
(114) The twofold nature of the means [to liberation]: that which is the ultimate means for this [liberation] is established in two ways.
One way is knowledge (*jñāna*), while the other way is merit (*dharma*). (13.12)
The relationship between these two is that of cause and effect; indeed, the relationship of cause and effect is traditionally taught for these two modes.
This constitutes the twofold nature of knowledge.
But knowledge therein has a cause, and that is established in two ways.
One is said to consist of direct realization, while the other is indirect;
between these two as well, the relationship of cause and effect is established, and this state of being both cause and effect is described for both. (13–14)
That which is indirect because it possesses a cause is called the "cause" (hetu).
The fact that actions are the cause of knowledge is the quality (dharma) of these two types of knowledge; that is what is proclaimed as the "cause. (13–15)
When that which is to be accomplished is perceptible, it is a direct cause; when it is imperceptible, it is a cause by way of that [perceptible result].
Those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the treatises on reality have observed a twofold division of actions, and for this [cause] as well, two types are seen. (13–16)
One [form] consists of direct worship, while the other is through mediation.
That supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord endowed with power, is the infinite nature of mediated action. (13–17)
That which is known as Nārāyaṇa is eternal, possesses the six attributes, and is imperishable; Brahmā and all others down to the immovable objects are his manifestations. (13–18)

Intermingled with the threefold meditation and manifested through that Sudarśana, that prosperity which was previously described by me as arising from a ten-millionth part of Śakti—[is now fully revealed]. (13-19)
From a mere fraction of that [splendor], Brahmā and the other gods were manifested through the expansion of Viṣṇu’s volition;
indeed, [this is attained] by men who are free from desire, through the gateway of this manifestation.
That which is performed as an offering to Brahman is dharma characterized by mediation;
the supreme Brahman, possessed of glory, is the very nature of unmediated dharma itself, existing without mediation. (13-21)

That by which the yogin is gratified is held to be Dharma itself. The entire teaching of the Sāttvatas, which is the Pāñcarātra, is directly devoted to that Dharma and serves as its means of realization. (13.22)
Regarding the Veda together with its ancillaries (*śiraska*), that which is the prior portion of the triple Veda has become subservient to the purpose of the subsequent portion;
it is that [prior portion] which defines the dharma for those free from desire. (13.23)
(116) The Pāśupata [system] is devoted to the dharma that has the single manifestation as its object:
"The dharma residing in the single manifestation is remembered by me in the Pāśupata;
it is constantly accomplished for the sake of pleasing Brahmā by men through fierce vows. (13.24)
That which is both direct and indirect, resulting in indirect knowledge, is the means to liberation;
that indirect knowledge is called *prasaṃkhyāna*, and it is contemplated by the Sāṃkhya. (13.25)
The Vedāntas result in immediate, direct knowledge when preceded by devotion and faith, along with the internal auxiliary means such as tranquility;
thus, the direct realization of Brahman is brought about through the Upaniṣads. (13.26)

Yoga, as defined in the *Yogānuśāsana*, consists of the restraint of the modifications of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*) and has as its primary goal the limbs of yoga, such as *yama*, which lead to direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*); it possesses a collection of limbs known as the external (*bahiranga*) and internal (*antaranga*). (13.27)
Through constant practice, dispassion, and devotion to the Supreme Lord, it bestows the pure liberation known as the perfected manifestation of direct realization. (13.28)
In all cases, every teaching is presented according to the relationship of primary and secondary importance;
thus, the knowledge of reality as it has been described, accompanied by various methods of reasoning, and the manifold nature of Dharma—all of this is explained by all [the scriptures]. (13.29)
An explanation of the underlying intention behind the teaching in the treatises of various other means for achieving various other results: (p.
117) "For the purpose of thinning out the evils of people who are engaged in what is beneficial..."
It is like the instruction on Ayurveda for those motivated by attachment and aversion. || 13-30 ||
For the sake of attaining various forms of fruits, dharmas differentiated by various observances are prescribed by the scriptures; likewise, cognitions are of various forms. (13.31)
The presentation of the two worldly human goals (puruṣārtha):
Thus, those two human goals have been described in detail;
now, another pair of worldly human goals is described by the scriptures. (13.32)
Of these two, *kāma* (desire) is traditionally said to be that which arises from sense objects;
*artha* (wealth) consists of the fruits arising from the acquisition of cattle, land, gold, and so forth. (13.33)
The discernment of the mutual relationship between the means and the ends within the three aims of life is as follows:
wealth is the means for dharma and for kāma, and likewise, it is also the means for artha;
dharma is the means for dharma and for kāma, and likewise, it is also the means for artha.
Desire is the means for achieving dharma and likewise for artha;
artha and kāma are everywhere means for achieving [their respective ends] through deviation.
Dharma is invariably the means for accomplishing everything that is to be accomplished;
these three together are declared by the wise to be the "trivarga" (the three aims of life). || 13-36 ||
(p. 118) Liberation is always that which is to be accomplished, and liberation itself is indeed an object to be accomplished; thus, there are four goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
This concludes the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*).
The science of government (daṇḍanīti), together with the four Vedas and their auxiliary branches, constitutes that [Vārttā]. || 13.37 ||
That which is designated by the learned as a means of valid knowledge for the attainment of wealth and pleasure—
namely, the subsidiary Veda (Upaveda) known as Itihāsa-Purāṇa— is indeed that which acts as an auxiliary to the knowledge of reality derived from the Itihāsas and other sources. (13.38)
He attains the state of being an auxiliary to the scriptures for the sake of knowing reality; thus, the fourfold aim of human life has been briefly described to you. (13.39)
Regarding the internal means for dharma and the other goals:
"O Nārada, listen to its internal means.
Unfeigned and unadorned compassion is the means for dharma. (13.40)
The cause for the arising of an object is its presentation at the proper place and time;
the cause of desire is intention that is sincere and unadorned. (13.41)
But the cause for liberation is the renunciation of everything, preceded by knowledge.
For those [other means], external instruments such as dharma and the like are appropriate; indeed, dharma is said to have external instruments. (13.42)

The external means for the attainment of an object consist of considerations such as the application of the *tantra* method; in the case of desire, the taking of hands [in marriage] and so forth is declared by the wise to be an external limb. (13.43)
The performance of duty without desire and so forth is the external means for liberation;
this fourfold aim of human life is the manifestation of worldly existence.
Volition is indeed Vaiṣṇava; it is said to be the cause of its manifestation.
This concludes the meaning of the chapter. Thus, the entire supreme course of the authoritative scriptures has been declared to you.
Along with its means and its modes—what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Meaning of Authority," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra. 13.
Chapter Fourteen, titled "Description of the Causes of the Soul's Transmigration and the Method for Its Liberation," beginning from verse 783.
Therein, first, Nārada asks again concerning the subject of liberation:
"To Him whose brilliance from the eye on His forehead burns away the darkness of ignorance..."
Salutations to you, O enemy of Tripura; salutations to you, O adversary of Antaka.
All human goals have been heard of, categorized as primary, secondary, or alternative;
among them, the primary human goal is heard of as that which is designated by the term "liberation. (14.2)
And liberation consisting of the nature of the Blessed One was proclaimed by the Enemy of Tripura;
and its direct means of accomplishment, which is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), exists in two ways. (14.3)
And its means of accomplishment is said to be dharma free from ulterior motives;
