O Moon-crested One, explain that liberation further in detail.
Tell me both that from which liberation comes and that which constitutes liberation;
for I ought not to ask anyone other than you, the all-knowing one.
A Brief Summary of the Nature of the Jīva: Ahirbudhnya says—
The Person (Puruṣa) is beginningless, indivisible, and composed of consciousness and bliss.
O Blessed One, this [world] is indeed composed of you; it is always permeated by your being. (14.6)

Regarding the individual soul's status as a minute fraction of a portion of the Lord’s power: "That power which is the Great Being (mahāsattā) is the attribute-bearer of Viṣṇu; from a billionth part of that [power], two powers of yours are said to have arisen. (14.7)
"Existence" and "action" are designated as the object to be produced and the producer;
that existence is made to move by action, just as a flame is stirred by the wind. (14.8)
The manifestation of *bhūti* was previously described as possessing various divisions;
it is twofold according to purity and impurity, and that which is pure has been declared in many ways.
The other power, consisting of time, is the male (puṃśakti); he is declared to be the Puruṣa.
Because of his subjection to time, he attains saṃsāra; abiding in the transformations of the power of time, he certainly wanders in transmigration. || 14-10 ||
Through the completion of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there is the manifestation of one's true nature; having attained this scriptural path, one is born by means of oneself.
Regarding this, however, there is a further question:
Nārada: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Śaṅkara, destroyer of Tripura!
Residing within the transformations of the power of Time, how does that eternal being transmigrate?
Or, having attained the means, how is the person born by his own [power]? (14.12)
Ahirbudhnya states that the Lord’s sovereignty is not subject to questioning:
"That divine sovereignty of the Lord is not to be questioned by anyone."
Even though he has attained all desires, the self-controlled one sports like a king.
The fivefold division of the Blessed One’s resolve:
that which is called his resolve is named Sudarśana;
although it possesses infinite forms, it manifests in five ways. (14–14)

By means of the functions of creation, maintenance, and destruction, which consist of restraint and grace, the power of restraint causes the concealment of the individual soul's form and other attributes; that power of concealment is designated as "restraint" (nigraha). (14–15)
She herself causes the male being known as the *jīva* to become concealed by means of her activity that conceals form, sovereignty, and discernment.
Synonyms for that which conceals are *māyā*, *avidyā*, *mahāmoha*, and *mahātāmisra*; furthermore, *tamas*, *bandha*, and *hṛdgranthi* are also synonymous terms. (14–17)
Due to the concealment of its form, the soul's atomicity and other qualities are asserted; (p.
123) due to the concealment of its sovereignty, its powerlessness is traditionally taught. (14.18)
The ignorance of the person is declared to arise from the contraction of consciousness;
the person is veiled by the power (śakti) which consists of the volition of Viṣṇu.
It is called "atomic" (aṇu), "doing little" (kiṃcitkara), and "knowing little" (kiṃcijjña).
Due to its atomicity and other qualities, it is known as impurity (mala) and bondage (bandha); thus, these three are declared by the wise to be the threefold impurity and the threefold bondage.
Through ignorance and the other [afflictions], there is an increase of impurity;
thus, for one who has come under bondage by the power of concealment belonging to Viṣṇu, ignorance, egoism, attachment, and the rest accumulate that impurity. (14–21)
Afflicted by such defilements as ignorance and the rest, which torment those who desire the attainment of the pleasant and the avoidance of the unpleasant,
he is driven by the impulses of seeking and rejecting, failing to follow the traditional scriptures.

Eager for the attainment of desired objects and the removal of the undesired, the one possessed by desire performs that action which results in the arising of auspicious or inauspicious fruits. (14.23)
Through the power of karma, there is the attainment of birth, lifespan, and experience;
therefore, abiding in the ripening of karma, impelled by destiny, he undergoes births, lifespans, and their consequences, which are mixed with the auspicious and the inauspicious. (14.24)
It gradually accumulates various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as pleasure and so forth;
this is the succession of concealments of the power of restraint. (14-25)
In the process of concealment, there are two auxiliary causes called Time (kāla) and Power (śakti), which follow after the manifestation [of the soul].
Through these two, the [power] consisting of restraint brings about the concealment of the person (puruṣa). (14.26)
The creation and other processes are rooted in accumulated karma;
however, by means of this power, the unborn [Lord] possesses three powers of creation and so forth, which proceed through those various powerful accumulated karmas. (14.27)
The bondage accompanied by its cause is beginningless; this bondage is declared to be beginningless, while the cause of bondage possesses a beginning.
[Yet] there is the manifestation of the Lord’s grace toward the bound soul.
Thus, while the wheel of saṃsāra revolves, beings are whirled about by their own karmas.
When a living being is overwhelmed by suffering, a certain grace of Viṣṇu arises;
for that grace is said to consist in the descent of the power of favor, which is the fifth power, having the nature of Viṣṇu’s volition. (14.29)
That supreme Vaiṣṇava power is indeed compassion, whose nature is grace;
that is called the descent of power (śaktipāta) by those established in the Āgamas of Viṣṇu.

(125) When the living being who is the object of compassion attains the equilibrium of karma, he is indeed accepted by Viṣṇu through His power consisting of grace, which takes the form of Sudarśana and consists of a rain of mercy. (14.31)
Beheld at that time by her whose form is a rain of compassion,
the individual soul (jīva), when gazed upon by Viṣṇu, indeed attains the equilibrium of karma.
That descent of power (śaktipāta) indeed delivers the living being from transmigratory existence;
for there, when the two karmas have become equal, they attain a state of silence.
The demonstration, with an illustration, of how actions are indifferent:
"Just as, when a traveler has departed with his belongings, those who were robbers—having ceased their efforts at plundering—remain indifferent, being equal [to others]. (14.34)
But at the moment of the descent of that power whose nature is grace, those two actions— the auspicious and the inauspicious— become equalized and remain indifferent.
The manner in which one desiring liberation attains the means to liberation:

Immediately after falling [from a higher state], the living being becomes intent upon the contemplation of liberation, possessing evolving dispassion and a deep inclination toward discernment. (14.36)
Having reflected upon the scriptures and having also approached the gurus,
he became awakened by means of those various types of beings he encountered, thereby protecting his realization.
Wearing away ignorance through the awakening of the Guru, and likewise wearing away the afflictions and other obstacles;
discerning the essence from all sides and accumulating supreme wisdom. (14.38)
Absorbed in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, himself devoted to virtuous deeds,
observing rigorous vows, he was a man of knowledge, steadfast in the wisdom of Vedānta.
By means of these well-determined paths, both collective and individual,
one attains the station of Viṣṇu after enduring great hardship.
For one who has attained knowledge, there is the attainment of liberation; having acquired an abundance of knowledge and purified his consciousness,
he shall enter that stainless, unafflicted state of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Causes of the Soul's Transmigration and the Method of its Liberation," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 824:
The fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Qualified Practitioner.
Madhusūdana, situated in the center of the wheel, is meditated upon by those who have mastered their selves.
May the Supreme One protect us from the pit of cyclic existence, which takes the form of a well.
The question concerning the qualified seeker:
Nārada said—
O God of gods, O Śaṅkara, whose banner is the bull, salutations be unto you!
Through your grace, I have heard this divine, secret, and supreme knowledge.
Tell me the remainder of my question, which you were previously asked by me:
namely, those four goals of human life (puruṣārtha) that have been declared as having all things as their support.
"Who indeed are those who have authority over them? Tell me that in detail.
In response to that, Ahirbudhnya first sets forth the Sāttvika method:
For those who were previously mentioned as the ones named Manu, whose wombs are knowledge—|| 15.3 ||
The humans born from him are divided into Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; likewise, there are those who are both human and non-human.
(128) From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the Brāhmaṇas and others emerged;
they are remembered as the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (15.5)
These two [systems] exercise authority over these [beings] as appropriate:
those born of the human lineage and those who have been previously mentioned as the five universally accepted Siddhāntas belonging to the Pāñcarātra. (15.6)
Among those born in the human lineage, it is the Sāttvatas who exercise authority there;
through their steadfast devotion to Him, they attain the Blessed One.
[The following is] the thirteenfold action joined with the qualities of restraint. (15.7)
Performing the five-fold duties, they go to Puruṣottama.
Among them, O Nārada, the system of the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) is ordained for the three social classes; indeed, the fourfold order of life is prescribed there for those three.
Whether he be a student (brahmacārī), a householder (gṛhastha), a forest-dweller (vanastha), or even a mendicant (bhikṣu)— by serving them, a Śūdra attains the Blessed One,
because through service to them, the Śūdra accomplishes the work of the Blessed One. (15.9)
Free from passion, anger, and greed, they gradually proceed to the abode of Hari;

even for those situated in any of the other stages of life, there is the attainment of liberation, for they are indeed pure performers of the sacrifice to the Supreme Brahman, devoted to their own sacred study. || 15.10 ||

(129) The Brahmins who do not sacrifice to others, who have been eligible [for initiation] since the beginning of creation, and who, while young, were properly nurtured by their mother and father prior to the dawn of [discriminative] knowledge; 15.11.
Endowed with the methods of the teachers, they were intent on service; they correctly knew the seven categories, remained established in their observances, and were composed in mind.
Endowed with knowledge of the primordial nature, free from negligence, having abandoned desires, firm-minded, pure, and with their senses restrained. || 15-13 ||
The Siddhas are highly fortunate, having reached the final certainty of knowledge;
through their intellect they have perfected all actions, and they are endowed with auspicious conduct.
Having established themselves in one of the four stages of life until their completion,
they performed the five-fold daily rites without interruption for a hundred years.
Having attained at the end of their karma that supreme and auspicious intellect born of discernment, their higher knowledge shines forth and all worldly exertion is shaken off. (15–16)
They enter Vāsudeva— the Lord of a thousand rays, the Master, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the stainless one, and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of all beings.
The state of the householder is that upon which the other stages of life depend.
One stage of life is that of the family man who maintains the sacred fires and possesses abundant wealth;
the other three are recorded as being without fires, pure, and devoted to vows and the like. (15–18)
Those three who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) indeed support their families; thus, O Sage, the Sāttvika style has been briefly described by you as the Sāttvika manner. (15.19)
Now begins the exposition of the systems beginning with the Trayī:
"In this way, listen today to another system from me in detail;
the authority for the Trayī and the others belongs to those born from the mouth, the arms, and the thighs."
For indeed, the four castes emerged from the mouth of Brahmā and the other [parts of his body]. || 15-20 ||
They correctly authorize the fourfold system beginning with the Trayī;
for those established in the Trayī, there is the attainment of results, and for those established in Sāṃkhya and the others, there is the gradual ascent to Pañcarātra.
Those established in the triple Veda alone attain success, as do those in the three systems beginning with Sāṃkhya.

By your will, even they who were devoted to the Pāśupata dharma— those who previously followed the Vedic religion (trayīdharma) and were established in the Pāśupata system— attained the supreme Sāttvata teaching as they ascended. (15–22)
O Sage, they do not practice the Dharma established in the three Vedas;
having entered the Pañcarātra, they do not extend any other Dharma.
For the Sāṃkhyas, there is liberation through non-action;
the Sāṃkhyas are traditionally defined as those who are free from action and are solely intent on thorough discernment. For those established in Yoga, there is the performance of Vedic rituals.
The yogi, endowed with the constant and occasional rites and possessing the limbs of yoga, [should practice] with desire.
One who is most devoted to Brahman should perform Vedic rites—both daily and occasional—for the sake of attaining what has not been attained and for the increase of what has been attained. (15.25)
This path, beginning with the three Vedas, has been revealed by Nārada.
Listen to my exposition of the castes and stages of life, their respective duties, and the classification of those castes and stages along with their dharmas. (15–26)
The four castes (varṇas)—
those which are designated as the four castes in the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—
among these, the first three possess the study of the Vedas and the status of being twice-born (dvijāti).
The three castes, having first become twice-born, should study [the Vedas].
The service of the twice-born is the duty of the Śūdra, and he possesses a single birth as the fourth caste; I have ordained that he shall serve those [other castes].
Sacrificing, teaching, and receiving gifts belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone.
The caste called Brāhmaṇa is the first, which emerged from the mouth of Brahmā.
He should teach these three—the Brāhmaṇa and the others—in their proper order;
and he should officiate at sacrifices for them as desired, for the sake of his livelihood, without malice. (15.29)
And one may accept [gifts] from three [castes]; this indeed is the specific rule.
Wielding weapons and so forth, as well as the constant study of the scriptures, are the distinguishing characteristics of the Kṣatriya caste. (15.30)
(132) Protection from injury and the preservation of subjects according to the scriptures;
agriculture and so forth are the specific occupations of the Vaiśya, namely: cultivation, cattle-rearing, and trade. (15.31)
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are equal for the three [castes];
however, for the twice-born, sacrificing, studying, and giving are likewise equal.
This is always for the sake of dharma alone; therein lies the avoidance of violence and other such acts. (15.32)
Service is the duty of a Śūdra, and service alone is his means of livelihood; indeed, service to a Brāhmaṇa is the highest duty, while the other [services] are recorded as inferior. (15.33)
The common duties for the four [classes] are non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, devotion to one's own wife, and compassion.
This dharma is prescribed in common for these four. (15.34)
The four stages of life (cāturāśramya) pertain to the highest Brāhmaṇas and the Kṣatriyas;
the four stages of life pertain to the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, but in no way to the Vaiśya.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there are only the first three stages of life.
And the first three [stages of life] are the fixed characteristic of dharma for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
p. 133) For those of the three [upper] castes, there is freedom of action prior to initiation;
before their second birth [initiation], they are twice-born but not bound by vows.
Initiation is their second birth.
The birth from the preceptor through the Sāvitrī is held to be the second, divine birth.
The third [birth] occurs during the initiation for sacrifice;
having attained their third birth during the initiation for sacrifice,
those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas attain equality with the gods.
The Brahmins, remaining at the Soma-pressings, [should perform their duties] at the end of each pressing in due order. || 15-37 ||

All those three gods, remaining devoted to their own sacred study (svādhyāya), are thus described as the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma). Having explained these castes (varṇas) to you, now hear from me concerning the stages of life (āśramas) as well. || 15-38 ||
The duties of the *upakurvāṇa* student:

Having obtained birth from a teacher, dwelling there constantly until the end [of his studies], performing his duties, being devoted to him, being faithful to him, and making him his supreme goal. (15.39)
Having reported all matters to him, he should go outside that family seeking alms;
and, with the remainder of his ritual duties, he should desire to study the Veda without haste for the sake of his preceptor and others. (15.40)
One should perform the twilight devotions outside, bathing daily and free from malice, restraining the senses and showing compassion toward all living beings. (15.41)
Kindling the fire with sacrificial fuel at both twilights with a concentrated mind, he remained established in the conventions of those who know the Dharma, practicing his own vow.
The twice-born man known as an *upakurvāṇaka* attains perfection in his private Vedic study;

having completed his period of student life (*brahmacarya*), he may, according to his desire, enter another stage of life (*āśrama*)—whether he has bathed after completing the Vedas (*vedasnāyin*) or bathed after completing the vows (*vratasnāyin*)—while giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to his teacher. (15.43)
Having obtained permission from his guru, he may desire one of the four stages of life.
If he desires the perpetual student's dharma, that student shall remain in his own stage of life as a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*).
One who desires knowledge should serve the teacher alone with discipline until the fall of the body; such a student shall obtain the supreme knowledge. 15.45
"Otherwise, there would be a loss of merit; such is the instruction of the Vedas.
Now, if he should desire to perform the duties of a householder, he should practice the supreme dharma of the household life. (15.46)
Having received permission from his guru and having bathed, he should duly take a wife;
together with her, he should constantly practice dharma, remaining devoted to the study of the Vedas. (15.47)
One who performs ancestral rites, speaks the truth, is always fond of guests, follows a humble mode of livelihood, is free from malice, and is not greedy— (15.48).
Observing the vows of a *snātaka* and devoted to the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*),

even a householder must necessarily follow the *Pāñcarātra* dharma, remaining constantly engaged in the five-fold ritual cycle (*pañcakāla*) and abiding in compassion, forbearance, and fortitude. (15.49)

Established in freedom from anger, truthfulness, modesty, knowledge, purity, non-stealing, and self-restraint; free from exertion and devoid of meanness, he delights in the auspicious rites prescribed by the scriptures. (15.50)
One should perform all sacrifices through mind or even through action;
for even a householder who acts without desire attains liberation by means of a intellect that is not struck by desire and is free from egoism and greed. (15.51)
Having attained the impossible through the two eyes of right reasoning and resolute effort,
he remains constant in the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites, devoted to the obligatory and occasional duties.
A householder of this kind, desiring knowledge, having attained the unsurpassed wisdom and having acquired the realization of the Vedānta, takes refuge in the station of Viṣṇu.
For a householder who possesses desire, there is attainment of the world of Brahmā;
being solely constant in dharma, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. [Now follow] the duties of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Or else, one may resort to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) even before the stage of the householder (gārhasthya).
When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, and sees the offspring of his offspring, he should then resort to the forest. (15.55)
Having abandoned village food and subsisting on forest fare, he should be devoted to sacrifice, offering oblations either into the external fire or into his own self. || 15.56 ||
Year after year, one should duly perform the three types of austerity.
Even for a forest-dweller who has renounced desires, there is the attainment of liberation by practicing the meanings of the scriptures with a mind unassailed by desire. (15.57)
Practicing various initiations while established in his vows and composed in mind,
he was pure through the restriction of his livelihood and possessed by the desire to know reality.
Having attained the knowledge of reality, he resorts to the station of Viṣṇu;
for him who possesses desire, there is the attainment of the world of Brahmā,
provided he remains constantly devoted to dharma and undertakes the Great Departure.
Free from sorrow and fear, the forest-dweller is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having obtained the saffron robe, one should adopt the duties of a renunciant from the very beginning by means of these two [methods]. || 15-60 ||
After [the completion of] both or one of these, he should subsequently undertake the life of a wandering mendicant,
having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee.

Having obtained permission from his guru, or being weary of ritual action, the observer of the great vow (mahāvratī) should consign the sacred fires into himself and enter the fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama). || 15.62 ||
Liberated from all defects and dispassionate toward sense objects,
he investigates the high and low states of this inner self.
Constantly investigating the subtle Supreme Self by means of the self, he should be ever devoted to higher discernment and intent upon the knowledge of Vedānta. (15.64)

Whether he is constantly established in meditative concentration or devoted to severe vows, even if one person were to cut off his arm with an axe while another anointed the other arm with sandalwood paste, [he would remain equanimous]. (15.65)
Without considering either hostility or affection toward both, the sage remains established in himself like the wind, like space, with a mind as steady as the earth. (15.66)
With a mind moist like water, he is ever pure like fire;
unshakeable like a pool in the Ganges, his appearance is like that of an empty house.

Having contemplated all objects with his intellect, having abandoned all possessions through his intellect, having accepted the true scriptures through his intellect, he is satisfied by that perfectly pure intellect. (15.68)
The yogi who has granted fearlessness to all is likewise granted fearlessness by all;
seated in yoga after his private recitation, he should contemplate that recitation through yoga.
He did not say anything to anyone, even when the time for speaking had arrived;
he remained always equal toward all beings, like a mother and like a father.
Having become serene within himself, finding his own light and delighting in the Self, he has ascended the palace of wisdom and is liberated from all people. (15.71)
Like one standing on a mountain peak watching all those situated on the ground below, he was called "mute" by some and desired as "steadfast" by others. (15.72)
By some he was called "Who indeed? and by others he was addressed as "The Terrible One";
he is always embraced by equanimity, compassion, loving-kindness, and sympathetic joy.
Constantly surrounded by the attendants of discrimination, awakening, and contentment, subsisting on alms and filled with satisfaction, he is endowed with such virtues as these. (15.74)
For the renunciant, liberation is attained through the worship of the Supreme Person;
like a lamp with its flame extinguished, the wandering mendicant established in meditation reaches the state of Viṣṇu upon the destruction of the bodily impressions. (15.75)
This is the conclusion of the chapter's subject matter:
those duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life, endowed with their common and specific characteristics, have been declared to you in brief. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Qualified Disciple," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Sixteen: An Exposition on the Origin of the Nine Hundred Letters from the Beginning;
A Question Concerning Protection and Its Authorities.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, omniscient one whose banner is the bull!
We have heard the meaning of the means of valid cognition, along with its reasons and its exceptions. (16.1)
And what is the protection for all this, and who holds the authority over its protection?
O Blessed One, you should explain this pair of opposites in its various forms.
The commencement of the reply by Ahirbudhnya:
"The protection consisting of the Sudarśana belongs to the Lord Harimedhas."
Except for one's own resolve upon Viṣṇu, no other protection is ordained. (16.3)

That divine power of action, which consists of the capacity residing in the object and whose nature is Sudarśana, is the goddess named Sudarśanā; she arises from a portion of Viṣṇu’s power and performs all the tasks of the Lord. (16.4)

Know that all capacity arising from every category of object—whether of the principles (tattvas) or of their constituent elements (tāttvikas), and whether sentient or insentient—is composed of that [consciousness]. (16.5)
(140) Of the various means of valid cognition, of the pair of existence and non-existence, and of dharma, artha, kāma, liberation, and the three bonds. || 16-6 ||
Whatever possesses the capacity for its own specific function, that is the form of the Sudarśana;
having described the protective efficacy of the array of scriptures and weapons, [it is said that] those scriptures and weapons are the transformations of Viṣṇu’s volition.
By means of which the Lord of the World, Janārdana, descending or entering at the proper times, lightens the earth through [the manifestation of] living beings.
Even a mere fragment of mantra serves as a means for protection;
it consists of various mantras, is adorned with a treasury of yantras, arises from both the Vedas and the Tantras, and abounds in manifold productions. (16.9)

The supreme power of action of Viṣṇu himself, consisting of pure consciousness, resides in the protection composed of mantra. Only a Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all principles and is proficient in all branches of knowledge possesses the authority for this. (16.10)

One who is constant in non-spilling [of semen], observant of both obligatory and occasional rites, honored by those of pure lineage, pure in three respects, free from the three doubts, and one who has reached the further shore of the rules for the six duties. || 16.11 ||
A Brahmin who abides in the womb of Brahman, who is devoted to his own wife and is pure,
may undertake the supreme power of action consisting of the mantra of Viṣṇu.
Even for a Brāhmaṇa, there is an incapacity to provide protection when he is not supported by the king: "A Brāhmaṇa who is not supported by [the king] does not deserve to perform his duty here;
but having obtained the support of the king, he may act for the sake of the world. (16.13)
Praise of the King:
For the king is indeed the supreme being, the all-pervading one who embodies all the gods;
he is the locus of the power of action (kriyāśakti) and is composed of the essence of Viṣṇu. || 16.14 ||
For in ancient times, the Lord God created the king from his head;
therefore, he is consecrated on the head (mūrdhābhiṣikta) and stands above all beings. || 16-15 ||
The Brāhmaṇa is proclaimed in the Vedas and Śāstras as twice as venerable as the king.
He who, out of delusion, hates those who hate the king incurs sin both in this world and the next; that evil-minded person, by hating them, hates Hari himself. (16–16)
That man who, out of delusion, hates Hari, hates Lakṣmī;
but the evil-minded hater of Lakṣmī falls away from all dharmas. (16–17)
Fallen from all the worlds and excluded from the company of all the gods,
he remains for eternal ages in a bottomless, blinding darkness.
Therefore, a king of noble intellect who desires to attain prosperity in this world and the next must certainly hold the king in high esteem;
he should revere the king as the presiding deity of all the worlds. (16–19)
(142) The instability of fortune when residing in either a Brahmin or a king alone is as follows: Fortune does not dwell in a Brahmin alone because of his extreme gentleness;
fearing his excessive ferocity, she does not desire to abide in a Kshatriya alone. (16.20)
When those two, the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya, are united with Fortune (Lakṣmī), who is of the nature of Agni and Soma,
she dwells there with great delight, like one seeking coolness in a lake during the summer heat. || 16-21 ||
In this regard, the reason is as follows:
those two splendors, acting in conjunction, sustain the stability of the world;
for within them resides the entire power of Viṣṇu, which is of the nature of action. (16–22)
The illustration for this is stated through positive and negative concomitance:
"For just as the stream of a great river is not capable of being held by a small embankment, so too a weak man is not at all capable of sustaining the power of action. (16.23)
Just as a wise man receives a great vessel from the further shore to the near shore, so does the Kṣatriya, when conjoined with Brahman, receive the power of action. || 16-24 ||
A great lake, though being filled by a mighty river, may burst its banks; yet even so, a single [sense] cannot be satisfied by that [river]. (16.25)
An explanation of how even the power of action employed for the sake of the king is beneficial to all subjects, as follows:
"Just as in a great river flowing toward the ocean, it is certain..."
By means of that moisture, other lakes are filled to a great extent. (16-26)
When the power of action is applied, the wheel of the universal monarch indeed turns; for all subjects established upon that wheel prosper accordingly with prosperity.
The gradation of authority regarding the power of action for the universal monarch and others is as follows:
the universal monarch (cakravartin) presides over the first [power], the regional lord (maṇḍaleśvara) over the second, and the local ruler (viṣayeśvara) over the third power of action. (16.28)
Whether he be a high minister or a twice-born, he who protects many subjects—no single man alone could accomplish this for a single individual. (16.29)
The commencement of the exposition on the nature of the power of action (kriyāśakti):
The authority over action and its power has been demonstrated;
now, listen as I describe its true form exactly as it is. (16.30)
In general, the power of Viṣṇu is of two kinds; it is the supreme unfolding (unmeṣa) of power, which exists as a billionth part of a billionth [of his essence].
It is established as twofold through the distinction between the object to be manifested (bhāvya) and the manifestor (bhāvaka). || 16-31 ||
The practitioner is one whose resolve is fixed on Viṣṇu, and his other name is Sudarśana;
these are synonyms for Śakti—this very Goddess is called Kriyāśakti, Sāmarthya, and Yoga as well. (16-32)
(144) By such words as "the state of the Supreme Lord," "great splendor," and "the yoga of Māyā," that volition which possesses the capacity for various modes is designated. (16-33)
The agent of manifestation is the initiator of the portion of existence; that which is called "the object to be manifested" (bhāvya) is celebrated as "existence" (bhūti).
It has already been demonstrated previously that this [existence] consists of both purity and impurity. (16.34)
Like the flame of a fire, she is extended by his volition;
the god Nārāyaṇa is one, and she follows his state of being. (16.35)
Listen to the state of that Goddess, the power of action (kriyāśakti), which consists of mantra: as the power of action arises, she assumes the nature of sound (nāda). || 16-36 ||
The sound is similar to the resonance of a long-bell;
know that supreme sound to be like the resonance of a long bell.
Its object of perception is accessible only to yogins.
That [reality] is directly realized by the supreme yogis within their own hearts.
In some cases, through its manifestation, it assumes the form of a *bindu*;
like a bubble in the ocean, it attains manifestation in certain instances. Furthermore, because it moves with rapid strides, it is called *bindu* by yogis. (16.38)
(p. 145) The *bindu* is twofold by way of its nature as *nāma* and *nāmi*; that *bindu* is divided into two according to the essential form of *nāma* and *nāmi*. *Nāma* is the *śabdabrahman*.
There, having attained its manifestation as name, the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) proceeds.
Having attained the state of being the manifestation of the *nāmin* (the name-bearer), the previously mentioned *bhūti* (manifestation) proceeds toward the arising of the *nāman*.
This is the beginning of the exposition on the production of phonemes (*varṇa*).
O Sage, now hear from me this path of mantras, which is the source of my renown.
For that power, consisting of the Bindu, has assumed various names by its own will;
though it is without letters, it was previously of a single nature, consisting of the Absolute (Anuttara).
The *bindu* is twofold, distinguished by the division into vowels and consonants; it is established in these two ways.
Now hear further in detail about this power of the *bindu*.

This supreme [power], known as emission (visṛṣṭi), consisting of the creation of sound, arises; it possesses manifold meanings through its unity and multiplicity, and undergoes transformation through various phonemes. (16.43)
She is the manifest embodiment of the moon itself, the verbal body of Lakṣmī;
she undergoes transformation in the form of vowels and consonants.
p. 146) Its manifestation as the essence of the letter *a*—that is, the manifestation of *a* and so forth—is proclaimed as the Absolute (*anuttara*).
This is because the letter *a* possesses the nature of all speech.
All speech is indeed this one [Self] alone, appearing with the various distinctions of those respective forms.
The manifestation [of consciousness] occurs through the nature of the vowels *bindu*, *ī*, and *u*;
it is known as *icchan* when clearly manifesting, and as *unmiṣan* (emerging) when [manifested] as *u*.
Thus, these three aforementioned phonemes possess the capacity to manifest all vowels.
These three phonemes alone are the manifestation of all sounds. || 16-46 ||
The attainment of length for those [vowels] is supreme; that Ānanda attains the state of *ā*.
By his own will, that Īśāna attains the state of *ī*. (16-47)
The vowel *u*, opening slightly and possessing a deficient form, attains the state of *ū*.
The production of *e* and *o* occurs from the conjunction with the unsurpassed Will (*icchā*); thus, that which is called *ai* is born. (16.48)
From the unsurpassed state, one further attains the state of non-existence;
from the unsurpassed unfolding of the divine, that which is called the syllable *Oṃ* is born. (16.49)
From the unsurpassed state, it further attains the state of non-existence;
these four peaks (kūṭa), whose nature is the twilight (saṃdhyā), are declared to be the diphthongs (saṃdhyakṣara). (16.50)
The explanation of the meaning of their individual components is as follows:
through union with the desire for the unsurpassed (*anuttarecchā*), he is remembered as *E* (the Increaser);
furthermore, through union with the unsurpassed, he is also remembered as *Ai*, the possessor of sovereignty (*aiśvaryavān*). || 16-51 ||
From this unsurpassed divine unfolding, the syllable *o* is everywhere remembered;
having arisen from that unsurpassed state, it has attained the state of *au* through its sovereign power. (16.52)
Regarding the origin of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*:
through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the first and third parts of *ar* and *al*, the wise have declared that *ṛ* arises;
likewise, from *a* and *l*, the nature of *ḷ* arises, while the vowel *ā* is supreme. (16.53)
Furthermore, she is likewise remembered as "Leaping" due to her unsurpassed exertion;
thus, through fourteen types of exertion, she manifests in various forms. (16.54)
Like an actress, the primordial Kuṇḍalinī energy of Viṣṇu unfolds;
her two subtle forms are the cause of creation and dissolution. (16.55)
The Great Being is inexpressible; that power of action, gradually evolving through the nature of sound, first attains the state of creation.

(148) By such terms as *sṛṣṭiḥ*, *sargaḥ*, *visargaḥ*, and *visarjanam*, [the state] at the navel of Kuṇḍalī is called *paśyantī*. Rising from the *mūlādhāra*, she is *śāntā* (tranquil) and *nirañjanā* (stainless). 16-57.
Being polished by various refinements with ointments, it attains the nature of both the seer and the seen, and turns away from being merely the referent of words. (16.58)
That which is called Paśyantī resides in the navel; it has attained the emergence of the vision of Yoga.
It is indeed the Vaiṣṇava power (śakti), the existence (sattā), the mother of mantras, and the one who bestows grace. (16.59)
Having reached that state through their intellect, yogis attain the exhaustion of all karmic entitlements.
Within the lotus of her heart, there is an expansion;
she is the splendor on the verge of blossoming, the perceiving power (paśyantī) consisting of action.
Having been refined by the formative forces (saṃskāras) and having attained the transformation known as "capacity," she expands within the lotus of the heart, humming like a female bee.
When [the power] has become liquefied through the relationship of signifier and signified, consisting of action,
then all grammatical refinements (saṃskṛtayaḥ) residing in the signified nourish the Smṛtis.
In the region of her throat, there occurs a transformation into the nature of the *visarga*;

such is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which, according to the desire to express various objects of denotation, assumes the form of sound, though it is fundamentally immutable and devoid of manifestation. (16.63)
Touched by the Unsurpassed (Anuttara), that power which emits emission (visargiṇī) goes to the throat; then, abiding again in the Unsurpassed, it manifests as the fourteen [vowels]. (16.64)
She proceeds higher and higher until she reaches the throat; this is the manifestation of the *hetu*.
Then, having become composed of the *sādi*, she is endowed with the consonants of the beloved. (16.65)
Consisting of the unsurpassed, it further becomes firmly established in the *bindu*.
The *bindu* is said to be withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), while the emission (*visarga*) is called creation (*sṛṣṭi*). (16.66)
These two processes of creation and dissolution have been briefly illustrated to you;
O Sage, hear from me further concerning the various series of vowels.
An examination of the internal subdivisions of the vowels:
That triad of primary vowels previously described as the foundation of the vowels is held by yogis to be eighteenfold in each case. (16.68)
Those two previously mentioned clusters of vowels and consonants, namely *ṛ* and *ḷ*:
the first has eighteen varieties, while the latter possesses twelve. (16.69)
Thus, there are eighty-four combinations of the five vowels;
such is the classification of the four vowel-complexes (svarakūṭas).
Three hundred and twenty-four verses;
thus, there are five thousand eight hundred *anuṣṭubh* verses. (16–71)

The vowel *ai* has been correctly explained by those expert in the principles of phonetics (*śikṣā*), as well as the vowel *o* and likewise the vowel *au*; these many varieties have thus been proclaimed. (16.72)
"Delightful and fair, they are 'Yam'—thus the number, having come together, resides in the junction;
yogis perceive that, while men conceive it with their minds. (16.73)
When combined, their own number is indeed twenty; these are the two fixed [vowels] and the letter *ya*.
It should be known that there are twice as many vowels, distinguished by creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). (16.74)
Those which are joined with *sarga*, joined with *bindu*, and those that are *kevala*—these three types, when combined as "body," "object," and "attachment," constitute fourteen. (16.75)
Emission (sṛṣṭi) is declared to be the Moon, while the Bindu is proclaimed as the Sun.
Regarding the vowels, they possess the nature of the rays of the Sun and Moon;
the first seven vowels are celebrated as the rays of the Sun. (16–76)
The rays of the moon are to be known as the vowels beginning with *ā* and so forth, which follow [the consonants].
Of these two, they are the initiators of day and night; for the sun, moving through the *piṅgalā* channel by means of the vowels, brings about the day. (16.77)
The Moon, moving by means of its own *iḍā* through its own vowels, creates the night;
for the vowels are the movement within the *suṣumnā* of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), which is the radiant, immutable power of Viṣṇu. (16.78)
(151) "By means of the *suṣumṇā*, she moves about, expanding the *Śabdabrahman*.
Thus has the supreme course of the vowels been described to you in brief. (16.79)
The commencement of the discourse on the creation of the consonants:
Now, O Sage, listen as I describe to you the creation of the consonants;
[I shall explain] how the Visarga possesses the form of Vāsudeva.
That which is the unsurpassed, supreme creation has been previously declared as "Ha. (16.80)
That is the body of the god Vāsudeva, the primordial array;
it is Acyuta joined with the Bindu, obstructing the primary substratum.
At the commencement of yoga for practitioners, he kindles the sound together with the fire;
this Acyuta, joined with emanation, performs the upward emanation.
Acyuta, being engaged in emanation, performs this external creation;
from that arises the birth of the *ūṣmans*, and their fourfold nature [is derived] from *h*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *ś*.
From those, the *śakti-ūṣmans* are eternally proclaimed. (16.83)
This is declared as the fourfold self (cāturātmya), designated as the "four Brahmans.
Because those [letters] together with the letter *kṣa* are denoted by the word "Brahman," they are designated as the "five Brahmans" through their conjunction with the *kūṭa* [of *kṣa*]. (16.84)
In the Sāttvata doctrine, *kṣa* is declared to be the seed of truth;
others, however, call *kaṣakūṭa* its eternal counterpart. (16.85)
The origin of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) and their three designations are from the letter *śa*; therefore, *la* is taught as the first, and from *la*, *ra* is produced.
That which begins with *ya* should be known as *dhāraṇā*, because it supports the universe (*viśva*). (16.86)
They are called "the intermediate" (antaḥsthā), for they reside within the Person who dwells in the intermediate;
and they are called "the states" (avasthā) in the sequence of the Lord's descent.
The arising of the letter *ma*:
from the power of the Lord situated in the letter *ya*, that which is called *ma* is born; the supreme among the unsurpassed is designated as *ma*, the bindu. (16.88)

Its nature is that of the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of all consciousness, and it is designated by the term "jīva. Indeed, it is declared to be the collective totality of all conscious beings; this is the referent of the word "we" (asmadartha), and it is the Supreme Person (uttamapūruṣa). (16.89)

The letter *bha* arises from that [letter *ma*], and its nature is to denote the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*). When [the subtle body] increases through subtle observation, that *prakṛti*, in the form of objects of enjoyment, is distinguished as the gross [element] *bha* from the letter *ma*. (16.90)

O Great Sage, the thirteen letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *ṭa* arise in the form of external objects of enjoyment and their instruments; manifested through the internal and external arrangement, these letters starting from *ba* and ending with *ṭa* consist of thirteen [phonemes]. (16.91)

The three musical instruments represent the Mahat-tattva, the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the mind (manas); the retroflex consonant group (ṭavarga) represents the organs of perception; and by the wise it is said: "Intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkṛti), and mind (manas)."
The triad of organs of action has been indicated; however, the organs of cognition begin with *n* and end with *t*. (16.92)

The *ṭa*-group signifies the organs of action (*karmendriya*); however, from *ṇa* to *ṭa*, they are called "action" (*karman*). Furthermore, the emergence of the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*) is twofold;
the origin of the *ca*-group is its denotation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
From *ñ* to *ant*, however, the pentad of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) unfolds.
The origin of the *ka*-group [of consonants] belongs to that [earth]; it denotes the great elements.

The sequence of letters beginning with *ṅa* consists of the five great elements, while other successions of letters [denote] the remaining [elements]. One should remember that from whichever letter a particular [element] arises, that [letter] corresponds to it in the creation of the principles (*tattva*).
The arising of the letter *la*: when there is a difference in the articulators (*karaṇa*) of *la* itself, that which is called the letter *la* is produced. The diversity of consonants.
Thus, thirty-four letters have been declared; they consist of consonants.
(154) Thus, through combination with each individual vowel, there would be many variations;
O Sage, fifty-four forms beginning with the letter *ka* have indeed been specified therein. (16.96)
O Sage, there are thirty-six syllables consisting of *ki*, *ku*, *kṛ*, *kḷ*, and *ke* sounds; the taste is the intellect. (16.97)
Yogis have recorded such *kokāra*s by way of their number; likewise, the *kaikāra* is remembered by yogis as signifying "this [person] is stiff and intent only on his own self-interest. (16.98)
And likewise, seven *kaukārās* of that same number, when combined together, are reckoned by the supreme seers as "the body," "the object," and "attachment. (16.99)

O Sage, the body, its meaning, and its divisions along with its limbs arise through the enumeration of the *vegas*, *vyañjanas*, and *saṃkhyās*, as well as through the enumeration of *nītimat*, *pratibhā*, and *heti*. (16.100)

This enumeration has been proclaimed as the combination of vowels and consonants, according to the successive combinations of consonants, one by one, two by two, three by three, and so forth. (16.101)
Then, the rule for the enumeration of the individual phonemes together with their vowels is prescribed;
the alphabet (mātṛkā) is permeated by the power of the Lord, and it abounds in various buds such as words, sentences, means of valid knowledge, and so forth. (16.102)
The power of sound (śabdaśakti), which has color as its pillar and knowledge as its root, belongs indeed to Viṣṇu;
for it was created by Viṣṇu himself, the god of gods, who is possessed of that very power.
This succession of phonemes is pervaded by [the levels of] gross, subtle, and supreme;
(p. 155) by the command of the Blessed One, even Rudra, as a portion of the Lord, possesses the presiding authority over the phonemic alphabet (*varṇamātṛkā*).
By his command, through various Rudras who are our own portions,
this goddess— who is the source of mantras— is always presided over by the Mātṛkās.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Castes," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1004:

The seventeenth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Designations of Phonemes," which eternally bestows happiness upon those who meditate, [describes Him] whose locks of hair are matted with flames.
Let us meditate upon that certain divine splendor known as Sudarśana.
The Question Concerning the Form of the Presiding Deity of the Alphabet of Phonemes:
Nārada said— Salutations to you, O Śarva, omniscient one, destroyer of all asuras!
Just as the phonemes are presided over by entities that are gross, subtle, and supreme. || 17-1 ||
O Śaṅkara, you ought to tell me that supreme state which was [attained] by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, and by the Rudras who are portions of Bhava.
His promise to provide an answer was made by Ahirbudhnya:
"The phonemes consist of the power of Viṣṇu and are manifested through the creative will of Viṣṇu."
Listen to me as to how it is presided over by various states of being.
The forms of Viṣṇu who preside over the letters are as follows: the first is Aprameya (the Immeasurable), and Vyāpaka (the Pervasive) is said to be the letter *a*.
Ānanda (Bliss), Ādideva (the Primordial God), and Gopana (the Protector) are remembered by the wise as the letter *ā*. (17.4)
The letter *i* is recited as *iṣṭa*, *iddha*, and *rāma*;
Viṣṇu, the five dots (*pañcabindu*), and Māyā are said to be the letter *ī*. (17.5)
The letter *u* is also the arising, the unrestrained one called "the world," the support of wisdom, and the Lord of the World; it is called *ūrja*. (17.6)
The letter *ṛ* is Ṛtadhāman, as well as Satya and Aṅkuśa;
it is Jvālā, Prasaraṇa, and indeed the one named Viṣṭara. (17.7)
The letter *ḷ* is declared to be the Savior (*tāraka*), the Lord who is the essence of the *liṅga*;
the letter *ḹ* is the Long-Nosed One (*dīrghaghoṇa*), as well as Devadatta and the Virāṭ.
The letter *e* is the womb of the world, a triangle, and indeed the physical form;
the letter *ai* is likewise sovereignty, as well as the yogi and Airāvaṇa. (17.9)
Odana and Autadeva, having displayed their prowess, are called the syllable *ukāra*;
Aurva, known as Bhūdhara, and Auḥ, whose nature is medicinal herbs, are likewise remembered as *auḥ*. (17.10)
The pervasive syllable *oṃ* is the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds;
the syllable *aṃ* is declared to be the creator of emanation, and the *visarga* is the Supreme Lord.
The letter *ka* is Kamala, Karāla, the supreme Prakṛti;
the letter *kha* is Kharvadeha, the soul of the Vedas, the creator of the universe. (17–12)
The letter *ga* is the destroyer of disease (*gada*) and Govinda, the wielder of the mace (*gadā*).
The letter *gha*, moreover, is the sun (*gharmāṃśu*), as well as the radiant and luminous one. (17.13)
The letter Ṅa is known as Ekadaṃṣṭra, the self of beings and the creator of beings;
it is proclaimed as the letter Ca, which is the moon-rayed, the flickering one, and the wielder of the discus.
Chandaḥpati is the destroyer of deceit; he indeed made Chanda. Ajita is the destroyer of birth; the letter Ja is remembered as eternal. (17.15)
The letter *jh* is known as *jhaṣa*; he is the singer of the Sāmans and the reciter of the Sāman hymns.
The letter *ñ* is called *uttama*; he is the Lord who upholds the principles (*tattva*). (17–16)

The letter *ṭa* is the moon that nourishes the universe and is declared to be joy; the letter *ṭha* is the bearer of the stream known as Nemi; and the letter *ṭha* is considered to be the Kaustubha gem. (17–17)
Mausala and Daṇḍadhāra; the letter Ḍa is Akhaṇḍavikrama;
the letter Ḍha is Viśvarūpa, Dṛḍhakarmā, and Pratardana.
The letter *ṇa* is proclaimed as the teacher who bestows fearlessness, Vaikuṇṭha;
and the letter *ta* is Tālalakṣman, Vairāja, and likewise Sragdhara. (17–19)
Dhanvī and Bhuvanapāla are the letter Tha; Sarvadhāraka, Dattāvakāśa, Damana, and Śāntida are known as the letter Da. (17–20)
The letter *dha* is proclaimed as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Abode, and Mādhava;
the letter *na* is declared to be Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the Path. (17–21)
The letter *pa* is Padmanābha, the Purifier, with a face turned toward the west;
the letter *pha* is Phullanayana, the wielder of the plow, known as Śveta. (17–22)
The letter *ba* is Vāmana, short, and he is said to have complete limbs; the letter *bha* is known as Bhallātaka, which certainly bestows success. (17–23)
The letter *ma* is proclaimed as the crusher, time, and the primary principle; the letter *ya* is the fourfold state of existence, and it is called the extremely subtle conch. (17–24)
The letter *ra* is the support of all worlds without exception, the fire that is the conflagration of time;
the letter *la* is known as Vibudha, the Lord of the Earth, and the Sovereign of Puruṣa. (17–25)
The syllable *va* is remembered as Varāha, the support of nectar; the syllable *va* is known as Varuṇa;
the syllable *śa* is proclaimed as Śaṅkara, the peaceful Puṇḍarīka. || 17-26 ||
The letter ṣa is Nṛsiṃha, the form of fire, and likewise the Sun;
the letter sa is proclaimed to be nectar, satisfaction, and the Moon. (17–27)
The letter *ha* is the sun, while the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is proclaimed as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The letter *kṣa* is Ananteśa; it is the end of the classes of consonants and is remembered as Garuḍa. (17–28)
The *bindu* is said to be withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), while the *visarga* is called emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
These consist of the power of Viṣṇu and are of the nature of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
One hundred and fifty entities, beginning with the "Immeasurable" (aprameya), have been proclaimed;
these are the phonemes (varṇas) which are the fierce forms presiding over the phonemes, and they are presided over by those portions of mine known as Rudras. || 17-30 ||
O great sage, learn of those illustrious ones who abide in the Imperishable:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ānanda, Sūkṣmeśa, Trimūrti, and Ameśvara. (17.31)
Aṅghri, Īśa, Bhārabhūti, Tithi, Sthāṇu, he who is called Bhava, Caṇḍīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara. || 17-32 ||
Akrūra and Mahāsena—these are the forms of the vowels.
Then follow Krodhīśa, Caṇḍīśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama. (17–33)
Likewise, there are Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, Āhvaya, Caturānana, Ajeśa, Sarva, Someśa, Lāṅgalin, and Dārika. (17.34)
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍha, Daṇḍin, Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and likewise Śikhī. (17–35)
Calagaṇḍa and Dvigaṇḍa, as well as Mahākāla and Vālin; Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākī, Khaḍgīśa, and likewise Baka. || 17-36 ||
Śveta, Bhṛgu, Vakulīśa, and Saṃvartaka—these are declared to be my forms as Rudras, the protectors of the castes. (17–37)
Description of the Wheel of Letters and the Lotus:
Likewise, learn from me concerning the wheel consisting of letters and the lotus as well.
The *praṇava* (Om) is designated as the axle, and *śakti* is declared to be the hub.
The vowels (a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ), the sibilants (ś, ṣ, s), and the aspirate (h), along with their respective homogeneous groups, constitute the spokes;
the consonants from ya to ma are designated as the rim, and the letter ha is called the hub. (17.39)
The Praṇava is said to be the pericarp; Śakti is the row of filaments;
and the vowels, the eight groups of consonants, the semivowels, and the sibilants [constitute the petals]. (17.40)
This is declared to be the eight petals; Garuḍa is said to be the radiance.
Thus, the garland of letters of the Mātṛkā resides in the center of the lotus of the wheel. (17.41)
The Great Goddess Vaiṣṇavī is the source of mantras and consists of the six qualities.
She is described as the very nature of the Vaiṣṇava power whose essence is the Mātṛkā letters;
her limbs are fashioned from the primordial syllables, and she is adorned with the ornaments of the consonant groups.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, holding a conch and a lotus,
her body was fashioned by Praṇava, Śakti, and Śrī.
Her face was filled with her own radiance; she had two hands fashioned from hair, two feet fashioned from bell-metal, and a beautiful belly fashioned from lead.

The goddess whose vital breath is heat, who wears the letter *la* as her excellent necklace, who is beautiful with the letter *va* as her girdle, and who bears the letters *śa* and *ṣa* as her earrings. (17.45)

The goddess Vāṇī, whose heart is within the syllable *ha*, who is the inner self, whose radiance is like that of the moon, who is garlanded with colors, and whose fingertips hold a noose and a goad, should be meditated upon by the wise man.
First, one should worship the power of Viṣṇu;
prior to that, one should worship the Goddess with the mantra to be described hereafter.
Next follows the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra).
p. 162) Having then received permission from the Goddess and having worshipped the lineage of gurus, || 17-47 ||
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should then extract the desired mantras.
A wise person should extract the Vaiṣṇava mantras using the forms of Viṣṇu, and should extract the Vaiṣṇavas with dispositions such as "the Immeasurable" (Apremeyādi).

One should extract the Raudra mantras with forms that are fierce, and the Śakti mantras with forms that are Śakti; thus, one should extract the Raudra mantras by means of the Rudras and the Śākta mantras by means of the portions of Bhāratī.
O great sage, although mantras are all-pervading and eternally perfected, [they must still be practiced]. // 17.49 //
Thus, through the contemplation of creation, the mantras become endowed with power.
There is transgression in overstepping the stated sequence; for that dull-witted person who extracts a mantra while abandoning the stated sequence [incurs sin]. (17.50)
The mantras of one who transgresses the scriptures become givers of curses;
there is prosperity when they are not violated.
That wise person who extracts the mantra without abandoning the entire sequence [attains success].
By the mere recitation of that, the mantra bestows accomplishment.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Designations of the Varnas," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 1055:
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras" (Mantroddhāra).
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
The extraction of the Śakti-mantra:
Ahirbudhnya says—
first, one should extract the Śakti, which exists in the nature of Agni and Soma.
She who dwells in Viṣṇu, who dwells in the Supreme Self, who touches all, and who is all-pervading once again.
Having taken the heart of Vāṇī, one should join it with the inner self;
having joined it again with the Heart-mantra, one should join the pair of the Sibilants (Ūṣman).
Then one should meditate upon the great power Pañcabindu as her seat; furthermore, one should again contemplate her with the intellect as she rests within Vyomeśa.
In brief, its power is as follows:
This divine, great power, adorned with the moon, sun, and fire, is the body of Viṣṇu known as Māyā, radiant and bestowing sovereignty over the three worlds. (18.4)
This power has been demonstrated through its gross, subtle, and supreme aspects;
O great sage, it is the source of the Sudarśana mantras.
(164) Those others on earth who are Vaiṣṇavas, whose forms consist of the resolve (saṃkalpa) of Viṣṇu—this is that supreme power, this is the supreme *ahaṃtā* of Hari. (18.6)

It is the bud of the respective conceptualizations of various words and meanings, formed by the six vowels at the beginning and end [of the two groups], joined with the six [consonants] at the end of the pairs and the beginning [of the next]. (18.7)

The arrangement of the limbs has been fully described; having extracted the ten-syllable *Sudarśana* mantra by means of one's own innate power (*śakti*), one should mentally practice that Vaiṣṇava power until the limit of perfect contentment is reached. (18.8)
With undistracted mind, one should extract the great mantra of Sudarśana;
one should describe it as the immeasurable nectar that has become the heart of Śakti.
One should directly unite that divine inner self with the supreme self by means of the first [mantra] alone; indeed, one should attain the exclusive satisfaction residing therein. (18.10)
The wise one should meditate solely upon that moon situated there, and upon that bliss situated there, which is the support of all worlds. (18.11)
Taking the fire of Time, which is a flame for the fuel of wicked sins, one should unite it with the all-pervasive [breath] that manifests in various ways. (18.12)
A brief description of its power:
This ten-syllabled Great Vidyā is the Śakti of the Sudarśana;
it possesses gross, subtle, and supreme forms, and its nature is the volition of Viṣṇu. (18.13)
O Viṣṇu, the supreme state of Sudarśana follows all beings; it manifests according to the existence or non-existence of various individual volitions. (18.14)
The subtle power of Sudarśana follows the distinctions of the manifestations from ether down to earth; it is that which differentiates the causes and their effects. (18.15)
Consisting of the destruction of the darkness of the multitude of various wicked Daityas,
enriched by the nature of the gross wheel, that is the volitional state of Viṣṇu.
This four-syllable mantra is filled with the combinations of vowels and consonants;
it is the source of all accomplishments and is beyond gain and loss. (18.17)

Since its [the mantra's] final portion generally resides in the peak (kūṭa) consisting of three syllables, this six-syllabled vidyā, by means of those two [portions], is the creator of the world. || 18-18 ||
One should apply the statement of the fivefold seed-syllables in three ways by means of the rising [breath], taking up the Supreme Self;
one should again touch the Pradhāna with the supreme fifth seed-syllable.
The Sun, enriched by unrestrained Time, is said to be its subtle seed-syllable;
it possesses vital breath, is the support of the worlds, and crushes the sins of Rākṣasas. (18–20)
The fifth seed-syllable is the gross, unsurpassed *saudarśana*.
The description of the sixth seed-syllable is threefold:
that which is the *sāṃkarṣaṇa*, the terrible plow, the supreme weapon. (p. 166) 18.
One should join it with the immeasurable and with the moonlight alone;
that supreme, sixth [state], radiant and beautiful to behold, is the highest.
O Nārada, this supreme state within the seed-syllable has been shown to you as the immovable essence of the meaning of all scriptures, an immeasurable splendor. (18–23)
That form with blossoming eyes, which is encompassed by blooming eyes, is celebrated as the first to have been entered; it is radiant and performs the dissolution of the universe.
The subtle sixth seed-syllable of the Sudarśana is declared to be supreme;
for, having severed both external and internal evil, it leads one upon the true path. (18–25)
It expands again and again through growth and also nourishes the entire universe;
this is your sixth subtle intermediate state that has been demonstrated. (18–26)
The one called Śvetā is pervaded by Vyāpaka and characterized solely by bliss;
the sixth is designated as Sthūlā. These, O Sage Nārada, are your sixfold divisions.
Just as one who constructs an irrigation field first cuts down the stumps and burns them, and then spreads the seeds for the attainment of fruit with water; || 18-28 ||
Having been nourished, with its heat stilled and pervading various fruits, it attains extreme delight; this, O Sage, is that supreme sixth [flavor]. (18-29)
Thus has that eternal power, the sixteen-syllabled Sudarśana-gāyatrī, been shown to you; indeed, this very Gāyatrī is said to be fully pervaded by its own power. (18–30)
Furthermore, regarding the majesty of the Śakti-mantra:
this Śakti of the Sudarśana is the destroyer of the seeds of worldly existence;
when recited, worshipped, offered into the fire, and meditated upon, she certainly delivers the practitioner. (18.31)
Its own specific seed-syllable is the fourth, the supreme peak (kūṭa).
Its specific power is remembered as Sati, whose nature consists of the nectar of the moon. || 18-32 ||
From the first and second syllables of the Śakti-mantra, the Puruṣasūkta and Śrīsūkta manifest;
from the first syllable of this [mantra], the Pauruṣa-sūkta has emerged.
O Sage, that which is called the Śrīsūkta is produced from the second syllable.
A brief description of the meaning of the mantra:
that knowledge which is remembered as "saha" is called the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*).
"Saha" is declared to be strength (*bala*), because it flows forth (*sravati*) in its entirety. (18.34)
That is declared to be the thousandfold, and it is the infinite vital breath;
it is declared to be the spoke of knowledge, eternally pure and stainless. (18.35)
The power whose nature consists of knowledge and action is the *kalā* of the Sudarśana; having attained its own unrestrained emergence for the sake of the world, it manifests spontaneously. (18.36)
Having become the nature of the vital breath and the sun, she is the very form of the Supreme Self;
having eternally destroyed all evil, she also nourishes the entire universe.
The Śvetā, being predominantly serene, rejoices repeatedly by herself through sentences, phonemes, and even words, whether they are withdrawn or articulated. (18.38)
The comprehension of its meaning has been stated only in brief; it cannot be fully expressed in detail.
This seven-syllabled *Sudarśana* mantra, when presided over by the *praṇava* (OM), is known as this very "Seven-Syllabled One. (18-39)
This eight-syllabled [mantra] of Sudarśana,
when pervaded by its own power, is known as this eight-syllabled [mantra];
[it is also] the nine-syllabled [mantra] of Sudarśana.
This very nine-syllable mantra, when remembered again, is endowed with prosperity.
Now, for the sake of the accomplishment of the limbs, there is the limb-mantra.
Now, listen to one limb for the sake of her accomplishment of the limbs:
first, one should extract the digit of the moon (caṃ) and adorn it with the immeasurable (pra). (18.41)
One should extract the second peak-syllable, which is the support of all worlds without exception, joined with the supreme primordial nature (paraprakṛti), and pervaded by bliss. (18.42)
Then, having taken the fourfold path, one should adorn it with the immeasurable;
thereafter, having also taken the nectar, it is adorned by the support of nectar.
After joining it with Ānanda, one should extract the Supreme Self;
this mantra, filled with bliss, is the king of all limb-mantras.
With an exceedingly flickering and blazing fire, resembling a blossoming lotus,
possessing the splendor of a thousand suns and fires, he has a radiance equal to that of the Primordial God.
Ever-satisfied and having the mantra as its essence, it is described as being in a subtle state;
it possesses the luster of a formidable form and color, and is endowed with tens of thousands of throbbing wheels.
Having destroyed all evil through her own vital breath and splendor,
she becomes the essence of both the moon and the sun and protects the three worlds.
Thus has the gross, divine course of the wheel-mantra been shown.
Now listen as I explain how one should apply this wheel-mantra with various seed-syllables (*bīja*) throughout the sequence of the heart and the other limbs. (48)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, within the *Tattva-rahasya* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Nineteen, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras of the Limbs and Sub-limbs," from the beginning: Verse 1103.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
The heart-mantra of Ahirbudhnya:
That which consists of knowledge, divine, the supreme source of the qualities (guṇas).
But for the five beginning with the powers, it is eternally pure and stainless. (19.1)
Since that name is the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) consisting of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya),
the wise man should mentally extract its expressive form (ākāra).
Because it is knowledge, it is immeasurable; it is remembered as the first and all-pervading. Bliss, the primordial deity, and concealment—these are the sixfold [aspects]. (19.3)
Having gradually withdrawn that unsurpassed Sāṃkarṣaṇa-knowledge, through union with each respective particularity, he is always the object qualified by it and becomes identical with it. (19.4)
Thus, through union with non-existence, the King of Mantras himself, whose nature is gnosis, should subsequently apply "Hṛdayāya Namaḥ" for the sake of manifestation. (19.5)
The Head-Mantra (p.
171): Delightful and well-kindled is that which is the eternal will of the God;
it is everywhere unimpeded, divine, and indeed distinguished as the support of the nectar of immortality. (19.6)
That sovereignty of Hari is indicated by the seed-syllable *vī*;
and that sovereignty, which is situated at the head, stands above all else. (19.7)
That which is of the nature of non-obstruction is the supreme form of desire;
kindled and delightful, it is the ultimate abode of immortality.
One should join the head [of the mantra] with that seed-syllable which indicates its departure;
thus joined, the wheel-mantra is augmented by sovereign power. || 19-9 ||
Kindling his desire, he clearly manifests as the minister; then, for the sake of manifestation, he should employ [the mantra] with "svāhā" for that head. (19-10)

The Śikhā-mantra is Amṛtā, who is of the form of Soma; she is the supreme one consisting of satisfaction, the sovereign Prakṛti of the universe, the power of Viṣṇu, both transcendent and immanent. (19.11)
The unbridled and stainless arising in the form of that world is designated as "Su"; thus, Śakti is said to have arisen by means of that. (19.12)
It distinguishes the eternal Wheel-mantra by means of its form;
differentiated by that power, it shines forth as the essence of power.
That Kuṇḍalinī power which is said to reside in the heart, that which is the crest-lock (śikhā) of yogis, is divine, in the form of a lamp, and supreme. (19.14)
It spreads upward and shines in the location of the crest (śikhā); therefore, the placement (nyāsa) of that Śakti in the location of the crest is traditionally taught. (19–15)
One should employ the mantra "Vaṣaṭ to the tuft (śikhā)" for the purpose of manifestation.
The armor-mantra (kavaca) is declared by the name Ūrja; it is Viṣṇu’s own powerful strength. (19–16)
The capacity to sustain wisdom is supreme and consists of eternal contentment;
for one who is fully engaged in all duties indeed finds satisfaction in the absence of weariness. (19.17)
The power that supports all worlds without exception is celebrated as *tad-bala* (that power); within that power, the sustaining force (*dhāraṇā*) kindled by *bala* bears the entire universe. (19.18)
That which is proclaimed as consisting of the four states of existence for living beings is said to be the fourfold movement consisting of the vyāna, apāna, and the other vital breaths. (19.19)
The vital breath consists of the four states of existence; that is proclaimed as strength, by which the unconquered Lord, the infallible One, conquers everything. (19–20)
That great Vaiṣṇava force, endowed with these qualities, is immeasurable and beginningless; it is celebrated by the word "Sūrya. (19–21)
The mantra, split apart by force, remains as the essence of power;
and that vast, great power is concentrated throughout all his limbs. (19–22)
Its manifestation occurs in the two shoulders; therefore, one should place it right there. For the sake of its clear manifestation, one should employ the mantra "kavacāya hūṃ. (19–23)

The mantra of the weapon (astra-mantra) possesses greatness and the absence of deficiency; it is moreover unchanging. Its own volition is unimpeded, and its excellent meaning has been thus defined. (19–24)
He who, while contemplating the entire universe—both sentient and insentient—through his own volition, remains unmodified, that state of his is the Mahāsudarśana. (19–25)
That power is declared in the scriptures as being of the nature of subduing the wicked;
it grants peace from all evils and brings welfare even to the worlds. (19–26)
The Supreme Self, the crusher of the Daityas, is free from all transformation;
His power is thus described in many ways as "Mahāsudarśana. (19–27)
The mantra, pierced by vigor, abides as the very essence of vigor;
therefore, one should place it there in the position upon the palm of his hand. (19–28)
Then, for the sake of manifestation, one should employ [the mantra] "Astrāya Phaṭ.
This is the Eye-mantra (netramantra), which is of the nature of internal consciousness and destroys the darkness of primordial matter (prakṛti). || 19-29 ||
The upward-flaming radiance of him who blazes like the sun is the sovereignty and disinterestedness of all persons without exception. (19.30)
That which is the nature of the support of immortality, which incessantly destroys rebirth, and which exists through independence—that is declared to be *tejas*. (19.31)
By the word "flame" (jvālā), that Vaiṣṇava splendor is indeed expressed in many ways;
the mantra, pierced by that splendor, remains in the form of splendor. (19–32)
Since the eye is the locus of light, one should place that [light] there;
one should recite "vauṣaṭ netrāya traya" in reverse order for the sake of manifestation.
Thus has this succession of limbs, consisting of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), been shown to you; likewise, the succession of subsidiary limbs (*upāṅga*) should be applied by the wise man. (19.34)

The subsidiary mantra (*upāṅgamantra*) consists of the letters beginning with *śa* joined with the pervasive [vowel *au*] and combined with the [five] starting with Knowledge (*jñāna*), along with *namaḥ*, on the belly, back, pair of shoulders, thighs, knees, and pair of feet. (19–35)

One should install [the mantras] as the very essence of the six qualities; thus the body of the mantra is born. It is immeasurable, the destroyer of disease, and the path to both heaven and liberation.
For that state which consists of desire, expanded by the volition of Viṣṇu, is called "fire" by the wise because it burns away all evils without exception. (19.37)
The mantra, when split by the fire-syllable, abides as the very nature of fire;
with that, one should fashion a rampart all around in the shape of a flame.
Standing in the midst of a wall of fire, he becomes difficult to behold,
while recollecting the Cakra-Gāyatrī and [protecting] all around with the Cakra-mudrā.
One should seal the exterior of oneself with the form of upward, downward, and transverse [flames];
first by means of the "fire-wall" (agniprākāra), or else by the "wheel-seal" (cakramudrā). || 19-40 ||

The *cakragāyatrī* is the heart [mantra]; then, "we know the first word for the Wheel" (*cakrāya vidmahe*), and "we meditate upon the subtle one, the lord of the mantra, beginning with the word 'eye'" (*netrādipadaṃ sūkṣmo dhīmahi*). (19.41)
The first and the ninth [syllables] of the Gāyatrī, and thereafter the unimpeded;
then the tenth foot of the Gāyatrī, which indeed possesses the form of the totality.
The Cakragāyatrī has been declared, celebrated as consisting of twenty-seven syllables.
Now, learn from me these mantras of the Sudarśana weapons.
The mantras for the weapons, beginning with the discus, are as follows:
Oṃ namo bhagavan viṣṇo, [the mantra] common to all begins thus:
"O you who bear the form of the discus" (cakramūrtidhara), and likewise, "O you who bear the form of the mace" (gadāmūrtidhara). (19–44)
"O you who bear the form of Śārṅga," "and O you who bear the form of Khaḍga," then the four weapons beginning with the discus, and then the word "Senāpati" (General). (19–45)
Having recited [the name] uniformly for all, one should then utter each individual [name].
Thus, the Lord of Mantra in the wheel consists of six syllables, as does [the mantra] for the mace and other implements.
One should utter "Kaumodakī," "Mahāśārṅga," and "Mahākhaḍga";
then one should employ the armor and weapon mantras—this is the sequence for the rule of silence.
These four *gāyatrīs* have been declared for the discus and the other [weapons];
now learn from me these mantras for the conch and the other four.
The mantras for the conch and other implements (p.
176): Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, who is equal to all from the very beginning;
likewise, [the mantra] "O you who bear the form of the conch" and "O you who bear the form of the plow. (19.49)
One should utter "bearer of the mace-form" and likewise "bearer of the trident-form," followed by the title "General," which is to be pronounced identically for all of them.
"Mahātha pāñcajanyāya svāhā"—this mantra is recorded as having one syllable in excess; "mahāhalāya svāhā"—this mantra also is remembered as having one syllable in excess. (19.51)
Then there is the mantra "And to Mahāmusalāya svāhā," which is an additional mantra; and "To Mahāśūlāya svāhā," which is also an additional mantra. (19.52)
These four Gāyatrīs for the conch and the others have been shown;
now learn from me these mantras for the eight [emblems] beginning with the staff. (19.53)
The mantras for the weapons, beginning with the staff, are as follows: *Oṃ namo bhagavate viṣṇave*, which is common to all at the outset;
then *daṇḍamūrtidhara* (bearer of the form of the staff) and likewise *kuntamūrtidhara* (bearer of the form of the spear). (19.54)
"O bearer of the form of Śakti," "O bearer of the form of the noose," "to the bearer of the form of the goad," and "O bearer of the form of the thunderbolt. (19–55)
Then "bearing the form of the axe," and then "the hundred-faced one," and likewise "bearing the form of fire"— such is the sequence of individual words.
Afterwards, one should utter the word *senāpati* (General) equally for all;
then the mantra *mahādaṇḍāya namaḥ* is traditionally taught as the additional [mantra]. (19.57)
Furthermore, the mantra "namo mahākuntāyai" is remembered as one additional [mantra];
and the mantra "namo mahāśaktaye" is also remembered as one additional [mantra]. (19–58)
Then, "Obeisance to Mahāpāśa" is remembered as one additional mantra; likewise, "Obeisance to Mahāṅkuśa" is also said to be an additional one. (19–59)
And likewise, "Homage to Mahākuliśā," and also such [a mantra] as "Homage to Mahāparaśave. || 19-60 ||
"O you with a hundred great mouths!"—thus [ends the invocation] for the Fire; then "salutation.
