This mantra consists of thirty-three syllables and possesses the brilliance of ten thousand fires. (19.61)
Thus, these mantras for the weapons have been shown to you according to their form. Regarding that which has not been stated here, one should take it from another *saṃhitā*:
the worship beginning with the support (*ādhāra*) and the seat (*āsana*), and ending with the gateway (*dvāra*). (19–62)
The various forms of mudrās, whatever they may be for whomever,
as well as the ritual of consecration, initiation, and the rules of discipline.

The ritual for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as well as the various meditations—all that has been heard in the Jayā [Tantra] must be performed, with the exception of those specific [details] belonging to each respective [tantra]. (19.64)
O Great Sage, for weapons such as the staff (daṇḍa) and others that lack specific mudrās here,
a divine Śakti-mudrā must be employed in conjunction with the Astra-mudrā.

(78) Thus, O Sage, this sequence of the ritual procedure for the Sudarśana has been briefly declared to you. This method for the seizing [of the mantra] and so forth shall now be explained; listen to it. (19.66)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras for the Limbs and Sub-limbs," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1169:
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for Initiation Beginning with the Reception of Mantras.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins amounting to many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Ahirbudhnya describes the characteristics of an Ācārya:
"One who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas, and is proficient in the branches of knowledge..."
He was skilled in the methods of reasoning and refutation, and devoted to the rites for the gods and the ancestors.

He is one who does not speak slanderous words, who does not commit evil deeds, who is free from envy toward the excellence of others, and who is devoted to compassion for the suffering of others. (20.2)
Compassionate toward all beings, rejoicing in the rise of others' happiness, endowed with sympathetic joy regarding meritorious deeds, and maintaining equanimity toward those of evil intent. (20.3)
Abounding in austerity, contentment, and purity, he is devoted to yoga and self-study;
he is knowledgeable in the rules of the Pāñcarātra and expert in other tantras.
He is one who knows the inner meaning of the tantras, understands the true nature of the functions of mantras,
is learned in words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition, and is skilled in the discourse on logic.

One who knows the general rules and their exceptions, who is skilled in mechanical devices, who understands the distinctions between sacrificial pits and mandalas, and who is proficient in ritual actions and procedures. (20-6)
Skilled in the knowledge of the inner self, tranquil, self-controlled, with senses conquered, born of a noble lineage— such is the Vaiṣṇava known as an Ācārya.

A disciple seeking his own welfare, being well-composed, disciplined in conduct and vows, a twice-born man, refined and pure, should take refuge in a teacher who possesses the characteristics of a master. (20.8)
Devoted to the holy life, wise, and intent upon his own wife, he should report exactly what he has done and left undone without guile. (20.9)
Standing in the midst of the embers of saṃsāra and being cooked by my own karmas, I have come to you for refuge; I am prostrate before you—teach me, O Lord! (20.10)
In this manner, the disciple should approach the most excellent teacher;
such is the sequence of initiation for the disciple who has approached him and speaks without deceit. (20.11)
To You who are of a single form, purified through manifold limiting adjuncts—both perceptible and imperceptible—and who are hidden by the secret tradition; 20-12.

Having thus examined him thoroughly from all sides with his intellect for one year— to ensure he is not deceitful, not envious, and does not serve greed, delusion, and the like— [he may initiate him].
To one who is unwavering, he should impart whatever knowledge there is and of whatever kind it may be.
Having first performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), he should project the Goddess, consisting of the *mātṛkā*, upon his own body. (20.14)
One should perform the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) with the syllables of the mantra;
one should wipe each forearm three times with the mantra that has a threefold form.
In this manner, one should then place [the fingers] upon the two palms; with the tips of both middle fingers, one should touch both palms.
One should place Tāraka, Tārikā, and Lakṣmī, situated at the beginning and end of the Praṇava, [on the fingers];
and one should place Soma, situated at the beginning and end of the Praṇava, on the middle joint of the thumb.
One should place the vital breath (prāṇa) together with the bindu on the joint of the index finger;
one should place the letters beginning with the third [vowel] on the joints of the other fingers.
One should then place the plow, the supreme weapon, upon the upward-pointing fingers.
Regarding the specific locations for the seers and so forth: one should assign the seer to the head and the meter to the region of the mouth. (20.19)
One should meditate in the heart upon Nārāyaṇa, the deity who is without beginning or end.
Regarding the sages of the supreme, subtle, and gross mantras: the Supreme Self is traditionally held to be the sage of the mantra of the supreme form.
Saṃkarṣaṇa is remembered as the Ṛṣi of the subtle and the gross "I" (ahaṃ).
Furthermore, the Sudarśana mantra is the very essence of the Atharva Veda.
O Great Sage, there are five branches of the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]. (20–21)
Within those [waters], the divine Kṛtānta, the king of mantras himself,
remained hidden by the command of Saṃkarṣaṇa; that extraction was performed by me, Ahirbudhnya, after I had practiced austerities for ten thousand years at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
By divine command from Saṃkarṣaṇa, through supreme meditative absorption,
the entire Atharva Veda was churned forth very gradually.
From that [source], as it was being churned, this eternal mantra—with its retinue, its limbs, and its sub-limbs—was extracted like clarified butter from curd. (20–24)
Then they declared me to be the Ṛṣi of the gross Mantranātha;
Gāyatrī is said to be the metre, divine, Brāhmī, and likewise Ārṣī. (20–25)

The Supreme Deity is subtle, as well as gross, and the Supreme Self; one should then perform the sequence of withdrawal and placement within the body, and install the eternal Lord of Mantras upon the limbs. (20–26)

One should contemplate the triad beginning with the *praṇava* as the rays of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, in their subtle and other states, [placing them] at the crown of the head and the Moon specifically at the forehead. (20–27)
One should place the syllable *sūrya* in the mouth, *srāṃ* in the throat, *raṃ* in the heart, and *huṃ* at the navel;
likewise, the syllable *phaṭ* in the *mūlādhāra*, and the triad beginning with *tāra* (*oṃ*) in the heart.

The syllable *haṃ* with its root [the vowel *u*] is at the navel; *srāṃ* and *raṃ* are at the feet; *huṃ* is in the mouth; and *phaṭ* is in the region of the head. After that, the ritual is performed with one’s whole being. (20–29)
The ritual placement of the limbs and sub-limbs (aṅgopāṅganyāsa):

one should place the primary limbs, such as the heart and so forth, upon their respective locations; likewise, one should perform the placement upon the sub-limbs using the constituent syllables of the mantra. (20–30)
The body is to be contemplated in three ways—as gross, subtle, and supreme; thus one should know the body to be threefold.
That which is rich with limbs, minor limbs, and sheaths, and is perceptible, is called the gross. (20.31)
The subtle body, known as the *puryaṣṭaka*, is said to consist of atoms;
it is filled with a tumultuous roar of flames resembling ten million fires and suns.
In this threefold Lord of Mantras, one should contemplate a threefold body:
the divine splendor, the great and pure, which resides in the mind and is imperishable within the heart.
One should meditate upon the Self as consisting of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of lights;
then, within the center of that wheel, [one should meditate] upon the essence of the moon, sun, and fire.
Having immersed one's own self, one should then extract it as being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*).
Thereafter follows the ritual placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*), consisting of the eternal Lords of Mantras who abide in the states beginning with the Supreme (*parā*).
By that very same sequence of yoga, one should again emit those bodies;
having caused the self to enter into them, one should once more perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (20.36)

The ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands, body, and so forth, as previously described, is completed; next follows the inspection of the disciple, who is the divine body of mantra, whose essence is mantra, and for whom mantra is the charioteer. (20–37)
Bearing the form born of Viṣṇu’s resolve, the body of the Sudarśana,
he should look upon the disciple with eyes consisting respectively of fire, sun, and moon.
The dissolution-placement (saṃhāranyāsa) of the disciple:

Then, by means of the mantra and with that [same] mental focus, one should burn the disciple’s self within the Supreme Self through the gross state and so forth, according to the sequence previously described. (20.39)

One should perform the entire sequence beginning with "having immersed" (nimajjayitvā) as the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*; likewise, one should do so in the body of the disciple, which has arisen from being dried and burnt, by means of the mind. (20–40)
Then, one should mentally perform the deposition of the mantra (mantranyāsa) in the proper sequence.
Next, the instruction of the mantra must be imparted to him— the leader of the mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga).
The caravan, along with its practice, and whatever entity was previously mentioned—[all this occurs] as soon as the eternal Lord of Mantras has been thus apprehended. (20.42)
A divine sign arises spontaneously in the mind;
thus, by means of this mantra when correctly grasped, the knower of mantras performs the duty of a disciple. (20.43)
Considering himself to have achieved his purpose, he should then offer himself, as well as whatever belongs to him, to the teacher. (20.44)
One should offer everything to him except for evil and undesirable things;
having thus offered it, one should think to oneself, "I have achieved my purpose. (20.45)
For one whose intellect is thus, the mantra shines forth by its own power through its unerring nature;
according to the degree of one's spiritual disposition, there are the various means such as initiation and so forth.
Having initiated him with initiation, or having made him a worthy recipient through his intellect,
or having purified him by means of Atharvaṇic consecration or by means of mantra.
This mantra should be imparted by the Guru to one who serves the Guru; thus, with the practice perfected through such mastery, one should remain restrained in speech. (20.48)
With this perfected mantra, the wise one should perform what is for the benefit of the world.
This mantra should never be employed for a trivial purpose, whether for some minor matter or for one's own sake alone. (20.49)
(186) Regarding worldly matters, a ritual injunction should be performed, for that is considered a minor task;
these are the applications of mantras for the protection of the three worlds, or for the sake of the earth-disk. (20.50)
Whether for the sake of the kingdom, the king, or a high official, the ritual must be performed solely for the purpose of prosperity, never for the purpose of ruin. (20.51)
The rule for the location for the purpose of *puraścaraṇa* is as follows:
on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, or in a temple of Viṣṇu; or in a hermitage of the seers (*ṛṣis*), or even in the abode of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (20–52)
Or else, in a cow-pen or even in a fire-sanctuary,
one should purify the body through the *kṛcchra* and other penances;
having purified oneself with three *kṛcchras*, or by a million recitations of the *gāyatrī*.
Or else, by means of three ablutions performed with *brahmakūrca* water as enjoined by the Sāttvatas,
one should observe the restrictive rules that constitute the limbs of the *puraścaraṇa* rite for one day, gazing at the image of Hari from head to foot.
Then, subsisting on alms-food or sacrificial offerings, he should live on barley-gruel; or else, observing a milk-vow, he may eat sacrificial food, or whatever else a man may be able to manage.

The number of mantra recitations and so forth (p. 187): The practitioner of mantra should recite six hundred thousand [times], offer oblations sixty thousand times, and likewise satiate [the deities] with water; thereafter, he should gratify the Brāhmaṇas. (20.56)
Through non-deceit regarding past events, there is the accomplishment of mantras;
the Lord of Mantras becomes pleased,
and by that, the world is protected.
Then, with a clear mind and out of compassion for the world, he performed the protection by means of the mantra.
"Indeed, [this practice] should be performed when requested by the king, and never out of a desire for wealth.
Thus has the detailed exposition of the Lord of Mantras been correctly shown to you,
for those who are qualified for the mantras.
This is not to be heard by those who lack self-restraint, nor indeed by those who are merely ordinary.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for Initiation Beginning with the Reception of Mantras," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrī-pāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1227:
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Radiant Protection.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly removes a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
The question regarding the method of protection:
Nārada said—
Salutations to the one who ordains the welfare of the entire host of gods.
Salutations to you, O enemy of Tripura; again, salutations to the Guru of Gaurī.
"This divine and most wonderful [teaching], difficult to find even in the Vedāntas, has been heard from the words of the Blessed One; indeed, by this I have attained my life's purpose. (21-2)
Furthermore, I desire to hear the supreme nectar of your words:
what kind of protection must be provided by a counselor through the use of mantras? (21.3)
Ahirbudhnya states that protection is twofold:
"Protection, however, is of two kinds: the mantra-based [protection] for the wise one who is constant in the use of mantras."
First, that which consists of light should be fashioned, and afterwards, that which consists of speech within it.
That which is the conception of the senses is the divine, great, imperishable light, the eternal Brahman;
it is the sun beyond the sun, and that which is the moon beyond the moon. (21.5)
The fire of fire, beyond radiance, it is the splendor even of splendors;
eternally satisfied, ever-blissful, and devoid of rising and setting. (21.6)
The wise one should then conceive that as the divine axle and meditate upon the navel;
that conception of the navel is the power (śakti) of Brahmā, which possesses his attributes and never departs from him. (21.7)
She who always perceives the world as formless and incomparable;
she who takes refuge in the etymology and the designation of the word "Śrī" for her own power; she who is herself Śrī, and who both hears and listens [to all].
She is great bliss, great splendor, changeless, and free from desire;
she is the fullness of the sixfold attributes of Śrī, possessing knowledge, power, sovereignty, valor, brilliance, and majesty.
Her form is infinitely infinite, indivisible, and the divider of all;
she is Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Pūrṇā, Riktā, Amṛtā, and Harā.
She who possesses the three forms and yet is formless, who is acknowledged by all as direct perception;
she who cannot be negated by negations and cannot be enjoined by positive injunctions. (21.11)
One should conceive of the five functions of that Śakti as the unutterable, the vocal, the eternal Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; these are the spokes and the five acts. || 21-12 ||

One should fashion the state of concealment (tirobhāva), as well as emission (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhṛti), and grace (anugraha); one should likewise fashion the arrangement of the spokes (nemikalpana), the array (vyūha), the further array (vyūhāntara), and the state of the rim (nemibhāva). || 21.13 ||
It is the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, characterized by motionless motion;
it is the locus of all activity, yet pure and served by that which is the locus of non-activity.
It exists at both rising and setting, yet it is devoid of rising and setting;
it is eternally free from states, yet perpetually established in four states. (21.15)
It is trackless and without footprints, yet it stands upon the fourfold path; it is weaponless and free from agitation, yet it is endowed with all weapons.
Expert in the treatises, the meaning of the treatises, their distinctions, and the arrangement of their fruits—
[he was] like a multitude of thousands, tens of millions, hundreds of millions, and trillions of moons, suns, and fires.

One should contemplate the flames situated outside the rim as belonging to Vibhaveśa and the others— flames whose mass of own-radiance has destroyed the arising of all evils— and one should visualize the placement of Vibhaveśa and the rest in the positions outside the rim. (21.18)
[He saw] those who possess the splendor of a thousand moons, suns, and fires, whose characteristic is consciousness and bliss,
who possess all forms yet are formless, and who bestow the fruit of all desired objects.
One should meditate upon the lords of the *rakṣas*, *daityas*, and *dānavas* being licked by the mass of flames of his splendor;
and one should contemplate the impure creation, consisting of smoke and rising masses of flame,
as well as the three worlds, the earth, the discus, the mandala, or its presiding lord.
If one desires to protect it with wisdom, one should conceive of it as being situated within the sense-faculties. (21.21)
For one who meditates in this way, there is an incidental benefit which the practitioner, intent on the meaning of the mantra, should reflect upon:
therein, both evil deeds and mental afflictions as well as physical diseases are destroyed. (21–22)
Calamities and enemies do not find a foothold, nor do afflictions;
the king is ever victorious, and his ministers always remain devoted. (21–23)
Friends always rejoice, well-wishers likewise find happiness, kinsmen bind affection, and the virtuous remain ever-present. (21–24)
Those who are to be supported thrive, they attain wealth and even prosperity;
their subjects always prosper, being well-disposed toward one another.
Through desires they bind laws to objects of wealth in manifold ways;
through objects of wealth they likewise bind desires and laws without exception. (21–26)
Men bind themselves to objects through religious duties, and likewise to desires without exception;
they pursue desire through both duty and wealth, and likewise the other two through desire and wealth;
and men always accumulate wealth through both duty and desire. (21)
The statement of the primary result:
likewise, all [beings] devoted to their own duties shall be partakers of auspiciousness. (21–28)
Having attained the knowledge of the Blessed One, they reach the supreme state. (p. 192) Thus concludes the summary of the chapter's meaning:
the protection consisting of light has been shown to you in brief.
Now listen as I recite the protection consisting of speech that has been proclaimed.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection Consisting of Light," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Twenty-two, titled "The Description of Protection Consisting of Mantras," from the beginning: verse 1256.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Therein, first, Ahirbudhnya [expounds] the fourfold Brahma-wheel:
"Listen to the protection consisting of mantra, which is declared to be composed of speech."
In which this entire universe, including the gods, asuras, and humans, is woven like a thread.
That Lord of Mantras who was indeed proclaimed of old as the six-syllabled one is the fulfiller of desires for the best of practitioners, augmented by inconceivable wonders. (22.2)
One should conceive of that mantra as strung together with the *tāra*, *śakti*, and *śrī* seed-syllables;
one should encircle it three times with the *tāra*, and likewise with the *śakti* and the *śrī*.
One should further write the mātṛkā (alphabet) intertwined with [the mantra] all around;
on the outer perimeter, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), interlaced [with the mantra]. || 22-4 ||
Outside, one should again draw Mantreśvara, along with Tāra, Śakti, and Śrī;
this divine arrangement of syllables is very difficult to obtain even for the gods.
One should visualize the navel in the form of the syllable *srā*, vibrating with the syllables *śakti* and *śrī*;
one should then encircle it with the Lord of Mantras, likewise strung together with the syllable *srā*. (22.6)
One should draw the Mātṛkā externally, strung together with the Śakti and the Tāra;
then, first the immeasurable Tāra, and after that the Śakti as well.
One should first draw the spokes in sequence as "vyāpaka" and "śriyam";
on the two sides, one should inscribe the mantra strung together with "aprameyeṇa."
One should draw the southern course in the sequence beginning with Uddāma;
one should draw the western course in the sequence beginning with Prāsāda.
In this manner, one should draw the subsequent movement according to the sequence beginning with Vyomeśa;
this divine four-spoked [diagram] is well-worshipped even by the gods. (22–10)
One should write the syllable *ra*, the letter of the mantra, at the beginning and end of the *arās*;
the four *aras* shall possess a luster equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*).
One should fashion the rim all around as the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra,
strung together with the seed-syllables of Śakti, Tārā, and Ramā, and encircled by the armor-mantra (varma).
One should draw the *śakti*, *tāra*, and *ramā* three times each all around; furthermore, one should write the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) interwoven with *phaṭ*, *śakti*, *tāra*, and *śrī*.
On the ground, one should draw this wheel known as the four-spoked Viṣṇucakra with six spokes;
this wheel, which is the essence of the Tāraka, one should fashion into an axle.
One should draw the previously described wheel all around it, with the Lord of Mantras strung together by the seed-syllables *tāra*, *śakti*, and *ramā*. (22.15)
One should write the letters of the name on the outside, interspersed with the three [syllables] beginning with Tārā;
the Lord of Mantras is strung together with the six-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra.
One should draw [the design] all around on the outside; beyond that, one should write the Mātṛkā together with the Darbha grass. One should contemplate all this as the syllable Akṣa.

One should visualize the navel as being most wonderful and shaped like the letter *srā*, strung together with the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra, along with the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Tāraka.
One should also write the Mātṛkā arranged in its various forms all around;
[specifically] the letter *ra*, the *praṇava*, the letter *ra*, the *praṇava*, and the *śakti* itself.
O great sage, one should first write the letter *repha* and then the *praṇava*, followed by *śrī*;
and having written *repha* first, one should then write the spoke (*ara*) possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
One should draw the fiery mantra agitated by the *praṇava*:
the letter *ra*, *viṃ*, the *praṇava*, *ra*, *viṃ*, *śakti*, and *ra* itself. (22–21)
One should draw the southern spoke thus:
*Śrī*, *Repha*, *Repha*, *Ṣṇa*, *Praṇava*, *Repha*, *Ṣṇa*, *Śakti*, and *Repha*.
One should also draw the southwestern spoke thus: *Ṣṇa*, *Śrī*, and *Repha*.
Repha, Veṃ, Praṇava, Repha, Veṃ, Śakti, and Repha alone.
One should likewise write the letter *ra*, which belongs to Varuṇa, followed by the syllable *śrī*. (p.
196) One should write the letter *ra*, *na*, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), the letter *ra*, *na*, the *śakti* (*hrīṃ*), and the letter *ra* again;
then *na*, *śrī*, and the letter *ra*—thus one should write the spokes belonging to Vāyu.
The syllable *repha*, *moṃ*, the *praṇava*, *repha*, *moṃ*, and *śakti*, and indeed *repha* once more.
One should likewise draw the syllable "moṃ" for Śrī, the letter "ra" for Aiśāna, and the vowel "a";
one should write the mantras assigned to those respective syllables on their two sides.
Each of these six [syllables] consists of ten vowels;
this indeed is the divine Ṣaḍarī, highly honored even by the gods. (22–27)
The wise one should draw the eight-syllable mantra around the rim;
he should draw the syllable *haṃ* on the rim, adorned with the *śakti*, *śrī*, and *tāra*.
One should draw the syllables Śakti, Tāra, Ramā, and Astra three times around the outside;
on the exterior, one should draw the Mātṛkā arranged with the syllable Phaṭ.
This six-spoked wheel is fashioned from twenty-six syllables;
one should fashion this six-spoked wheel as the eight-spoked Nārāyaṇa wheel, which is the axle of great splendor.
With an eight-syllable mantra, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel,
possessing great strength and great dread, with a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
Understand correctly the ritual procedure for this wheel:
one should write the mantra around it, interspersed with the three syllables beginning with *tāra*.
One should write the letters of the name on the outside, interspersed with the three [syllables] beginning with Tārā;
the Lord of Mantras is strung together by means of the eight-syllable mantra. (22-33)
One should draw [the design] all around on the outside; beyond that, one should write the Mātṛkā together with the Darbha grass. One should contemplate all this as the syllable Akṣa.
One should imagine the navel, most wonderful in form, strung together with the eight-syllable mantra and the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Tāraka. (22–35)
One should also write the Mātṛkā arranged in its various forms all around;
this is designated as the navel, and outside of it, one should write the eight syllables.
One should first write "repha," then the *praṇava*, then the *tāra*, then "repha," then the *tāra*, then the *tārikā*, then "repha," then the *tāra*, then "Śrī," and finally "raṃ. (22–37)

The wise one should likewise conceive of the syllable *raṃ* as the Savior (*tāraka*), the syllable *raṃ* as Power (*śakti*), the two *raṃ*s as Prosperity (*śrī*), and the syllable *raṃ* as the Fire-god (*āgneya*). Thus he should arrange the *ara*. (22.38)

The wise one should write, in sequence: the syllable *repha*, *moṃ*, the *tāraka*; the syllable *repha*, *moṃ*, the *śakti*; the pair *repha* and *moṃ*; and *śrī*, the syllable *repha*, and the southern *ara*. (22–39)

One should write the syllable *raṃ*, then *nāṃ* as the *tāraka*, then *rephaṃ*, then *nāṃ* as the *śakti*, then *rephaṃ* again, then *nāṃ* as *śrī*, and finally *rephaṃ*; thus one should draw the *nairṛta* [mantra] along with the *ara*.
One should write the syllable *ra*, *rāṃ*, the *tāraka*, the syllable *ra*, *rāṃ* for Śakti, and the syllable *ra* again;
likewise, *rāṃ* for Śrī and the syllable *ra*—thus one should draw the *vāruṇa* and the *ara*.
One should write the syllable *raṃ* as the Savior (*tāraka*), the syllable *raṃ* as Power (*śakti*), and likewise the syllable *raṃ* as Fortune (*śrī*);
thus one should write the western [syllable] as *raṃ*.
One should write the syllable *ra* as the Savior (*tāraka*), the syllable *ra* as Power (*śakti*), and likewise the syllable *ra* as Fortune (*śrī*);
thus one should write the syllable *ra* as Kaubera. (22.43)

One should write the syllable *ra* as the Savior (*tāraka*), the syllable *yaṃ* as Śakti, and likewise the syllable *ra*; the syllable *yaṃ* as Śrī, and the syllable *ra* as Aiśāna—thus one should write the *ara*.
That mantra, joined with those syllables on both sides of the spokes, is eight-spoked, of great merit, and saluted by gods and asuras. (22.45)
One should fashion the marvelous twelve-syllable rim all around;
one should write "Hūṃ" outside, strung together with the *tāra*, *atāra*, and *anutāra* [syllables].

One should draw the syllables Śakti (Hrīṃ), Tāra (Oṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), and Astra (Phaṭ) three times around the outside; then, one should draw the Mātṛkā alphabet encircled by the syllable Phaṭ on the outermost layer.
This is the great wheel of Nārāyaṇa, proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa himself.
Having made this twelve-spoked wheel the axle, one should draw it on the outside;
listen now to the procedure for that great wheel of Vāsudeva.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Protection Consisting of Mantras," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1304.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Yantras of Vāsudeva and Others.
Even a single meditation [upon these] swiftly removes a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Ahirbudhnya is the twelve-spoked wheel— this sequence of the twelve-spoked wheel is thus proclaimed.
Evil deeds are utterly consumed by the mere remembrance of him. || 23-1 ||
The practitioner of mantra should fashion that wheel called Nārāyaṇa, which was previously described, as its axle according to the procedure to be explained.
One should draw the leader of the mantra, strung together with the syllables *tāra*, *tārā*, and *anutārā*, all around the outside of the wheel called Nārāyaṇa.
One should write the letters of the name on the outside, interspersed with the three [syllables] beginning with Tārā;
the Lord of Mantras is strung together by means of the twelve-syllable mantra. (23.4)

One should draw [the design] all around on the outside, and beyond that, the Mātṛkā together with the Darbha-grass; one should write all of this and contemplate it as the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 23-5 ||
One should conceive of the navel, most wonderful and shaped like the letter *srā*, as strung together with the twelve-syllable mantra and the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Tāraka. (23.6)
One should also write the Mātṛkā, strung together with its phonetic forms (srākāra), all around; this is designated as the navel. Then, one should draw twelve spokes.
One should write two *rephas* in each of the cardinal directions and likewise one in each of the intermediate directions;
[the sequence is] the *repha*, the syllable of the mantra, the *tāra*, the *repha*, the syllable of the mantra, and the *tāra*.
By this method—namely, the syllable *repha*, the syllable of the mantra, and *lakṣmī* (the letter *la*)—there are twelve spokes through the twelve-syllable vidyā. (23.9)
The best of mantra-knowers should arrange [the deities] starting from the east and ending with the northeast,
and he should also place the mantra joined with its respective syllables on both sides of the spokes.
This great Vidyā of twelve spokes is beloved by the Lord of All; one should arrange the great mantra known as Jitantā around the rim.
One should draw "Hūṃ" outside, strung together with the syllables Tāra, Tārā, and Anutārā;
one should then write the Śakti, Tāra, Ramā, and Astra mantras three times each around the exterior.
One should draw the Mātṛkā alphabet encircled by the syllable *phaṭ* on the outside;
this wheel, called Vāsudeva, is praised by the gods.
The majesty of this wheel cannot be described by those such as I.
Having made the axle the thirty-two-spoked wheel called Ajita, one should draw this wheel with its thirty-two spokes. (23.14)
This wheel named Ajita is honored by gods and asuras;
the ritual procedure for this wheel is now taught according to the rules. (23.15)
One should fashion the axle of this [chariot] as the discus called Vāsudeva; listen now to the procedure for its construction according to the prescribed rule.
The practitioner of mantra should write the leader of the mantra, strung together with the syllables *tāra*, *tārā*, and *anutārā*, all around the outside of the one called Vāsudeva.
One should write the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), strung together with the seed-syllable *tārā* and others, on the outside;
then, one should write the mantra, strung together with the syllable *jitam*, all around that on the outer perimeter.
One should write the *mātṛkā* on the outside, interlaced with the pairs [of syllables];
the wise man should know this to be the correct arrangement of the letters for the Ajitacakra.

One should conceive of the navel as being strung together by the mantra known as Jitantā, along with the Śakti, Śrī, Bīja, and Tāraka mantras, in the form of a *srā* [the letter *s*], most wonderful to behold. (23.20)
One should also write the Mātṛkā arranged in its various forms all around;
this is declared to be the navel, approved by Puṇḍarīkākṣa.
One should draw a circle around the thirty-two spokes;
one should then draw four [lines] in each of the eight directions in due order.
The syllable *repha* is the mantra-syllable *tāra*; the syllable *repha* is the mantra-syllable and *tārikā*;
and the syllable *repha* is both the mantra-syllable and *lakṣmī*. In this manner, by means of this direction [of interpretation], one should understand the syllable *repha*.
One should thus correctly draw thirty-two spokes with *samyagjitā*;
moreover, the mantra joined with those respective syllables should be placed on both sides of the spokes. (23–24)
That divine thirty-two-syllable [mantra], which bestows victory upon the God of gods,
should arrange the supreme Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh as a rim all around it.
One should draw the syllable *hūṃ* outside, strung together with the *tāra*, *atāra*, and *anutāra* mantras.
One should then draw the *śakti*, *tāra*, *ramā*, and *astra* mantras three times around the exterior.
One should draw the Mātṛkā on the outside, strung together with the syllable *phaṭ*;
this wheel, known as Ajita, is approved by Puṇḍarīkākṣa. (23–27)
By means of which the lotus-eyed one conquers all the Daityas today;
this most wonderful discus is indeed called the glory of Viṣṇu.

The true mantra-practitioner who is ever-yoked here conquers the entire world; having taken this Nārasiṃha wheel of thirty-two spokes as its standard, indeed, every other wheel operates accordingly. (23–29)
O sinless one, listen to this procedure for that which consists of Mahāviṣṇu—terrible yet auspicious, and the crusher of death—as it is being told by me. (23–30)
One should draw the leader of mantras, known as Ajita, surrounded on the outside by the [syllables] tāra, tārā, and nutārā, within the great wheel.
One should write the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) outside, strung together with [seed-syllables] such as *tāra*;
and the Lord of Mantras (*mantranāyaka*), strung together with the *ugravīra* and other mantras. (23–32)
One should draw the Mātṛkā syllables, joined together, all around the exterior;
for this is the auspicious axle of the wheel, consisting of Mahāviṣṇu. (23–33)

One should fashion the navel, which is most wonderful and shaped like the letter *srā*, as strung together with the *ugravīra* and other mantras, along with the seed-syllables of Śakti and Śrī, and the *tāraka*. (23–34)
One should also write the Mātṛkā, strung together with its various forms (srākāra), all around;
this is declared to be the navel, consisting of the supreme Mahāviṣṇu.
One should draw thirty-two spokes around the navel of the wheel;
one should then draw four [syllables] in each of the eight directions in due order.
The syllable *repha* is the mantra-syllable *tāra*; the syllable *repha* is the *tāraka* among the mantra-syllables;
and the syllable *repha* is the *lakṣmī* among the mantra-syllables—in this manner [one should understand] the syllable *repha*. (23–37)
One should thus write the thirty-two spokes with the *nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh* [mantra],
and the respective mantras joined with their syllables should also be written on both sides of the spokes.
This thirty-two-syllable vidyā is the destroyer of wicked daityas;
one should assign the three meters to the rim of this wheel.
One should draw the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Anuṣṭubh meters outside, strung together with the Tāra, Atitāra, and Anutāra mantras, along with the syllable "huṃ. (23-40)

One should draw the syllables Śakti (Hrīṃ), Tārā (Oṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), and Astra (Phaṭ) three times around the outside; then, one should draw the Mātṛkā alphabet encircled by the syllable Phaṭ on the outermost rim.
This most wonderful and formidable great discus of Nārasiṃha, which slays the wicked Dānavas, is known as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death). || 23-42 ||
Pretas, apasmāras, kuśmāṇḍas, daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas; ḍākinīs, bhūtas, yoginīs, and whatever other cruel species there may be—(23.43).
By the constant recollection of this wheel, [all obstacles] perish.
Having taken this wheel as its axle, the wheel of light (jyotiścakra) revolves. || 23-44 ||
The three luminaries are undoubtedly the three meters, beginning with the Gāyatrī; listen to the procedure for that wheel as prescribed by those who know the ritual rules. (23–45)
That which is this celebrated, supreme light manifest in the heavens—this Gāyatrī is it, the transcendent mother of the Vedas. (23.46)
"That light which carries the oblation situated in the Agnihotra—this *jātavedase* verse is a *triṣṭubh*, a body consisting of fire. (23.47)
That which nourishes the universe with its flavors and delights the eyes with its light—that is the body consisting of the *anuṣṭubh* meter and the *indu*, known as *Triyambaka*. (23-48)
The universe is sustained by lights that awaken, heat, and gladden;
it consists of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, whose natures are formed by mutually opposing processes.
The practitioner of mantra should fashion the axle of that great wheel, which was previously described as consisting of Mahāviṣṇu, by means of three supreme lights.
One should first fashion the axle with Vedic meters, strung from the *tārā* onwards;
outside the [area] consisting of Mahāviṣṇu, one should inscribe the leader of the mantra.

Outside [that], the practitioner of mantras should also write the letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), strung together with the seed-syllable *tāra* and so forth; and outside of that, he should write the mantra composed in its respective meter.
One should write the Mātṛkā on the outside, interlaced with the two [mantras];
this, O Nārada, is declared to be the syllable of the Jyotiścakra.
One should conceive of the navel as being most wonderful, shaped like the letter *srā*, and strung together with the first three meters—the Śakti, Śrī, and Bīja Tārakas. (23.54)
One should also write the Mātṛkā, strung together with its various forms (srākāra), on the outside;
this is declared to be the navel, worshipped by the Vedas and the Vedānta.
Let there be a hundred spokes for this [wheel]; hear from me its arrangement:
from Vāyu to Agni, within the range of Śarva, it is the domain of the Rākṣasa. (23–56)
Having laid down two cords and divided [the space] into four parts,
one should draw five spokes each and one field for each.
There may be as many as one hundred spokes; hear from me the procedure for that.
One should write there the three meters beginning with Gāyatrī.
The syllable *repha* is the mantra-syllable *tāra*; *repha* is the *tāraka* among the mantra’s letters;
and *repha* is the *lakṣmī* among the mantra’s letters—in this manner [the term *repha* is applied]. (23–59)
One who is composed should inscribe the Gāyatrī at the beginning of the Gāyatrī;
likewise, one should inscribe the Triṣṭubh for the spokes using the Triṣṭubh itself.
One should likewise inscribe the *anuṣṭubh* meters of the gods using the *anuṣṭubh* [meter] itself, following the sequence starting from the east and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna. (23.61)
That mantra, joined with those respective syllables on both sides of the spokes,
is the hundred-spoked [wheel], which is highly meritorious, supreme, and composed of the Brahma-weapon.
By means of feet, words, and syllables, and indeed by reversing [the order] in three ways,
he manifested the splendor consisting of the Brahmadaṇḍa, the Brahmaśiras, and the Brahmāstra.
The wise one should fashion the inner portion of the rim with the Gāyatrī,
which has the nature of the Āgneya weapon and is recited in reverse order (pratiloma).
The best of mantra-knowers should fashion the middle portion as the rim;
he should fashion the third portion as the rim with the Anuṣṭubh [meter].
The wise one should write those [syllables] in reverse order, interwoven with the mantra of the Traiyambaka weapon, which consists of the letters in reverse order.
One should draw "Hūṃ" outside, strung together with the syllables Tāra, Tārā, and Anutārā;
one should then draw the Śakti, Tāra, Ramā, and Astra three times around the exterior.
One should draw the Mātṛkā alphabet, interwoven with the syllable *phaṭ*, on the exterior;
this is the supreme wheel of the three lights, renowned throughout the three worlds. (23.68)
The stainless light of Brahman, intermingled with various groups of weapons,
is the Wheel of Brahman (brahmacakra).
Outside of this wheel, the five Hotṛ priests together with the Grahas are traditionally taught.
The *saṃbhāras*, the *patnīs*, the *dakṣiṇās*, and the *hṛdayas*;
outside of that are the *Śatarudrīyas*, and outside of those are the five *Brahmans*. (23.70)
Outside of that, one should recite the Tvaritā mantra, as well as the Puruṣasūkta;
outside of that, the Śrīsūkta, the Gāyatrī, and the three Vyāhṛtis.
One should write these rows around the *praṇava* in succession;
this is the wheel consisting of Brahman, fashioned from all the meters. (23.72)
It pacifies all suffering, eradicates all evil, and always bestows the desired objects upon everyone through mere remembrance. (23.73)
From this, the thousand-spoked wheel of the *mātṛkā* proceeds outward; it is the supreme *mātṛkā*-wheel.
One should write the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of the Moon, the Sun, and the Fire-bindu all around it. (23.74)

The practitioner of mantra should draw the leader of the mantra strung together with the syllables *tāra*, *tārā*, and *anutārā*; outside of that, he should again draw those [syllables] beginning with *tārā* in a strung sequence.
One should write the letters of the name on the outside; outside of that, interspersed with the mantra;
and on the outermost layer, one should write the Mātṛkā along with the Mātṛkā bound together.
This is declared to be the syllable (akṣa) arising from the wheel of the Mātṛkā,
together with Tārā, Anutārā, and the Mother of Syllables (varṇamātṛkā).
One should fashion the navel as knotted, having the form of a *srā*, most wonderful;
and one should also draw the *mātṛkā* externally, likewise knotted in the form of a *srā*.
This is declared to be the navel, consisting of the supreme Śabdabrahman;
it has a thousand spokes—listen now to its description. (23.79)
In the previously described divided plots of the field according to the sūtras, one should fashion fifty-five spokes in each respective section, as before.
With fifty and twenty [syllables], the base of the thousand-spoked wheel (sahasrāra) is formed;
likewise, by means of the three beginning with vāgbhava, along with tāra, atāra, and nutāra.

By means of the four primary *mātṛkā* seed-syllables, with the vowels beginning with *au* and ending with *ū*, and by means of the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, which are combined with the first two groups of seven [vowels]. || 23.82 ||
By five hundred syllables endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds, and by as many [syllables] ending with creation, combined with a thousand [syllables]. (23.83)
One should thus fashion a thousand fire-drills; hear now the procedure for that:
the syllable *repha* (the letter *ra*), the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), the *repha*, the mantra-syllable, and the *tāraka* (the syllable *oṃ*).
By this method— namely, that the syllable *ra* is both the letter of the mantra and *lakṣmī*—
one should write one thousand [squares] in the sequence starting from the east.
This thousand-spoked [wheel] is declared to be the supreme [state], consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
Sovereignty, conjoined with the Bindu, is proclaimed as the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (23.86)
The Māyā residing in the place called Karālavibudha is endowed with Vyāpi;
the seed-syllable consisting of Kāmarāja is joined with Somaurvavyāpi. (23.87)
This is the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī; these three begin with Vāgbhava.
[She is] she who moves through the wind, like the sun within the lotus situated in the fire of time. (23.88)
Māyā is conjoined with Vyāpinī; she is the primordial seed-syllable of Mātṛkā, the support of all worlds, and she dwells within the sun and fire. (23.89)

The second seed-syllable is said to consist of five points joined with the pervasive [vowel]; it is the union of the subtle state situated between the moon and the fire, which is blissful and all-pervasive. (23.90)
The third seed-syllable has been indicated; now hear from me the fourth as well:
it is the protection consisting of the Moon, the Tāla-mark, the subtle, the situated Time, and the Fire.
The fourth seed-syllable, which is formed by the *kūṭa* and joined with *vyāpin*, is the most excellent;
these four seed-syllables, O great sage, are within the *mātṛkā*.
The practitioner of mantras should write the mantra joined with those respective syllables on both sides of the spokes, according to the procedure for the thousand-spoked wheel.
The mantra-practitioner should write the Mātṛkā in reverse order, strung together with the syllables of the mantra,
and the practitioner should write the syllable *hūṃ* surrounded by [the mantra] beginning with *tāra*.

The wise practitioner should draw three times the [triangles] of Śakti, Tārā, and Rāmā on the outside; he should also inscribe the Mātṛkā, strung together with the syllable *phaṭ*, around the periphery.
This is that Mātṛkā-cakra upon which everything is established;
one should draw a protective rim (pradhi) outside that seed-syllable which begins with the letters of the Mātṛkā. (23.96)
Then, one should draw the Cintāmaṇi on the outside, and beyond that, the Parā;
beyond that, the Parāvarā, and beyond that, one should draw Śrī.
Outside of that is the Tārakā, and outside of that is the supreme Tāraka;
outside of that are the goads (aṅkuśas) three times three, and the nooses (pāśas) three times three, further outside.
One should draw the limbs, beginning with the wheels (cakra), all around the outside of that;
and beyond that, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha). Listen now to its form.
Then [the mantra] is "svāhā to the Person (puruṣāya)," followed by the name of the direction and "amarṣaṇa. After that, one says "saha," and finally, directed toward the direction, "I bind. (23.100)

Then, "To myself, svāhā!"—this is the name for the intermediate directions (vidiṅ), which is also called Amarpaṇa; and after that, saying "Saha," one then binds that which has gone to the intermediate directions.
One should draw the Gāyatrī of the wheel at the end with the enclosure of fire;
outside that, the sphere of space, endowed with its seed-syllable.
Outside of that, however, is the seed-syllable of wind, endowed with its own seed-syllable;
and outside of that, the seed-syllable of fire, likewise endowed with its own seed-syllable. || 23-103 ||
The watery mandala is on the outside, endowed with its own seed-syllable;
outside of that is the earth-form, endowed with its own seed-syllable.
Prāṇa, Sūkṣma, Anala, Vāruṇa, and Puruṣeśvara—these are the five seed-syllables of space and the other elements, pervading the left [side] in their respective order. (23.105)
Anala, Kamala, Bhāskara, and likewise Mardana;
Anala, Sūkṣma, Aurva, and Ūrja—these are the Piṇḍīkṛtas.
The seed-syllable that pervades all is remembered as this supreme Cintāmaṇi;
it is the Great Vidyā named Parā, which, abiding in the moon and the ocean, brings about creation.
Pervading the left side, Viṣṇu, who resides in the moon, is said to be this supreme and inferior [mantra].
One should encircle the earth with the Sudarśana peak. || 23-108 ||
Then one should encircle the womb of the Sudarśana with the Tārā mantra on the outside;
then Soma, Sūrya, and then Soma, followed by the pair consisting of Kāla and Pāvaka.
This peak of the Sudarśana [discus] consists of five *nirajas* and five *halas*;
this is the form of the Sudarśana, possessing a splendor equal to the fire of time.
One should pacify this deceptive [obstacle] indeed with the form of the nectar of liberation.
O Sage, this wheel consisting of fire and moon has been shown to you;
always meditate upon this wheel as the supreme Vaiṣṇava splendor.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Yantras of Vāsudeva and Others," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1415:
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation on the Deity of the Yantra.
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Regarding the brief description of the fruits of the eight previously mentioned wheels, Ahirbudhnya says:
"Blazing with the splendor of the moon, the sun, and fire..."
This wheel has been proclaimed by the Great Sage;
it consists of all that is composed of speech, is commensurate with all mantras, and comprises everything that has arisen as sound and the objects of sound. (24.1)
O Sage, that which is the inner wheel of Brahmā, arising as the sole bestower of stainless wisdom;
and that which is the wondrous wheel of Viṣṇu, arising [therein].
It bestows pervasiveness, beauty, intelligence, and valor. || 24-2 ||
That which is called the third wheel is most wonderful, bestowing radiant fame and wealth;
as for that wheel which is called the fourth—
O Sage, it bestows liberation and has been proclaimed by the hosts of sages.
The fifth bestows victory; the sixth grants fame and destroys fierce diseases and death;
the seventh provides spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*).
The eighth is for the sake of attaining prosperity and victory.
It is impossible to describe its greatness in detail; therefore,
this fruit has been briefly stated for each of the eight wheels of yours, which are worshipped by all the lords of yogis and sages.
Even in many tens of thousands of years, it is not possible for me to describe the full extent of this [reality], which is the self of all.
First, having discerned the distinctions between the states manifested by the syllables of the mantra,
the practitioner of mantra (mantrin) should worship those deities of the mantra according to the ritual rules, together with the forms, powers, retinues, ornaments, and weapons.
And one should contemplate them by way of the spheres of the power of vigor. || 24-6 ||
The detailed exposition of the nature, meditation, and so forth of the deities of each respective wheel [is as follows]:
the primordial, stainless [reality] stands ready with the acts of creation, protection, destruction, restraint, and grace for the entire world.
One should meditate upon Hari, who is within the scope of the Praṇava, resembling a great ocean with waves possessing full power, in the first cakra.
White, with a serene countenance, eyes as broad as lotuses, clad in yellow garments, with a broad chest, the self-born one,
holding the discus and conch with his thick and long arms—
Indeed, the Kaumodakī and the lotus are among Viṣṇu’s discuses. || 24-8 ||

I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial deity, the delight of the eyes, who is dark-complexioned, wears a crown, and holds in his four noble arms the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the water-born lily, and the excellent discus.
One should meditate upon Śrī together with him in the wheel situated at the third step.
With eyes as broad as the petals of a white lotus, fair as the moon and jasmine,
holding a pure rosary and the mudrā of stainless, rising awakening,
and bearing in his two arms the pure wheel and conch;
Contemplate him as Vāsudeva in the fourth wheel.
Holding a conch, discus, lotus, mace, goad, noose, bow, and the Saunandaka sword with eight fierce hands,
seated upon Tārkṣya, resembling a mountain of silver, the Ancient One—
One should contemplate the man who has entered the unconquerable wheel.
His body was smeared with the blood spurting from the chests of Daityas severed by the tips of his cruel, fierce, and curved claws;
he was difficult to behold due to his three eyes of a most terrible form.
O Sage, in the sixth [month], meditate upon the Lord Narasiṃha.
Situated in the midst of a thicket from which the rays of the moon, fire, and sun emerge, holding a lotus, mace, discus, and conch,
established in the meter, the immeasurable cause of the world—
O sage, contemplate Śrīśa, the ancient Puruṣa.

In the wheel of the Mātṛkās, Lakṣmī is to be meditated upon as having hands holding a white lotus, a conch, and a lotus as pure as the radiance of cow’s milk, a conch, moonlight, the celestial river, and jasmine; her complexion is stainless like the luster of a conch.
That Mother should be meditated upon with a smiling and serene face, eyes as broad as lotuses, atop her own wheel-abode. 24-14.
Holding a ten-pronged trident that is superior to the three ages with her own sixteen hands, possessing the luster of a hibiscus flower,
seated upon the Cintāmaṇi gem, and enriched by three eyes—
O Sage, one should contemplate with the mind that this power belongs to Hari. || 24-15 ||
The Goddess Parā, possessing the cool luster of the full moon, bearing the mudrā of awakening, enriched by the book of self-knowledge held between her arms— the divine power of the Supreme Puruṣa—
She is inconceivable, with a serene countenance and eyes like lotuses.
With hands holding a lotus, an arrow, a boon-granting gesture, a goad, and a noose;
clad in red garments; with eyes like the broad petals of a water lily;
she is born from the essence of the supreme and the subordinate, abiding in subtle radiance.
And that power, called both supreme (parā) and inferior (avarā), is also the power of thought (cintyā) and so forth. || 24-17 ||
With the entire multitude of living beings coiled by the noose held in her arms,
her bodily luster as red as the bandhūka and lotus flowers,
possessing full breasts and lotus-eyes rolling with intoxication—
This entire pantheon of deities has its abode at the side of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
The primordial power of Hari, established upon the divine goad, is praised by the multitude of living beings who bow down, pinned by her sharp-tipped, curved, and keen goad.
She of great power is to be meditated upon by one devoted to samādhi. || 24-19 ||

The detailed exposition of the limbs, mantras, deities, their meditations, and so forth is an ancillary part; however, that which was previously explained at the outset as being entirely identical in form to the deity consisting of the wheel is the primary wheel.
Gāyatrī also possesses a complexion like a blazing fire, a majesty equal to that of the Lord of the Discus (Viṣṇu), and is endowed with full, swelling breasts. || 24-20 ||
The virtuous declare that the rampart is indeed composed of fire, wherein the entire host of the enemies of the gods has been melted by the mass of flames;
even the Power (Śakti) stationed in the sky is a garland of thousands of suns.
She possesses the luster of a blue lotus and is to be meditated upon with the mind.
One should meditate on her as bearing with her body a garland consisting of the four states of existence, as the power (śakti) residing in the wind, possessing a smoky-colored form,
and appearing like a garland of thousands of youthful suns known as the fire of time (kālānala).
The power residing in fire should also be meditated upon as having a red body.
She whose form is composed of nectar, who possesses the power residing within the waters, who is to be meditated upon as wearing a garland fashioned from millions of boars,
who has the luster of molten gold, and who is enriched by the Lord of Men (Viṣṇu).
The power of the earth of the Primordial Person is to be meditated upon. || 24-23 ||

One should mentally contemplate the peak of the entire Sudarśana-wheel, which has the form of ten thousand times ten thousand fires of cosmic destruction; one should visualize that peak as being composed of the Sudarśana.
Its mass of flaming crests was thickened by the outpouring of the fat of all the enemies of the gods, which had been boiled while they were tormented by heat.
Meditation on the Power that is the root of all mantras of the Sudarśana:
she whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; who is the color of the rising sun;
who stands pervading the entire world without exception; and who is worthy of the worship of all.
She who bears a thousand discs with her multitude of arms, the source [of all], known as Sudarśanamanas—thus she is to be meditated upon. (24–25)
Among the aforementioned machines, the right to operate them belongs exclusively to the twice-born;
this noble protection has been briefly described for the welfare of all the world.
With the king's permission, the best of the twice-born,
remaining unwearied, should meditate upon this constantly.
The aforementioned yantras possess the quality of being means for achieving the supreme fruit, which is liberation preceded by incidental fruits;
evils never overcome them.
All planetary afflictions subside;
the earth flourishes with abundant crops, and there is no obstruction to the three aims of human life for mankind. (24–27)
Abounding in virtue, wealth, and pleasure, long-lived, and free from evils, they possess noble fame and majesty;
devoted to the scriptures and performing prescribed rites, they remain steadfast.
At the end, the stainless ones enter the Supreme Person. || 24-28 ||

O Sage, this divine procedure regarding the *saudarśana* mantras— which is free from obstacles such as the loss of progress— has been fully described; O Brahmin, it should be contemplated here by kings who have maintained meditative concentration.
In this world, even a man devoid of meditative concentration, though his actions may be charming, certainly obtains the fruit appropriate to his effort. || 24-29 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation on the Deities of the Yantras," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
Chapter Twenty-five, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sudarśana Yantra," beginning from verse 1444:
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
In order to demonstrate the majesty of the Yantra, Nārada restated the matter already explained:
"O Blessed One, you have correctly described it in detail, exactly as it is."
That which is the cause, that which is the support, and that which is the measure of this world; || 25-1 ||
Likewise, the nature and the means of achieving dharma, artha, and kāma;
as well as paravidyā and vidyā, and that which is designated as adhyātma. (25.2)
Liberation is declared to be supreme, as well as bondage and its means; likewise, the divisions of caste and stage of life, and their specific duties in particular. (25.3)
Likewise, the method of protection for all castes and for kings has been described;
indeed, this divine method of protecting kings has thus been detailed. (25.4)
How indeed, when the Kali age has arrived, shall there be a method for the protection of kings? [First,] a brief description of the nature of the Kali age:
the twice-born will neither perform sacrifices, nor give gifts, nor offer oblations. (25.5)
In the Kali age, not everyone will apply their minds to their own duties;
the powers of all mantras will fall into disrepute. (25.6)
The kings will become devoid of vigor and abandoned by their subjects; they will be impoverished, stripped of their kingdoms, and oppressed by bandits. (25.7)
When the Kali age has arrived, cows will yield little milk; and people, afflicted by hunger, will be oppressed by droughts during the Kali age. (25.8)
Devoted to heretical doctrines, those people who are mostly immersed in darkness and lack true knowledge will engage in censuring and other such acts against the Blessed Lord Janārdana.
In such a Kali age, the question arises regarding the means for the protection of kings:
"How can the method of protecting kings be accomplished in this time that is a locus of faults by Brahmins who are powerless and devoid of strength? (25.10)
O Omniscient One, tell me with certainty that means by which protection may be achieved; O Maheśvara, who else but you is able to speak? (25.11)
The commencement of the reply by Ahirbudhnya:
"Excellent, excellent, O Nārada, that you have asked this!"
This is true: in the Kali age, the method of protection by means of mantras is not effective.
Nevertheless, I shall tell you of one who is devoted; listen to him:
he is [the foremost] of all beings, and especially among kings. (25.13)

The narration of obtaining the Sudarśana Yantra from Nārāyaṇa for the sake of pacifying the great sin of having severed the head of his own grandfather, which is the supreme secret method of protection and the highest essence of the tantras.
This was told to me by Nārāyaṇa at the meritorious Badarikāśrama.
For the pacification of the great sin of severing the head of the Grandfather (Brahmā), it is the allayer of every affliction and the warder-off of all suffering. (25.15)
This is a summary of its greatness:
it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*), is the sole cause of all prosperity, pacifies the malevolent magic of others, grants the sovereignty of others, and is auspicious. (25–16)
It removes the defects of the Kali age and destroys all enemies;
by its mere remembrance, the enemies of men perish. (25.17)
Like robbers whose territory has been lost, they flee in the ten directions;
for him in whose house this yantra is placed, everything becomes successful. (25.18)
Whatever king should have this machine constructed with devotion in his home, the entire circle of the earth shall come under his control; of this there is no doubt. (25-19)
The greatness of the Sudarśana Yantra has been described by me;
[this is] the demonstration of the fruit of the Sudarśana-Nārasiṃha Yantra (p.
223). The Yantra of Nārasiṃha joined with Sudarśana. (25–20)
Even another world shall be subject to him who causes this to be done;
by the mere writing of this, everything is accomplished for men. (25.21)
Demonstration of the Fruits of the Viṣṇupañjara Yantra:
By the mere performance of the Viṣṇupañjara Yantra, all the deities are always pleased; how much more so, then, humans and others? (25–22)

The fruit of these three yantras combined is impossible to describe: "O Nārada, even by an omniscient one, it is not possible for me to describe the entire result of the combination of these three yantras. (25.23)
The Fruit of the Mahāsudarśana Machine:
By constructing this Mahāsudarśana machine here, O twice-born one, a man attains the three worlds; how much more so, then, the circle of the earth? (25.24)
In one place, the Sudarśana-Nārasiṃha with imagined limbs; elsewhere, the Sudarśana alone with radiant body;
and in another, the one with two faces conceived and joined with a multitude of weapons.
This is the Śrīviṣṇupañjara, endowed with a multitude of mantras.

The Great Sudarśana, consisting of radiant energy and honored by all the worlds, is a single machine that bestows happiness upon those who take refuge in it, yet is unattainable for people who have not performed meritorious deeds.
One should have that performed if one desires victory over all the worlds. || 25-26 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sudarśana Yantra," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Twenty-six, titled "The Characteristics of the Mahāsudarśana Yantra," beginning from verse 1470:
A single meditation [upon it] removes a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
In detail, regarding the question on the characteristics of the Mahāsudarśana yantra,
Nārada said:
"The configuration and the characteristics of this yantra [shall be explained] in detail."
I wish to hear this, O Blessed One; explain it to me as I ask.
The promise of that reply was made by Ahirbudhnya:
"I shall explain in detail its essential nature as well as its characteristics."
O divine sage, listen as I describe the mechanism of this machine to you.
The practitioner should fashion the materials for constructing the machine from silver, gold, metals, or even stone,
and according to his qualification, he should perform the worship of the machine. (26–3)

One should draw this yantra on a cloth using substances for the preparation of the drawing, namely the juices derived from metals, sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and agallochum, or else with a golden needle. (26.4)
p.
226) One who is composed should place the *tāra* (the syllable Om) in the center of the moon disc within the yantra;
in its center, one should draw the red-colored deity Sudarśana. (26.5)
The description of His essential nature:
the all-pervading Lord, of great splendor, with reddish-brown eyes, endowed with reddish-brown hair, wearing red garments, and possessed of either sixteen or eight hands. (26.6)
He is endowed with a noose, a goad, a lotus, a mace, a bow, a conch, a club, and a discus—
these excellent and terrifying weapons— and is the foremost among victors.
That is the supreme form of Viṣṇu, eternally composed of radiant light,
His face adorned with the sprouting flames of the seven-rayed fire spat forth from His fangs.
Adorned with various ornaments, terrifying and hair-raising, he filled the entire world with his own splendor, possessed of great strength. || 26-9 ||
Greedy for consuming the blood of the Daityas as they were being pierced,
resembling hundreds of rising suns, and renowned for its prowess.
Constantly supported by the principle of the mind through its impetuous force,
it is skilled in the essence of service to the lotus-hand of Nārāyaṇa.
Through the speed of the thought of Viṣṇu, he is the supreme guide for those devoted to him; by mere remembrance, he is the means of accomplishing both seen and unseen goals. (26.12)
The slaying of those who are hostile to one's own devotees is honored by the gods;
its deeds are praised by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas. (26.13)
His state as the refuge of all, his faultlessness, and his nature as a mine of auspicious qualities are described thus:
"He is the protector for those seeking refuge, intent on crushing the enemies of his devotees;
he is an eternal, boundless ocean of faultless and auspicious qualities. (26.14)
Having thus inscribed the name of the practitioner at the edge of its foot, which is ever-blissful and auspicious,
one should place the name of the practitioner around the perimeter of that lotus-foot. (26.15)
Then, on the periphery, one should draw a six-pointed wheel;
on the periphery of the lunar disc, one should inscribe a six-pointed wheel, which is fiery, of immeasurable splendor, infallible, and effective for all practitioners. (26–16)
Therein, regarding the placement of the six syllables:
one should place the six syllables of the mantra in the directions starting from the east and in the corners.
This is the placement of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra-nyāsa).
One should place the mantras of the limbs in sequence within the six intermediate corners.
Then, one should draw a four-petalled lotus;
outside of this, likewise, a lotus endowed with four petals. Therein, the syllables are to be placed.
One should place "sabinduvama phaṭ" upon these petals in their respective order.
In the intermediate spaces,
the practitioner should likewise arrange the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*);
then follows the drawing of a sixteen-petaled lotus with eight filaments.
There, on the outside, is an eight-petaled lotus, and within it, one with sixteen filaments.
Regarding the placement of the sixteen vowels on the filaments:
one should write the sixteen vowels upon its filaments in sequence;
as for the petals, there is the placement of the eight-syllable mantra.
One should inscribe the great eight-syllable mantra upon its petals.
The drawing of a lotus with thirty-two filaments and sixteen petals:
it has thirty-two filaments, and outside of that, sixteen petals;
on the filaments, there is the arrangement of the letters from *ka* to *sa*.
One should write the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa* upon its filaments.
The placement of the sixteen-syllable mantra on the petals:
one should indeed write this Vaiṣṇava sixteen-syllable mantra upon the petals;
[one should also perform] the drawing of a lotus with thirty-two filaments and petals.
One should draw thirty-two petals with filaments on its exterior.
Regarding the placement of the syllables of the Vārāha Anuṣṭubh mantra upon the filaments: (p.
229) "One should correctly inscribe the supreme Vārāha Anuṣṭubh mantra in due order upon the filaments of this lotus, starting from the east. (26.23)
The placement of the syllables of the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh mantra upon the petals:
one should inscribe this Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh great mantra, which is unfailing and effective for all practitioners, sequentially upon the thirty-two petals. (26–24)
The drawing of a sixty-four-petaled lotus:
outside of that, one should draw a lotus endowed with sixty-four petals;
upon those petals, there is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Pātālanārasiṃha mantra.
One should place the mantra known as Pātālanārasiṃha upon its petals.
Furthermore, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus; having again placed a lotus surrounded by eight petals,
one performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight-syllabled Nārasiṃha mantra upon those petals.
One should inscribe the eight-syllabled Nārasiṃha mantra upon its petals.

Outside of that, one should conceive of the Maheśvara mandala; outside of that, one should construct the Maheśvara mandala, adorned with vajras, blazing intensely by its own nature, and decorated with all ornaments. (26–27)
Outside of that, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of its seed-syllable together with the name of the practitioner.
On the outside of that, in the cardinal directions starting from the east, the wise one should place that seed-syllable in due order, conjoined with his own name. (26–28)
The placement of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) in the outer corners:
one should likewise arrange the semivowels in the four outer corners;
in the intervals between the corners, there is the placement of their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
One should again place that seed-syllable within the interior portions of the corners.
Around that, there is an arrangement of the vowels in reverse order;
one should draw all those vowels around it in reverse order.
Around that, there is an arrangement of the letters beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'kṣa'.
One should likewise arrange [the letters] beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'ka' all around.
One should perform the encirclement with one's own name and the noose and goad;
interwoven with one's own name, one should place the final pair [of syllables] all around.
The afflicted person should then encircle this with the noose and likewise with the goad. (26–31)
One should unweariedly construct an encircled *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) on the outside of that;
everywhere, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms beginning with Keśava.
One should place Keśava and the others in their embodied forms all around it. || 26-32 ||
A Description of the Form of Keśava (p.
231): Resembling molten gold, with eyes as broad as white lotuses, possessing boundless compassion, and bearing the lotus, conch, discus, and mace. (26.33)
The god wearing yellow garments, adorned with a forest garland,
and graced by necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings.
One should first place the Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, who has four arms, noble limbs, and a serene countenance.

Then one should fashion Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of Nārāyaṇa himself, bearing the conch, lotus, mace, and discus, with the complexion of a dark blue cloud, and adorned with all ornaments. (26–36)
Then one should meditate upon Lord Mādhava, who bears the lotus, the mace Kaumodakī, the conch, and the discus; he is imperishable and dark blue like a blue lotus. (26–37)
One should depict Govinda of immeasurable splendor, resplendent with the discus, the mace Kaumodakī, the conch, and the lotus as his weapons, resembling the orb of the moon. (26–38)

One should depict Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, who possesses the form of Viṣṇu, bearing the mace, lotus, conch, and discus as his weapons, highly adorned, and resembling the filaments of a lotus. (26–39)
One should meditate upon Madhusūdana,
the ocean of compassion, who bears the discus, conch, lotus, and mace,
and who resembles the petals of a red lotus. (26.40)
One should depict Trivikrama as the Lord attended by the discus, the mace Kaumodakī, the lotus, and the conch, resembling brilliant gold in appearance. (26.41)
Then one should meditate upon Vāmana,
who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, who is supremely adorned,
and who resembles the rising sun. (26–42)
One should contemplate the Lord Śrīdhara, who possesses the form of Śrīdhara, bearing the lotus, discus, mace, and conch, an ocean of excellent qualities, and resembling a white lotus. (26.43)
One should visualize Hṛṣīkeśa, who possesses the splendor of lightning and lotus-like eyes, bearing a mace and the Sudarśana discus, as well as a conch and a lotus. (26.44)
One should have Padmanābha fashioned, radiant, bearing a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus, resembling a thousand suns in brilliance. (26–45)
Then one should meditate upon Lord Dāmodara,
who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus, who resembles the bandhūka flower,
and who is easily accessible through devotion alone. (26.46)

One should write down each of those names ending in "namas," and having thus placed them in this sequence, one should also place their names [surrounded] on all sides with the formula: "O such-and-such one, protect, protect! ending in "namas. (26–47)
One should perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bījākṣara) in a clockwise direction starting from the east and the other cardinal points:
*yaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *raṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, as well as *laṃ*, *saṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *haṃ*—two by two—in the great directions beginning with the east, proceeding in a clockwise manner. (26–48)
The placement of the seed-syllables (bījākṣara) is performed in an anti-clockwise direction starting from the northeast; namely *yaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *raṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, as well as *laṃ*, *saṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *haṃ*—
these should be placed in pairs in the corners beginning with the northeast, moving counter-clockwise.
Furthermore, there is the encircling with the noose and the goad;
having encircled it with the noose, one should also encircle it with the goad. All of this is surrounded by the *hṛllekhā* mantra together with its seed-syllable. (26–50)
One should place Viṣṇu, the immutable, together with his weapons— the discus, the mace Kaumodakī, the bow Śārṅga, and the sword— in due order in the four directions starting from the east. (26–51)
The conch and discus, his excellent weapons, are common to all. (p.
234) Regarding the placement of Hṛṣīkeśa in the corners starting from the southeast:
"Then one should place Hṛṣīkeśa in the corners beginning with the southeast. (26.52)
One should place their specific weapons— the conch, the plow, the mace, and the trident— among these;
and in the eight intermediate corners, there is the placement of Janārdana.
Likewise, one should then place Janārdana in the eight intermediate corners.
Their specific weapons were the staff, the spear, the javelin, the noose, and the goad;
likewise the thunderbolt, the axe, and the hundred-mouthed fire.
One should draw these [symbols] upon their hands in the proper sequence;
on each respective side, one should draw the corresponding retinue, placing the individual members of the retinue at the sides of those [deities]. || 26-55 ||
Then, one should remember the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) together with the Earth upon the Earth—
the God in the form of a boar, bearing the conch, discus, and mace—
and one should meditate upon Puruṣottama as being united with the Earth upon the Earth. (26–56)
In the sky, one should perform the recollection of Narasiṃha; indeed, one should contemplate Nārasiṃha of immeasurable luster—
terrifying, adorned with many ornaments, and having torn asunder the Asura.

One should perform the recollection of the discus, mace, bow, and sword in the east and other directions. (p. 235) The wise one should visualize the discus situated within a great flame in the eastern direction; likewise, he should visualize the mace situated within a flame in the southern direction. (26.58)
One should visualize the Śārṅga bow situated in the midst of extremely fierce flames in the western direction;
likewise, one should visualize the most formidable sword in the northern direction.
For the construction of the other part of this yantra, one should arrange a wheel with twenty-four spokes in the middle;
then, in the middle of the other part of the yantra, there should be a lotus situated within a wheel.
A wheel with twenty-four spokes, with a beautiful rim and a radiant form.

In the center of that, one should draw a twelve-petaled lotus; one should place the wheel (cakra) within the lotus, which is endowed with twelve petals. Upon its pericarp (karṇikā), there is the placement of the fire-maṇḍala (āgneyamaṇḍala).
One should place the fiery mandala in the position of the pericarp of the lotus within the wheel.
In the center of that, one should draw Yoganṛsiṃha;
in the center of that, the eternal Nārasiṃha, with four arms, holding four discs, the Supreme One, whose limbs are bound by a yogic band (yogapaṭṭa). || 26-62 ||
He was seated at the foot of an aśoka tree, possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction,
adorned with all ornaments, and the remover of the suffering of all devotees.
The great ocean filled with boundless and innumerable auspicious qualities,
eternally compassionate toward his devotees, and the sole leader of all the worlds.
The placement of those two attendants at the edge of his feet (p. 236):
