having thus arranged them, one should place both of them at the edge of his feet—those two formidable executors of his command, whose forms are like dark blue clouds. (26.65)
One should place two excellent [deities] with uplifted bodies, fearsome eyes, and terrifying weapons,
their faces made formidable by fangs and their eyes round.
One should then meditate upon the eight Śaktis of the wheel in the directions beginning with the east;
one should contemplate those eight women surrounding the wheel,
their hair tied up high, who have attained the bloom of youth.
Adorned with all ornaments, two-armed, and holding a garland, one should visualize the goddess Jayā of yellow complexion in the eastern direction. (26.68)
In the southeast, one should recollect the goddess Mohinī, who is dark-complexioned and has long eyes;
and in the south, the goddess Vijayā, who has a dark form.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the supreme goddess Hlādinī of red color in the southwest, and Ajitā of yellow color in the west. (26–70)
In the northwestern direction is Māyā, eternal and black in color;
in the northern direction is Aparājitā, red in color. (26–71)
Thereafter, one should visualize Siddhi of smoky color in the northeast.
Such is the majesty of the yantra with its aforementioned characteristics;
thus, this great yantra is the destroyer of great sins.
It bestows long life, health, and wealth; it grants sons, friends, and a wife;
it pacifies all obstacles and wards off all that is evil. (26.73)
Whatever one desires, by drawing that particular yantra, it bestows that very thing upon him.
One should fashion the yantra out of gold, enriched with gems, coral, and pearls.

If a king attains a kingdom free from thorns and disease, it is because of the efficacy of this yantra written even on birch bark; having written this on birch bark with saffron and sandalwood, [one achieves] the accomplishment of all fruits. (26–75)
Whatever mortal wears this upon his head shall have all his desires fulfilled;
indeed, the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas will quickly perish for him. (26.76)
Regarding the fact that the consecration of this stone yantra is a means to liberation:
"Whoever performs the consecration of this stone on the surface of the earth, having attained all desires here, shall obtain union with Viṣṇu. (26.77)
The fruit of fashioning a mechanical image from iron and other materials:
"Or the wise man who should fashion an image out of iron or silver attains the fruit of the three aims of life and, moreover, liberation before long. (26.78)

The fruit of the emanation of the sacred site (āyatana) consists of everything from the plowing [of the ground] up to the consecration; whoever performs these rites from the plowing through to the consecration, and his descendants as well, shall attain the unsurpassed worlds of merit. (26.79)
The Fruit of Recollecting the Yantra in Times of Fear and Other Circumstances:
(p. 238) Whoever should recollect this [mantra] when fear arises, in battle, or in debate, victory is already in his hand; no deliberation is required in this matter. (26.80)
The worship of the Yantra at the three junctions of the day is the means to liberation.
Whoever worships this unsurpassed Yantra at the three junctions is freed from the threefold suffering and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The commencement of the specific ritual for the protection of kings:

"But listen, O Nārada, to the special rule regarding the method of protecting kings—whether they are seekers of a kingdom, those whose kingdom has been seized, or those who have been humiliated by other monarchs. (26–82)
In that regard, first is the procedure for honoring the preceptor:
considering the Guru, the bestower of the *saudarśana* yantra, as superior to all others, one should worship him with great wealth. (26.83)

Then follows the procedure for the worship of the Blessed One; then [one should meditate upon] the god Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes are as long as lotuses, who is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with all ornaments. (26.84)
One should propitiate the four-armed [deity] according to the procedure taught by the preceptor. Then follows the construction of the yantra, made of refined gold and inlaid with jewels and coral.
One should have this supreme yantra fashioned, adorned with all ornaments. (p. 239) Regarding the fact that the construction of the yantra is the cause for attaining a kingdom:
"By the mere act of making this, one obtains a healthy kingdom. (26.86)
Regarding the fact that worship preceded by consecration is the cause for attaining the earth within the seven continents:
"One should worship this [deity] after having consecrated it with devotion; it bestows all accomplishments.
Thereafter, one obtains the earth consisting of the seven continents along with its cities. (26.87)
Ultimately, there is the attainment of the status of protector of the three worlds;
the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas become constantly submissive.
He protects the entire kingdom of the three worlds upon the surface of the earth. (26.88)
The accomplishment of turning back malevolent spells cast by others:
"Malevolent spells cast by others, failing to reach him, turn back in terror;
they enter back toward the practitioner like a river struck by a mountain. (26.89)
The accomplishment of warding off obstacles and the like occurs;
obstructions perish, enemies flee, and there is no fear from untimely death, wild beasts, snakes, thieves, diseases, and so forth. (26.90)
In his kingdom, O sage, there exists no force [of disorder] within that lineage;
for all, the accomplishment of their own duty prevails, and they always engage in their respective duties alone. (26.91)
By means of this yantra, Indra, who had been cursed by Durvāsas, regained his own position once again. (p.
240) Formerly, when the Lord of Śacī had been deprived of his kingdom due to the curse of Durvāsas, he regained the entire celestial realm through the grace of this [yantra]. (26.92)
The acquisition of the machine by the four-faced one from the presence of the Blessed One:
"In ancient times, Hari proclaimed this great machine to Brahmā;
then, by means of the four-faced one, Viśvakarman fashioned both the machine and the celestial chariot."
And Brahmā, having summoned Viśvakarman, caused this to be made.
From that time forth, the gods, gandharvas,
and dānavas established the protection of the machine itself; likewise, the ancient kings performed the rite of its protection by means of this.
Therefore, this is the supreme method of protection for all kings. || 26-94 ||
The conclusion of the chapter's meaning is like the brilliantly shining orb of the newly risen sun, resorted to by hosts of deities headed by the lotus-born Brahmā.

One should meditate upon the King of Machines (yantrarāja), which, though pervaded by the five elements, is served by the primordial nature (prakṛti), the great principle (mahat), and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Mahāsudarśana Yantra," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Tantra.
Chapter Twenty-seven, titled "Description of the Dhāraka Machine," from the beginning: Verse 1565.
Merely meditated upon once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Following a recapitulation of what has been stated, Nārada poses a question concerning the sustaining machine (dhārakayantra):
"The detailed description of the King of Machines, the God of gods, has been told."
Its essential nature, its means of accomplishment, its method, and likewise its fruit—[these are explained]. (27.1)
Today I wish to hear this, O Blessed One, Supreme Lord:
by whom is this most wonderful, divine ornament worn? (27.2)
I do not perceive in anyone the power to uphold this;
because of its extreme power, you ought to sever this doubt.
The commencement of his reply: Ahirbudhnya said—“It is true, O one of great splendor; it cannot be restrained by anyone.”
Except for this other instrument, O powerful divine sage. (27.4)
Listen now, O best of sages, to his true nature and prowess:
having first fashioned the great Indra-maṇḍala, he first created the Maheindra-maṇḍala consisting of the earth. (p. 242)

Adorned with all ornaments and marked with the insignia of the yantra, one should perform the placement of the syllables of the earth-seed (bhū-bīja) in its corners; one should place this supreme seed-syllable of Bhauma in its corners. (27–6)

Supported on all sides by the eight nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, [the seat is placed] in the eastern part of the mandala; there, in the eastern portion of this mandala, are the two terrifying ones with fearsome eyes, Śeṣa and Gulika. (27–7)
One should draw the remaining two *gulikas*, looking at one another;
on the right side, Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla, gazing at each other. (27–8)
The practitioner should likewise place them in the southern direction;
in the west, he should thus draw Takṣaka and Mahāmbuja— those two, Takṣaka and Mahāmbuja— in the western direction.
In the northern part, O Sage, one should draw Kārkoṭaka and Ambuja; to the north, one should draw Kārkoṭaka and Ambuja.
In the center of that, it is resplendent with a whirling garland of great flames.
In the center, one should conceive of a fire-maṇḍala (p. 243);
the fire-maṇḍala is endowed with six corners and joined with the seed-syllable.
In its center, there is the placement of the wind-maṇḍala.
And having drawn that, one should draw the Vāyavya mandala in its center.
Circular, joined with a *bindu*, and endowed with its seed-syllable; in its center, one should draw a ten-spoked wheel (*daśāracakra*),
and in the middle of that, an incomparable wheel with a brilliantly shining rim.
One should arrange the "Crusher of Enemies" (Arimardana) diagram, filled with ten spokes;
upon these spokes, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Sudarśana and Nārasiṃha mantras— namely,
one should place this mantra of Sudarśana and this mantra of Nārasiṃha.
One should place two syllables each in sequence upon the nine spokes;
indeed, one should place the word "hana" on the tenth spoke of this [wheel].
Regarding the drawing of an eight-petalled lotus in the center of the wheel:
"In the center of the wheel, one should place a lotus endowed with eight petals; it is beautiful, set with a pericarp, and adorned with filaments. (27.15)
The placement of the *praṇava* (syllable Om) in the pericarp:
one should write the *tāra* (Om), which delivers one from the cycle of existence, in that pericarp;
right there, one should also write the name of the desired object to be accomplished.
After that, [one should state] the name of the person for whom the desired object is to be accomplished. || 27-16 ||
By means of such a sustaining instrument (*dhārakayantra*), there is the accomplishment of all aims. (p.
244) This is the supreme, divine [means], the most auspicious of the auspicious, the purifier of purifiers, and the warder-off of the affliction of thieves. (27.17)
This formidable and unsurpassed [mantra], which accomplishes all aims and is worshipped by the universe—
by means of this yantra, Indra formerly attained victory over his enemies when the gods were overwhelmed by the Daityas. (27–18)
Having summoned Bṛhaspati, he then spoke these words:
"These Daityas and Dānavas are oppressing us most severely. (27.19)
"By what means, O Blessed One, shall we conquer the great asuras? O Blessed One, tell us how this loss of their strength will come to pass. (27.20)
Thus addressed by Maghavan, Bṛhaspati spoke this regarding the construction and other matters of the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha Yantra here.
"All enemies shall perish, O slayer of Bala!
Having spoken thus, he established the yantra in the city of Maghavan.
Rich with jewels, coral, and pearls, it was made of gold and possessed immeasurable luster;
from that time forward, the Daityas were deprived of their fortune and their splendor was destroyed.
Defeated, they flee in all directions, having lost their dwellings;
for this is that exceedingly powerful machine, highly honored by the gods.
This very machine possesses the quality of being the bearer of the previously mentioned Great Sudarśana Machine (p.
245). By means of this very machine, O divine sage, that supreme Sudarśana machine is borne in its manifold form as the Viṣṭara [the seat]. (27.25)
Thus have I described this great Sudarśana yantra;
by the power of this yantra, one possesses the heroic energy of both Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha. (27.26)
O King, while the land as a whole is capable of supporting the aforementioned machinery [of governance],
it is that very earth alone which is capable of supporting this distinguished [ruler],
he whose protector is a righteous king of firm prowess. (27.27)
Worshipping the gods, the twice-born, the preceptor, and the wise, and being supremely devoted to the sacred, this is the king’s constant rule for worship;
the king, unwearied, should worship this wheel-like form. (27–28)
Or likewise, it may have a human form with faces on both sides.
This is the special reason for the worshipfulness of the giver of this mantra;
the wise person should especially honor the giver of this mantra as distinguished. (27–29)

By means of this mantra-ritual, the procedure for the rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration is established. The king himself should cause these rites, from plowing to consecration, to be performed according to the path taught in this mantra. (27–30)
The unity of this tantra with those such as the Sāttvata is [established] by the path prescribed in the Sāttvata and other tantras;
O Sage, [this applies] to the mantra of Sudarśana or that of Nṛsiṃha. (27–31)
All ritual procedures performed according to the kalpas, when carried out in his presence, become entirely effective through his power. (27–32)
Therefore, having established [the deity] according to the aforementioned method, one should worship it.
By this worship, kings obtain their kingdoms and other such gains; the king shall attain sovereignty, victory, prosperity, long life, and health. (27–33)
For a king who worships constantly, there is a specific reward: this entire earth, consisting of seven continents and clothed by the ocean, shall come under his control. (27.34)
Regarding the construction of the temple and the sacrificial pit for the purpose of the *homa*:
having constructed a temple endowed with the proper characteristics as a supreme seat, one should have a sacrificial pit made right there according to the prescribed rule for this mantra. (27–35)

The practitioner, while accomplishing those rites which are for the king, should perform the fire-oblation and other rituals there; being composed, he should offer oblations into this sacrificial pit with this mantra. (27–36)
An alternative procedure for other locations (p.
247): If, however, the rite of protection for a king is to be performed with this very mantra, it should be done in a beautiful temple of Viṣṇu or in a decorated pavilion. (27–37)
Having constructed this very sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) right here and having honored the king with great wealth,
he should have the performer of his own rites act as the bestower of this mantra.
Furthermore, regarding the specific fruits of the worship of the yantra:
"By this, the king shall indeed have accomplished all his goals and obtain his kingdom;
he shall be free from disease, without rivals, and long-lived. (27–39)
His city shall be filled with many thousands of nāgas, with innumerable horses, with chariots, and with the best of men.
And whichever king should worship this unsurpassed sovereign of yantras, by that act all deities are worshipped, because it is superior to all mantras. (27.41)
For whatever purpose one might worship him, he strives supremely for that person's own sake;
he brings about the welfare of all beings as well as of the king. (27.42)
In this mantra and this yantra, the authority belongs only to kings;
this mantra and this yantra are prescribed for kings alone, O Nārada, while the various types of mantras are for the benefit of all people. (27–43)
Those mantra-practitioners who are devoted to the worship of this [deity] protect the king even from the mouth of misfortune. (27.44)

This [attainment] is the means for achieving those respective fruits even through prostration and so forth; whether by prostrating to Him, by worshipping Him, by chanting His names, or even by remembering Him.
One should constantly satisfy him in every way and see that all his desires fall into one's own hands. || 27-45 ||
Thus has been declared this summary of the chapter's meaning: this form of the Yantra, together with its mantra,
is engaged in the destruction of all evils for those who take refuge in it.
Therefore, in this world, a sovereign who has fulfilled his duties and attained his desires shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin) and obtain the entire surface of the earth.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Sustaining Yantra," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1611:
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Method for Worshipping the Blessed One."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of tens of millions of sins;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The commencement of the exposition of the rules for propitiation:
Ahirbudhnya says—
O Nārada, I shall describe the rules for propitiation in brief.
It bestows long life, health, victory, and land, and grants wealth and grain. (28-1)
It is the means for achieving fruits in this world and the next;
it is the supreme means for those desiring sons, cattle, and food;
it bestows enjoyment and liberation, brings peace, and is the cause of overcoming others. (28–2)
Therein, first is the procedure for bathing:
having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha) and taken earth from a clean place according to the mantra, one should divide it into two parts and perform the purification of the body with one portion. (28.3)
Having bathed and sipped water, one should take another portion of earth and divide it into three parts;
with one part, one should perform the binding of the directions upon the left hand.
Then, O Nārada, one should apply [the substance] as an ointment to the limbs with another portion;
thereafter, one should resolve upon using a third portion for the sacred bathing-place (tīrtha-pīṭha). (28.5)
There, one should remember the Gaṅgā as having issued from the left foot of Viṣṇu;
then, having offered this water of honor (arghya) to her, one should take up a handful of water.
One should sprinkle it upon one's own head three times, having consecrated it seven times with the mantra;
then, submerged therein, one should place one's head at the lotus feet of the God. (28.7)
One should recite the mantra according to one's capacity, being intent upon its meditation;
then, having emerged from the water, performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), and put on the lower garment and upper cloth.

Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should meditate upon the gods and others as being of the nature of Acyuta, satisfy them with libations, and perform the remainder of the daily rites according to the rules.

Then, having arrived at the sacrificial ground, the self-controlled practitioner, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should remain silent and begin the worship. || 28.10 ||
Having gone to that beautiful sanctuary provided with four gates, the self-possessed one should worship all the attendants stationed at the doors and then take refuge in the pavilion.
The description of the pavilion:
It was lofty, endowed with auspiciousness, and adorned with jeweled floors;
it possessed many golden pillars embellished with gems and coral. || 28.12 ||
It was provided with networks of lamps made of gold, surrounded by various banners and adorned with archways. (28.13)
It was resplendent everywhere with networks of jeweled bells and canopies made of fine linen,
and it was adorned throughout with jeweled pedestals.
Therein, in the center of that jewel-pavilion, was the construction of an altar,
supremely radiant and adorned with four pillars made of ruby.
It was provided with a canopy made of pearls and a jeweled four-sided platform,
featuring a lofty pedestal fashioned from lapis lazuli and furnished with lamps.
If one is unable to perform it in this way, the worshipper should meditate thus:
there, in the center of the four-pillared pavilion, upon a seat consisting of a lotus within a wheel, is the Blessed One together with his retinue. (28.17)

In the lotus supported by the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), Kūrma, Ananta, Dharma, and the others, which is surrounded by the moon, the sun, light, and the qualities of sattva and so forth; || 18 ||
Thus attended by his retinue in the manner described,
he was surrounded by the Vedas, mantras, as well as by weapons, missiles, and spears.

Seated upon that very seat, one should meditate upon the Lord seated upon His own seat, while offering prayers to the Blessed One: "I am yours; I worship You with the ritual offerings granted by You. (28-20)
One should say, "By means of those pertaining to touch," and "O God, by means of those pertaining to food.
The sequence of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) should dissolve the principles of the body (dehatattva) by way of the process of reabsorption (pratisaṃcara). || 28-21 ||
Then, having dried up this gross body, one should burn it;
with the first breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should place the mantra at the navel.
By means of the sound produced from that, which resides within the *suṣumnā*,
having reached the sphere of wind by means of that very wind arising therefrom— || 28-23 ||
O divine sage, one should then wither this gross body by means of the second [practice], prāṇāyāma; thereafter, one should place the mantra in the heart.
The preceptor should burn the body with the fire arisen from the mantra abiding within the maṇḍala;
he should burn his own self with the third, which is prāṇāyāma.
Placing it below the left lotus-foot of Viṣṇu,
one should indeed meditate upon oneself being bathed in the nectar spat from its big toe.
Then, having assumed a physical form through the five Upaniṣadic mantras,
the knower of mantras, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (nyāsa) with the mantras, should meditate upon the Sudarśana.
Having invoked [the deity] through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) from the solar orb into the heart-lotus,
one should then begin the worship after performing the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
One whose senses and mind are restrained should first perform the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga).
[Then] one should arrange the vessels and other items on one's right side with perfumed, purifying waters. (28–29)
One should place the filled vessel consecrated with the root mantra;
likewise, one should arrange all other ritual implements on the left side. (28–30)
Then, having spread out a perfectly pure cloth before him,
he should place the arghya vessel upon it in the southeastern direction.
Then one should place the vessel for water for the feet (pādya) in the southwest corner;
one should place the vessel for water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the northwest corner.
Then, one should place the vessel for the bath in the direction of Śaṅkara.
Furthermore, the substances to be cast into the *arghya* and other offerings are white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds.
Barley, fragrance, fruit, and flower—this is called the eightfold arghya.
Also [the eight items are] dūrvā grass, viṣṇuparṇī, śyāmāka grain, and lotus. (28–34)
One should prepare four substances for the water for the feet along with water;
for the water for sipping, the substances are cloves, nutmeg, and cardamom.
The wise one should prepare the bath materials, such as white mustard seeds and so forth, as previously described. (p.

254) Therein, having first recited the mantra, he should touch [the vessel] while saying, "I intend to offer the seat of the mantra, the expansion, and the water for honor (*arghya*)," and then offer the *arghya*. || 28-36 ||
O divine sage, one should speak thus in due order regarding the water-vessels for the feet and the others;
having filled all these vessels completely with fragrant water. (28–37)
Having taken a small amount of water from the *arghya* vessel with another vessel,
one should place it upon the right hand of the deity while reciting the root mantra.
Having offered a flower, one should then sprinkle the feet of the deity with water for the feet (pādya);
having wiped them with a cloth, one should then offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Then, one should pour the remnants of the water for the *arghya* and other offerings into another vessel;
thereafter, one should offer sandalwood paste, garlands, incense, and a lamp.
Furthermore, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) and mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa),
and thereafter betel (tāmbūla), one should then prostrate and perform the self-offering (ātmanivedana).
Having prepared a second seat for the bath, one should worship the bathing pedestal with scents, flowers, and other offerings; then,
having informed [the deity] and offered the sandals, the Lord proceeds to the bathing seat.
Thereafter, having removed [the deity's] garments, ornaments, and garlands,
one should offer a bathing cloth for the purpose of bathing, as well as water for the feet and water for sipping.
Then one should provide a footstool and offer a tooth-stick;
furthermore, one should provide a tongue-scraper and a means for cleansing the mouth. (28.44)
Again, the offering of water for sipping (ācamanīya), as well as the presentation of a mirror;
again, the gift of betel leaf (tāmbūla), and after that, the anointing with oil (tailābhyaṅga).
One should perform the rite of anointing with fragrant unguents, the gift of *āmalaka* fruit, and then the gift of water, as well as the gift of a comb and a cloth. (28.46)
Then one should provide for the deity a cloth for the purification of the body;
one should apply a coating of turmeric, and thereafter perform the washing.
One should give a garment for an upper cloth and likewise a sacred thread;
one should provide water for the feet and for sipping, as well as variegated sandalwood paste.
Incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, lamps, and water for rinsing the mouth, together with all auspicious elements such as dance, instrumental music, song, and so forth. (28–49)

Then one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), and thereafter the rite of lustration (nīrājana); then the bathing cloth, the garment, and the upper robe, and after that the sacred thread (upavīta).
Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) to the deity,
the preceptor should subsequently worship the third seat, the ornamentation seat (alaṃkārāsana), by means of sprinkling and other rites.
Having made the request and offered the sandals once the deity has taken his seat upon the mat,
one should then arrange the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings as before.
Then one should offer the *arghya*, the *pādya*, and thereafter the *ācamanīya*. (p.
256) One should perform the *arghya* and other rites with substances such as fragrant sandalwood and the like.
Then one should present variegated garments and ornaments.
Then follows the gift of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should also offer fragrant flowers and the presentation of a mirror;
likewise, one should give incense and lamps, and again the water for sipping (ācamanīya). || 28-55 ||
Then one should recite hymns of praise, followed by the display of parasols and chowries,
the sight of vehicles, and likewise the sound of the conch shell.
Likewise, one should listen to the sounds of the lute, the horn, the kettledrum, and other instruments;
then, one should worship with dance, instrumental music, song, and so forth, according to the mantra.
The preceptor should offer a flower to the deity with the root mantra,
presenting a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) in every direction while proceeding in a clockwise circumambulation.
Having given [the offering] and bowed again, one should indeed praise the deity with hymns and offer oneself to the Blessed One for the state of a servant. (28–59)
Then, having meditated, one should recite the mantra with concentration according to one's ability;
O Sage, one should then duly worship the preceptor with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (28–60)
One should present to him the mantras, complete with all ritual enjoyments;
then one should give mouth-perfume, betel, and the water-offering (arghya).
The fourth [rite] is the offering of the seat for the meal.
Having honored the seat for the meal and informed the Lord, one should offer the sandals;
once He has sat down there, one should then offer water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamana).
Then, having performed the worship, one should place curd, clarified butter, milk, honey, and fragrant substances into a vessel and perform the rites of drying and so forth. (28.63)
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the arghya water itself, one should then offer the madhuparka;
thereafter, the worshipper should give gold, a cow, and jewels.
The presentation of the sacrificial offering consists of well-prepared food, clarified butter, curd, milk, honey, roots, sweetmeats, unctuous side dishes, and fruits. (28.65)
Whatever [foods] are available at the proper time, pure, excellent, most delicious, abundant, and whatever others that are pleasing to the heart; || 28-66 ||
Having purified it by means of drying and other rites, and having sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering,
one should perform protection with the *astra-mantra*, preceded by the presentation of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and worship (*arhaṇa*).
Having formed the *mudrā* known as *surabhi*, one should offer this to the deity;
thereafter, one should present an incense burner (*anuvāsa*), and after that, a mirror.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya), as well as hand-cleansing materials, sandalwood paste, mouth-freshener, and betel leaf; and having offered these to him, one should prostrate.
Furthermore, the fifth is the seat of mantra (mantrāsana). Then,
having placed the seat of mantra and wiped it with the *kūrca* brush,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and after making a formal request, one should offer the sandals (*pādukā*).
When the Lord of Gods has thus ascended, one should remove the garlands and other offerings,
give water for the feet and water for sipping, and then present incense.
One should give him the sweetest fruits as well as betel;
thereafter, one should worship the deity with songs, instrumental music, dance, and so forth. (28.72)
Having performed circumambulation for him, one should then prostrate like a staff;
then, having worshipped the deity in the sixth posture, the paryanka (lotus) seat, one should address the Lord.
Then, after the god had taken his seat upon the couch by the offering of the sandals, [the worshipper],
being composed, again offered water for the feet and water for sipping.
O Mahāmati, having removed garlands, ornaments, and the like—
those garlands, ornaments, and fine garments suitable for the bed— (28.75)
One should give other items that are pleasant to the touch, as well as a sacred thread (yajñopavīta);
one should also give water for sipping (ācamanīya), and then offer fragrance and flowers.
Having offered mouth-freshener and betel leaf, one should praise him with hymns;
having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation, one should go for refuge.
Having performed a circumambulation, one should place the deity seated in the yogic posture upon the surface of the earth, together with the mind, intellect, and ego.
Like a tortoise, [I withdraw] my four limbs and my head as the fifth right there.
Whatever inauspicious act has been committed by me—whether through ignorance or even with knowledge—[is offered] as a prayer for service. (28.79)
"You ought to forgive all of that; accept me as your slave.
In this way, one should propitiate Hari in both ways. (28.80)

Sudarśana and Nṛsiṃha are forms of Viṣṇu; Sudarśana is thus the means for liberation for one who has performed such worship. Indeed, O Nārada, even for one who worships in this manner for but a single day— 28–81.
Liberation stands in his hand, let alone all desires;
by this it is established through a *kaimutika* argument that [this practice] is a means for achieving even incidental fruits, as well as all the world-protectors and the hosts of gods. (28–82)
Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and hosts of Apsarases—all these become subject to one's will here; how much more so, then, the humans on earth? (28.83)
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kuśmāṇḍas,
and vināyakas shall become the servants of that high-souled practitioner.

The procedure for the worship of the retinue: likewise, there is the worship of his attendants— the gods, the Śaktis, the women, the mantras, and the missiles and weapons— each by their own respective names.
And one should perform the sixteen services in sequence, ending with the word "namas."

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Worship of the Blessed Lord," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Twenty-nine, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Worship for Desired Ends," beginning from verse 1696:
A single meditation quickly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Nārada’s inquiry regarding the manner in which the worship of the Blessed One serves as a means for attaining secondary fruits:
"By these acts of worship, how and for whom do the gods and other deities [bestow results]?"
And others who have been mentioned come under one's control; tell me that according to the truth. (29.1)
The commencement of the reply by Ahirbudhnya:
"O great sage, because a Kṣatriya especially desires victory..."
By means of which specific mode of worship all beings indeed become submissive. || 29-2 ||
Listen; I shall tell you that in brief, exactly as it is:
how each particular mode of propitiation serves as a means for the conquest of those respective directions, should a lord of the earth desire victory in all quarters. (29.3)
Through specific modes of propitiation, one shall obtain victory over this or that [region].
In that regard, if a king desires victory over kings in the eastern direction, he should [propitiate] those from the east. (29–4)
One should propitiate the god Sudarśana with excellent offerings:
with white flowers, white garments, and white unguents as well. (29.5)
Having worshipped Sudarśana with rice cooked in milk and enriched with curd, in the pure, decorated pavilion previously described, in the presence of the deity; 29-6.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing the characteristics of a palace, which is surrounded by four corners,
one should then take fire and kindle it with wood from the bilva tree.
Seated there, facing the east, pure and composed,
O Nārada, he placed bilva fruits smeared with clarified butter upon it.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations with the root mantra into a blazing fire;
by these oblations, the entire earth as far as the ocean shall become submissive to the east.
By means of a *koṭi-homa* sacrifice with fruits made of *bilva* wood, he shall bring under his control the eastern region of Plakṣadvīpa along with its king. (29.10)
And by means of these two factions, O Nārada, Śālmalī shall bring the eastern region, along with its kings, under his control as if it were his own country.
Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and the one named Puṣkaradvīpa— these are indeed situated in order to the east, measuring one, two, three, four, five, and six [thousand yojanas] respectively.
They shall come under the power of the king through ten million fruit-oblations;
and among these islands, the city of Māghavatī lies in the east.
By ten koṭis of oblations, she will certainly come under one's control;
for the sake of protecting the worlds, Vāsava [will do so] with a single portion. (29.14)
He too will remain right there and provide him assistance with women, food, drinks, excellent horses, and elephants. (29.15)
Just as a king dwells without fear in his own city, that monarch will take delight in those very objects brought to him by mere thought. (29.16)
By its power, all the oceans will be solidified so that they shall become capable of being traversed by chariot, just like dry land.
And Vāsava himself shall bring him a divine necklace composed of all kinds of jewels, which bears the marks of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
If the desire for victory over the southern direction arises in the monarch regarding the region of the south,
one should lead the deity, facing southward, into the previously mentioned pavilion. (29–19)
Having worshipped the god— who wears red garlands and garments, is anointed with red sandalwood paste, and is clad in crimson robes— according to the prescribed method.
Having offered as an oblation to him rice mixed with jaggery and sesame seeds,
one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a half-moon according to the characteristics of a temple.
Adorned with kuśa grass, flowers, and parched grain, and remaining uninjured,
he sat there facing south, in front of the Lord.
Having taken fire with a mantra and kindled it with *khadira* wood, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with millions of red lotuses. (29.23)
Then that southern earth, extending to the edge of the ocean, would come under her control; and the kings of that region, bearing their offerings, were kept waiting at the gate. (29–24)
They will remain waiting for the time of that great-souled one;
then, they will be honored throughout the six continents in the southern quarter.
By means of ten million oblations of red lotuses, one gains mastery over one, two, three, four, five, or six [beings], including kings, respectively. (29–26)
To the south lies this delightful city of Yama, Saṃyaminī;
it shall come under one's control by means of ten koṭis of offerings of red lotuses. (29.27)
Yama too, being pleased by his disposition and with a joyful mind,
will not cause the king's desire to be otherwise.
No untimely death shall occur in that region for those who are subject to Yama in the city of Saṃyaminī.
They will all come under his control, without a doubt,
adorned with divine, beautiful, and red armlets that bear the marks of universal sovereignty.
But Yama himself, having taken it, joyfully bestows it upon him.
When a king desires to conquer the western region—that is, toward the western quarter—then [he should proceed]. (29–31) p. 264)
In the decorated pavilion, one should lead the deity facing westward,
wearing a variegated garland and adorned with diverse silken garments.
Adorned with variegated unguents and colorful ornaments,
having prepared an oblation of honey-rice, one should present this to the God.
Having constructed a well-adorned sacrificial pit in the shape of a lotus,
the self-controlled practitioner, having established the fire there, sits before the deity.
Then, having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks made of *śamī* wood,
one who is composed in mind should offer a million oblations of *karavīra* flowers smeared with honey while reciting the mantra.
Then the earth, including the oceans, to the west of Jambūdvīpa, along with its kings, will come under the control of that monarch. (29–36)
And by ten million oblations of *karavīra* flowers, and by twenty million, and by thirty, forty, fifty, and sixty million respectively. (29–37)
The six divisions of the western continents will come under the control of the king;
there shall be the city named Sukhā, situated in the west, delightful and supremely radiant. (29–38)
It was filled with foods, linctuses, and drinks always kept ready,
and it was adorned by Nandana groves endowed with divine trees.
It is adorned with lakes rich with ever-blooming lotuses, and endowed with pleasure-mountains embellished with various jewels. (29.40)
Adorned with palaces and lofty pavilions made of gold,
such shall be that city for the enjoyment of that king.
Varuṇa himself held a parasol adorned with jewels and coral,
strewn with strings of pearls, dripping with nectar, and worthy of worship.
If the lord of the earth is intent on conquering the northern region, the King, being pleased, will bestow that sign of universal monarchs upon him. (29-43)
One should lead the deity, who is facing north, onto a seat consisting of a lotus upon a disc;
he is wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow flowers.
Having prepared an oblation of ghee and rice, one should worship Sudarśana with it, adorned with coral ornaments and anointed with powdered saffron.
One should construct a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) in front of it, characterized by a circular temple-shape;
facing north, one should establish the fire in that pit situated within the pavilion.
Having kindled the fire with udumbara wood, once the flame is blazing,
one should first offer a million oblations of nandyāvarta flowers.
Therefore, this land of Bhārata, together with its golden mountains and its kings, will undoubtedly come under his control. (29.48)
By means of two hundred thousand oblations, the year known as Kiṃpuruṣa will undoubtedly bring that king, along with his subjects, under the control of that monarch.
With three hundred thousand [offerings], Harivarṣa together with its king shall be brought under control;
with four hundred thousand oblations, Bhadrāśva will come under one's sway.
For a lord of the earth who performs five, six, or seven hundred thousand oblations,
the regions of Ilāvṛta, Ketumāla, and Ramyaka shall come under his control.
In the golden region of Meru, together with eight and nine [others],
he will bring under his control a sovereign lord of the earth through one hundred thousand oblations.
O Nārada, the six islands whose mouths are like those of the Plakṣa tree are lands of enjoyment; they shall come under one's control through oblations performed ten thousand times the stated number.
To the north of all the continents and regions lies the supreme city,
renowned as Vibhāvarī, the most wonderful abode of Soma.
Through ten million oblations, she will come under his control;
likewise, those classes of deities who are subject to Soma shall also be under his command.
O Sage, they shall all remain under the control of that king;
by his power, Soma himself will take up the fly-whisks.
Resembling a mass of one's own moonlight, endowed with jeweled stalks,
the white insignia of universal sovereignty, beautiful to behold and cool.
The illustrious one, pleased with him whose deeds have inspired wonder, will grant [his boon].
Through the victory over the great quarters, he has become a perfected master of the intermediate directions; thus, victory belongs to the lord of the intermediate directions. (29.58)
The other world-protectors will present offerings if the king’s exertion toward conquering the upper worlds proceeded within the domain of the upper world. (29–59)
One should honor the deity upon the jewel-throne of the pavilion, seated facing the east,
draped with fragrant garlands and adorned with ornaments of pearl.

Having thus worshipped him according to the prescribed rite— his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and his body clothed in silken garments— one should offer milk-rice mixed with sugar-candy.
Having announced the oblation rich in clarified butter and provided with all kinds of cooked fruits,
[he should prepare] an eight-sided sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the temple, endowed with every auspicious feature.
Having consecrated it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), the knower of mantras, taking up fire,
should kindle the sacrificial fire (jātavedas) with wood made of black aloe-wood (kṛṣṇāguru).
There, one should indeed perform an oblation of clarified butter (ājya-homa) numbering one hundred crores;
by that oblation, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) will then come under one's control.
Then all those inhabitants of the world— the Siddhas, Gandharvas,
and Kinnaras, as well as the Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and Cāraṇas, together with their hosts of women— [approached].
With lutes, flutes, drums, and all kinds of musical instruments and rhythmic clapping, there were supreme rows of enjoyments containing his accounts of misfortunes and deeds. (29.66)
Singing as they surround him, they will gladden the lord of the earth;
and by ten million times ten million oblations, heaven shall become subject to his will.
There, even Mahendra, accompanied by the goddess Śacī and together with hosts of Apsarases, mounted the elephant Airāvata.
Having approached that high-souled one and descended [from his vehicle], filled with joy,
he placed him upon a jeweled throne and had the auspicious benedictions recited.
With dances, songs, and instrumental music, with the sounds of divine drums,
and with the blares of conchs and trumpets, Vāsava will consecrate the king to the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), accompanied by waters brought from sacred fords (tīrtha).
Then he gave him a jeweled crown, a single divine elephant, a horse equal to the wind, a celestial chariot resembling the Puṣpaka,
and a divine golden garland fashioned from lotuses.
And moreover, being pleased, he will grant equality with his own self. || 29-71 ||
Having caused the king, the sovereign of the entire earth, to perform a hundred horse-sacrifices,
and having bestowed upon him a hundred celestial nymphs;
The slayer of Vṛtra, together with the gods, shall go to the third heaven.
If the wheel-turning monarch desires to conquer the realm of the nāgas, and if he is born among the nāga worlds,
[he shall find it] adorned with divine ornaments made of rubies. (29.73)
One should worship the God, whose limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, with lotuses;
and having offered him an oblation of ground rice enriched with molasses.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) characterized by a palace and having six corners, with a blazing fire,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) of ten million times ten million cakes.
By that means, Bhogavatī, the supreme city of the principal Nāgas headed by Takṣaka, shall come under the control of this king as his own city.
Beholding his power, that Naga king brought forth great, brilliantly shining jewels;
two earrings made of gems, along with women—
Having taken hold of truth, he shall attain universal sovereignty.
The general conventions have been stated;
now hear, O Nārada, the characteristics of those both mentioned and unmentioned, by which the practitioner of mantra attains success in his desired objective. (29.78)
The monasteries consist of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine [units]; they have three, four, or five facades, and their width and height are equal. (29.79)
Thus, nine groups are proclaimed for the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the center;
five groups are likewise for the cardinal directions and the center, while the remaining ones are rows facing east.
One, two, and so forth, up to four [yogas] are proclaimed for the rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi);
while for minor rites, one, three, and so forth, up to nine, are used, excluding the ninth.
Palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, khadira, and other such trees fit for sacrifice;
as well as dūrvā grass and sesamum seeds and the like, are recommended for auspicious rites. (29–82)
The *kāraskara* and other such [offerings] are for minor rites; likewise, the *kaṭubīja* and others are used for [rites of] subjugation.
The types of fire-oblations (*homajāti*) range from one thousand up to a hundred thousand, and culminate at ten million. (29–83)
One, two, or even many officiating priests (ṛtvij) are prescribed according to one's supernatural power (ṛddhi);
if they should offer oblations into a single fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa), they should face the east or the north.

Auspicious rites are performed in the temples, gardens, and palaces of Vāsudeva; however, inauspicious rites are performed in places such as cremation grounds, according to the sequence of the rules for time.

One should perform auspicious rites during the conjunctions of the planets with the lunar mansions on the day; otherwise, it may be done differently—either by separating them, combining them, or according to one's own preference. (29.86)
Sacrifices such as the *lakṣahoma* and *koṭihoma*, performed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and other substances, are prescribed by tradition.
Having reflected thus, one should perform the means for attaining one's desired goal by means of the mantra. (29.87)
Whatever has not been mentioned [in one's own manual], one should perform according to what is stated in their own *gṛhya* text;
or the oblation (*homa*) may be performed as something unprecedented, without being accompanied by the *āghāra* offerings and other such rites. (29.88)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Worship for Specific Desires," in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā, a secret doctrine within the illustrious Pāñcarātra Tantra.
From the beginning, verse 1784:
The thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Births and Names of the Astras.
Contemplated even once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
The inquiry regarding how the divine weapons, beginning with the Brahmāstra, came to have gods as their attendants:
Nārada said—
How did the great and powerful weapons, headed by the Brahmāstra, [come to be so]?
The immeasurable missiles constitute the retinue of the God. || 30-1 ||
Regarding their births, there is this question: "O Maheśvara, why were these great weapons born?
What are the names of these? Tell them to me as I ask. (30.2)
In order to provide an answer to that, the narrative begins:
In ancient times, the god Nārāyaṇa himself remained established [in his own nature].
Before creation, he found no delight except in the instruments of his play.
For the sake of divine play, the Blessed One manifests as many;
therefore, for the sake of play, the Lord fashioned Himself into many forms.
This is the creation of Pradhāna presided over by Puruṣa.
Then, presided over by the Puruṣa, it [the intellect] created Pradhāna from itself. (30.4)
From Pradhāna comes the creation of Mahat;
from that, O Nārada, Mahat was produced from the Unmanifest (Avyakta);
from Mahat comes the creation of Ahaṃkāra.
Therefore, beyond that is the ego (ahaṃkāra), which consists of the three qualities (guṇatraya).
From the sāttvika ego (ahaṃkāra) arises the creation of the eleven organs; indeed, these ten organs consist of both cognition and action, and he produced the mind from that same sāttvika ego. (30.6)
From the *tāmasa* ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), there is the creation of the subtle elements and the gross elements.
O great sage, Janārdana created these ten—the gross elements and the subtle elements—from that *tāmasa* ego-sense. (30.7)
The creation of the cosmic egg, enveloped by seven coverings, brought forth that egg by means of these [principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas;
it was surrounded by seven coverings, each tenfold greater than the last.
Within that egg was the creation of the Four-faced One;
therein Viṣṇu himself created Prajāpati, the creator of high and low beings by means of his own powers. (30.9)

Time, which has become the power (śakti) of the Blessed One, acts as the auxiliary cause in creation; Hari, who consists of the universe, endowed with Time as his own power, performed the act of creation within the objects to be created, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat). (30.10)

Under the guise of the four-faced one, it is the Blessed Lord himself who, endowed with various powers, brought forth the manifold world— a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious— assuming the form of Brahmā. (30.11)
From the words of the Veda alone came the differentiation of the names and forms of the gods and others;
having examined the Vedas, Yama, the lord of beings such as the gods, fashioned their various names and forms just as they were before. (30.12)
The possibility of the Lord being a creator even though his desires are fulfilled:
although the Supreme Lord has at all times attained every desire, he nevertheless experienced the essence of the rasa of divine play (līlā) through the beings created by himself. (30.13)
Without even considering that the Blessed One himself is the protector, Hari himself, in the form of a partial incarnation, protects the entire world as another savior of the worlds. (30.14)
Without the elimination of the wicked, protection is impossible;
without the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas, it is not possible to protect the world consisting of gods, asuras, and humans. (30.15)

The Blessed One himself remains in the form of the discus for the purpose of destroying the wicked. Therefore, the Blessed Viṣṇu is established in the form of the discus; by that discus, all the Daityas and Dānavas are slain. (30.16)
The capacity of the gods and others to wear the Sudarśana:
"Due to the distinction between the gods, the celestial beings, and the rulers of the earth, it is not possible for them to wear the unsurpassed Sudarśana. (30.17)

Their classification is according to the nature of missiles (*astra*) and weapons (*śastra*); therefore, O Nārada, their various weapons and types of arms are manifold and many for the destruction of enemies. (30.18)
The origin of the weapons from the Sudarśana, which is identical with the Blessed Lord:
those weapons issued forth from the Sudarśana, which is the very form of Viṣṇu; they were unfailing, terrifying, and mighty. (30.19)
O great sage, the Lord of the Universe, in the form of a wheel, set his mind upon creating progeny and all weapons from his own form.
Therefore, the god assumed a terrifying and fierce form— tawny, with reddish-brown rolling eyes, and teeth from which fire issued forth, consuming wood like a blazing flame.
Terrible, with tawny hair that has the brilliance of lightning. || 30-21 ||
There, weapons born from his mouth [issued forth]:
the Nārāyaṇa, the Pāśupata, and likewise the Brāhma weapon;
the weapon named Brahmaśiras, Viṣṇu’s discus, and the Jṛmbhaṇa. (30.22)
Then [he gave him] the Kālapāśa, the Āgneya weapon, and likewise the Hayaśiras;
also the Prasvāpana, the Tāpasa, and the Kālāstra of immeasurable radiance.
The staff-wheel, the wheel of time, and likewise the wheel of dharma;
the trident of Śiva, the weapon of Rudra, and the terrible trident itself.
These principal weapons were born from the mouth of the Lord;
from his chest were born the Saṃmohana weapon, as well as the Aiṣīka, the Aindra, and the highly resplendent discus.
The two thunderbolts known as the Dry and the Wet, both terrifying to all; the Pānaka weapon, the Kaṅkāla, and the exceedingly dreadful Kāpāla.
The Saurya, the Vāruṇapāśa, the Saṃtāpana that subdues enemies,
the exceedingly fierce Vāruṇa weapon, and likewise the Dharmapāśa.
These weapons emerged from the chest of the god; likewise,
weapons born from his thighs,
two śaktis, the vāyavya weapon, and the mausala weapon [also issued forth].
The Gāndharva weapon, the Darpaṇa weapon, the Śoṣaṇa weapon, the Paradāraṇa weapon, the Tejaḥprabha weapon, the Paiśāca weapon, and the most terrible Aindra weapon. || 30-29 ||
The Yāmya, the Vilāpana weapon, the Vaidyādhara, the Amitrahā, as well as the Kaṅkaṇī, the Modakī, the Śikhara, and the Krauñca. (30–30)
He of vast prowess produced from his own thighs these weapons born of the feet:
the sword-jewel, the pacifier, and likewise the beloved of Kandarpa.
The Madana, Saumana, Satya, and Saṃvartana weapons, as well as the Māyādhara, Soma, Tvāṣṭra, and Śīteṣu weapons. || 30–32 ||
O Nārada, these Bhagāsra weapons were born from his feet;
the upasaṃhāra weapons were born from other parts of his body: Sandāmana, Satyavanta, Dharaṇa, and Dhṛṣṭa.
And likewise Bhṛśāśvatanaya, as well as Satyakīrti, Mohana, Rabhasāstra, and Sarvanāha, who had turned their backs in retreat. (30–34)
Jṛmbhaka, Pratihāra, and likewise the excellent Varaṇa;
Avāṅmukha, Dhana, Dhānya, Vṛṣākṣa, and Kāmarūpaka; Dṛḍhanāha, Kāmaruci, Sunābha, and likewise Makara.
He has ten eyes, possesses a circular form, and likewise another with ten faces.
Rucira, Daśaśīrṣa, Yogandhara, Amitrahā,
Anidra, Makara, Bhoktṛ, and likewise Kaṅkaṇī.
Śatodara, Saumanasa, Padmanābha, as well as Mahānābha, Pramathana, Jyautiṣa, and Krathana. (30–38)
I have likewise well meditated upon Trairāśi, Sārcimālin, Vimalā, Dhṛtikā, as well as Sṛṣṭi, Viṣāmāstra, and Sudhyātā.
Vidhūta, Kṛśana, Lakṣākṣa, and likewise Karśana—
all these weapons, which are of the nature of withdrawal (upasaṃhāra),
that god, the scorcher of foes, indeed brought forth from his own left side.
The conclusion of the chapter's subject matter:
"Thus have the names and the births been declared, O Nārada, as well as the majesty of the weapons and of this Yantra in brief. (30–41)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Births and Names of the Weapons," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1825:
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Limbs of Yoga: Restraints, Observances, and Postures."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly destroys the flood of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The question regarding the nature of the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga):
Nārada says—
first, the worship within the heart is superior to the external sacrifice.
You have mentioned its nature; you ought to explain it correctly as it truly is.
The commencement of the subsequent discourse by Ahirbudhnya:
"Well asked by you; O Nārada, listen to its true nature."
By which one pleases the Blessed One, who is honored by all the worlds. || 31-2 ||
The characteristic of the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga) is this:

whatever threefold means of accomplishment are used here to perform the external sacrifice, with those very same means—perfected through mere resolve—one performs the worship directed toward the Deity. (31.3)
This is declared to be the propitiation of the Heart, which accomplishes all goals;
it is equal to the internalization of the Self, or rather, it is the surrender of one's own self to that Blessed Lord. (31.4)
One should oneself offer the oblation of the self—pure and dissociated from primordial nature—to this supreme deity in the form of the wheel, according to the mantra. (31.5)
Nārada asks a question concerning the nature of the Self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti): "You should describe the form of the Self as it is dissociated from matter."
Tell me with certainty by what means that attainment is reached.
The commencement of the subsequent discourse by Ahirbudhnya:
Listen to that which is supreme, subtle, all-pervading, and likewise the sustainer of all.
It is of the nature of knowledge, without beginning or end, changeless, and free from affliction.
It is without eyes or ears, without touch, and without hands or feet;
it is eternal, devoid of name, genus, and so forth, and likewise without color or qualities.
All-hearing, all-seeing, with hands and feet everywhere, supreme, unattached, immovable, tranquil, self-luminous, and incomparable. (31.9)
Standing afar yet moving nearby, attainable through knowledge, stainless, the sustainer of beings, the light of lights, beyond darkness— (31.10).
The Imperishable, which abides in all beings—that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Yoga and action are the means for attaining the nature of the Self, which is distinct [from the world];
both yoga and action are enjoined by the Śruti as the means for attaining that. (31.11)
Regarding that subject, Nārada asked:
"What kind of action is to be known, and what is said to be yoga?"
By means of these two, the Self, which is entirely beyond primordial nature, is attained.
The commencement of the subsequent discourse by Ahirbudhnya:
"Listen; first, that action is said here to be of two kinds."
Karma is said to be of two kinds: one is impelling (pravartaka), and the other is restraining (nivartaka).
The actions that incite and those that restrain are, respectively, the means for attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
O divine sage, that which incites is said to be the means for achieving results such as heaven, while that known as the restraining action should be understood as the means for liberation. (31.14)
The conjunction of the individual soul and the Supreme Soul is the meaning of the term "eight-limbed yoga" (aṣṭāṅgayoga).
It is said that the union of the individual self and the Supreme Self is called yoga;
this is declared to have eight limbs, by means of which the Self is brought within the range of vision. (31.15)

The enumeration of the limbs of yoga (p. 282): I shall describe its eight limbs; listen to them individually. Restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*), and likewise posture (*āsana*) immediately following that. (31.16)

Then breath control (prāṇāyāma) is proclaimed, as well as withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and likewise absorption (samādhi); these, O Nārada, are the ancillaries.

The definition of the restraints (yamas): Truthfulness, compassion, fortitude, purity, celibacy, forbearance, straightforwardness, moderation in diet, non-stealing, and non-violence—these are the ten restraints. (31.18)
The definition of the nature of truth and the other virtues: Truth is speech that is beneficial and pertains to objects as they have been perceived.
Compassion is the constant inability to endure the suffering of all living beings. (31.19)
Fortitude is the steadfastness in performing one's own duties even in times of adversity;
and purity is the fitness of all the senses for performing actions prescribed by sacred law. (31.20)

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the avoidance of the notion that one's own wives are objects of enjoyment; forbearance (*kṣamā*), however, is the state of an unchanging mind even in the presence of causes for transformation. (31.21)
Straightforwardness is the uniformity of the activities of speech, mind, and body;
moderation in food, for those in the stages of life, consists of eating as enjoined by the Vedas. (31.22)
Non-stealing is the absence of longing for the wealth of others through speech, body, and mind; non-violence is the refraining from harming others through speech, mind, and body. (31.23)

The definition of the nature of the observances (niyama) is as follows: listening to the established doctrine, giving, discernment, worship of the Lord, contentment, austerity, faith, modesty, recitation of mantras, and likewise the performance of vows. (31.24)
These ten restraints (niyamas) have been declared as the means for accomplishing yoga.
Regarding the definition of the hearing of the Siddhānta and so forth:
the hearing of the Siddhānta is declared by the wise to be the hearing of the Vedānta. (31–25)
Giving consists of bestowing wealth acquired through righteous means upon a worthy recipient; faith in the prescribed action is what is called "discernment" (mati). (31.26)
Worship of Viṣṇu according to one's ability with devotion is the worship of the Lord; contentment with the thought "this is enough" is indeed delight in whatever comes by chance.
Austerity consists of emaciating the body through practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
faith is the firm conviction that there exists a reality accessible solely through the Vedas. (31.28)
The wise declare that shame (*hrī*) is the feeling of modesty regarding the performance of forbidden actions;
the practice of the study of sacred texts and mantras as instructed by the guru is known as *japa*. (31.29)
The vow consists of grasping the means taught by a true teacher.
Now, regarding the postures as the cause of physical steadiness, I shall describe the various principal postures. (31–30)
By resorting to one of these, yogis attain liberation.
(p. 284) [The enumeration of the primary seats: the wheel, the lotus seat, the tortoise, the peacock, and likewise the cock. || 31-31 ||
Vīrāsana, Svastika, Bhadra, Siṃhāsana, as well as Muktāsana and Gomukha—these, O Nārada, are the principal postures. (31–32)
One should place the left thigh upon the right ankle and the right [thigh] upon the other; with the body held straight, this is the supreme *cakrāsana*. (31–33)
Having placed both soles of the feet comfortably upon the thighs,
this is declared to be the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which destroys all sins. (31–34)
Pressing the anus with the two heels in reverse order, one who is composed performs the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana);
this is declared to be the supreme tortoise posture, which brings about the perfection of yoga.
Having assumed the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), with both elbows properly placed on either side of the navel region,
one should support the earth with the palms of the hands, standing like a staff in the sky.
The mayūrāsana is prescribed with the head and feet raised equally;
it destroys all poisons and wards off all diseases. (31–37)
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the hands extended between the knees and placed upon the ground, this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana) situated in the sky. (31-38)
Having placed one foot upon one thigh and then the other foot upon that thigh, and having settled the [other] thigh upon the foot— this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture. (31–39)
Having placed both soles of the feet firmly between the knees and the thighs, one should sit with the body straight; that is called the Svastika posture. (31.40)
Placing the ankles on either side of the perineum and firmly binding the forefeet with both hands— this is called Bhadrāsana, which destroys all sins. (31–41)
Having placed the two ankles on either side of the perineum in reverse order,
and having placed both hands upon the knees with all the fingers fully extended. (31–42)
With eyes fixed on the tip of the nose, mouth open, upright, and wise—
this is declared to be the lion’s posture (siṃhāsana), worshipped by all the gods.
Having placed the left ankle upon the right thigh and the right ankle upon the left, and having positioned both hands between the thighs, one assumes the *muktāsana* (p. 286). || 31-44 ||
This is declared to be the *muktāsana*, in which those seeking liberation remain.
For the *gomukhāsana*, one places both ankles against both sides of the back. (31–45)
Then, having crossed the hands and grasped them with the palms placed together, while the big toes are pressed from behind, this is called *gomukha*. (31.46)
The necessity of purifying the channels for the accomplishment of *prāṇāyāma*:

"O you whose wealth is austerity, for the sake of perfecting *prāṇāyāma*, one should thereafter perform the purification of the channels by means of the winds residing within the body together with fire. (31.47)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Limbs of Yoga: Restraints, Observances, and Postures," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 1872:
The thirty-second chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Purification of the Channels, Victory over the Winds, and the Limbs of Yoga such as Prāṇāyāma."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly removes the flood of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
Regarding the question of the number, location, and so forth of the channels (nāḍīs), Nārada says:
"How many channels are there? Of what nature are they? What is their measurement?"
Where do they reside within this body, and how is their purification accomplished? || 32-1 ||
The Question Concerning the Number and Other Attributes of the Winds:
How many winds abide, what are their names, and of what nature are they? What are their functions? You should explain all of that. (32.2)
The commencement of the subsequent discourse by Ahirbudhnya:
"Listen to this supreme secret with an undistracted mind."
The body of all living beings measures ninety-six finger-breadths; it is free from disease by means of these fingers. (32-3) [p. 288]
O divine sage, each [measurement] consists of ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
If you desire to hear, O great sage, the determination of the middle part of the body—that which is called the "middle of the body"—[then listen]. 32-4.
Listen: beyond two finger-breadths from the region of the anus, and below two finger-breadths from the region of the penis, the middle [channel] is said to be located. (32–5)
The nature of the fire-mandala residing within the body is four-cornered, triangular, and circular; these correspond respectively to quadrupeds, humans, and birds. (32–6)

The location at the root of the channels is nine finger-breadths above the penis; it is called the *kanda* (bulb) of the channels, measuring four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in length. (32.7)
It is egg-shaped, enveloped by fat, flesh, bone, and blood;
the location of the navel-wheel is right there, and upon it the twelve-spoked navel-wheel is established. (32.8)
Kuṇḍalinī dwells in that by which the body is sustained;
there is the placement of the syllables of the Sudarśana mantra upon the spokes of the navel-cakra—namely, those syllables which belong to the Saudarśana mantra. (32.9)
Having distinguished all those consonants as well as the vowels,
one should place them in this wheel in sequence upon the spokes starting from the east.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the remaining syllables in the center of the wheel; being composed, one should place the rest in the middle of this wheel.
The abiding of Kuṇḍalī is all around the navel-wheel (nābhicakra).
Then the eight-faced Kuṇḍalī revolves all around the wheel.
Enveloped by experience in the form of the eightfold prakṛti, the power of Viṣṇu indeed closes the aperture of Brahmā with the mouth of the suṣumnā.
The location of Alambusā and Suṣumnā within the cakra:
Alambusā and Suṣumnā both reside in the center of the cakra. The specific locations of the other twelve nāḍīs are as follows.
In the eastern part of the Suṣumnā, that channel named Kuhū resides.
In the pair of spokes immediately following [the first], there is Vāruṇā and Yaśasvinī;
and on the southern spoke, Piṅgalā exists in succession to Suṣumnā.
Immediately following those two, Pūṣan and Payasvinī proceed;
and in the western movement of Suṣumnā, the channel Sarasvatī is situated.
Śaṅkhinī and Gāndhārī are situated immediately adjacent to those two;
and on the northern spoke of the Suṣumṇā, the one called Iḍā dwells. (32.16)
Immediately following is Hastijihvā, and then Viśvodarā is situated;
thus, in a clockwise sequence, these are the channels (nāḍīs) upon the spokes of the wheel.
These twelve sons of Brahmā exist within the twelve [channels];
these are the names of the fourteen principal nāḍīs: Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī. (32–18)
Kuhū, Payasvinī, and Yaśasvinī the daughter of Varuṇa;
Viśvodarā, Hastijihvā, Gāndhārī, and likewise Śaṅkhinī. || 32-19 ||
Alambusā and Pūṣā— these fourteen are the primary ones.
The total number of channels existing within the body is seventy-two thousand.
There are three principal channels;
among them, three are most important: Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā.
Of these as well, Suṣumṇā is the most important.
Among them, Suṣumnā is the principal one; it is established extending up to the crown of the head.
The wandering of the individual soul within the wheel of channels:
"Mounted upon the vital breath, the individual soul always wanders in this wheel, just as a spider remains within the web of its own threads. (32.22)
The middle aperture of the *suṣumnā* is perpetually covered by the *kuṇḍalī*.
Of the five apertures, four belong to the *suṣumnā* and are filled with blood;
however, the middle one, the *brahmarandhra*, is eternally closed by the *kuṇḍalī*. (32.23)
Description of the dimensions of the channels:
The eastern side of the Suṣumnā extends upward to the forehead, while the western side reaches to the neck;
these are the two sides, the left and the right. (32.24)
This secret has been declared regarding the attainment of the head and the sides:
there is a channel called Alambusā, which is situated extending to the ends of the feet. (32.25)
The Kuhū, pervading all bodies and belonging to Varuṇa, reached the end of the penis;
then the illustrious Yaśasvinī reached as far as the big toe of the right foot.
The channel named Piṅgalā reaches the end of the right nostril;
Pūṣā and Payasvinī reach the right eye and ear respectively. (32.27)
The channel named Sarasvatī reaches the root of the tongue;
Śaṅkhinī goes to the left ear, and Gāndhārī to the left eye. (32.28)
The channel reaching the left nostril is renowned by the name Iḍā;
the channel Hastijihvā, however, reaches the big toe of the left foot. (32.29)
I have described the movement of the channels as they reach the universal belly;
the moon and sun reside in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* respectively: the moon abides in the *iḍā*, and the maker of light (the sun) abides in the *piṅgalā*. (32–30)

(292) Only two [channels] cause time; the Brahma-nāḍī consumes that time. Now hear the account of the movement of the bodily winds: the account of the winds situated within the interior of the body. (32–31)
In the body there are ten winds: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
The determination of the locations of the vital winds (prāṇas) and so forth:
The wind known as prāṇa always resides in the navel-cakra;
the prāṇa manifests between the mouth and the nostrils, and within the heart. (32–33)
The *apāna* wind generally resides in the anus, the penis, the thighs, and the knees; it is also present in the abdomen, the testicles, the waist, the calves, and the navel, like a lamp. (32–34)
The apāna wind manifests while standing between the anus and the fire-pit (the perineum);
the vyāna wind is located between the ears and eyes, as well as at the nape of the neck and the two ankles. (32–35)
Udāna dwells here in the nose, the throat, and the buttocks; there is no doubt of this. It is situated in all the joints, as well as in the feet and the hands.
The *samāna* [vital air], having pervaded all the limbs, remains established throughout them.
The definition of the functions of the vital airs (*prāṇa*) and so forth is as follows:
exhalation, inhalation, and the like are held to be the action of *prāṇa*. (32–37)
The very action of abandoning and taking up is intended as the action of vyāna;
that which consists of lifting the body and so forth is declared to be the action of udāna. (32–38)

The functions of the *samāna* wind within the body are said to be nourishment and so forth; that which has eructation and other qualities as its characteristic is proclaimed to be the function of *nāga*. (32–39)
O celestial sage, the closing [of the eyes] and so forth belong to Kūrma; sneezing belongs to Kṛkara; and the act of drowsiness is said to belong to Devadatta. (32–40)
The swelling and other ailments of Dhanañjaya, as well as all his activities, have been proclaimed; likewise, the entire course of Vāyu and their respective functions have been described. (32–41)
The procedure for purifying the channels:
thereafter, the self-possessed practitioner should perform the purification of all the channels;
this is the method for that purification.
Having filled the internal air with the *iḍā* [nāḍī] for sixteen *mātrās*, one should draw the external [air] in likewise.
Then, holding the breath in the abdomen for thirty-two measures (mātrās),
one should meditate on the fire within one's own maṇḍala, and thereupon on the letter *ra* together with the nasal bindu.
One should visualize the orb of the moon at the tip of the nose as showering nectar;
having visualized the letter *va* with its bindu upon the moon, one should then exhale.
Again, having filled [the breath] through the *piṅgalā* by the very same path as previously described,
and having held the vital air (*mātariśvan*), one should exhale again through the *iḍā*.
Thus, one should perform this three times daily at the three junctions of the day, always with a concentrated mind.
For one who purifies according to the stated sequence, the perfection of the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhisiddhi*) is attained within three months.
For one who practices thus while bound by the observances (*niyama*), all the channels— (32–46)
Those who know yoga understand that one becomes pure after three months; thereafter comes mastery over the vital air (vāyu),
and from that, one achieves victory over the winds residing within the body.
From mastery over the vital air comes steadiness of the mind;
thereafter, O Nārada, wherever the vital airs abide within the body, there the mind remains steady along with the fire.
The procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma):
one should then perform breath control, which destroys all sins.
Next is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six-syllable mantra upon the locations beginning with the crest-lock (śikhā).
Then, at the place of the crest-lock, in the navel-cakra, and in the heart-lotus.

One should contemplate the six syllables of the mantra in their proper sequence upon these locations: the pit of the throat, the middle of the eyebrows, and likewise at the root of the tongue. (32–50)
The method of breath control (prāṇāyāma):
Having filled the air with sixteen mātrās through the iḍā [nāḍī], one should meditate upon the imperishable Supreme Self in the form of a wheel within the center of the heart. (32–51)
One should recite this mantra of Sudarśana as many times as possible while remembering it;
then, one should exhale through the channel called Piṅgalā using sixteen measures (mātrās). (32.52)
Having inhaled by means of this [nostril] and held [the breath] by means of the other, one should exhale;
likewise, one should mutter the *praṇava* during inhalation, retention, and exhalation. (32–53)
Having recited the Gāyatrī ten times, fifty times, or one hundred and fourteen times respectively, one should perform [the rite] according to the path previously described.
One should perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in this manner every day;
these purify even a man who has committed a great sin within a month.
The Description of Pratyāhāra (Withdrawal):
Thereafter, one should perform pratyāhāra, endowed with its five ancillaries.
The wise [understand] the mind as that which by its very nature is engaged with the objects of the senses. (32.56)
Having withdrawn [the senses] from those [objects] by force through the perception of their defects, the settling [of the mind] upon the Blessed One is known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal). || 32-57 ||

The definition of concentration (dhāraṇā): Through detachment from sense objects, through practice, and by perceiving their defects, the restraint of the mind within the Supreme Self is known as concentration. (32.58)
The Description of Meditation:
