Thus, having steadied the mind, one who is self-restrained and applying the mind for the first time should meditate upon Janārdana in the form of a wheel within that [lotus]. (32.59)
The duties of the castes and stages of life constitute the procedural requirements for meditation (p. 296):
"In a delightful, pure, secluded place with water, in a forest, abiding in the dharma appropriate to one's caste and stage of life, with a serene mind... (32.60).
Tranquil, endowed with all virtues, seated upon an even posture,
with his body straight and his gaze fixed on the tip of his own nose, he was devoted to Hari.
By means of that very breath arising from *prāṇāyāma*, together with the internal fire,
one pierces the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī, which resides within the center of the *suṣumnā*.

Having opened the lotus of the heart, one should contemplate that form of wondrous appearance in the space thereof, at the location of the crest-lock (śikhā), in the midst of a flickering flame of fire.
An investigation into the essential nature of the object of meditation, which serves as the support for dhyāna:
Tawny-eyed, rich with tawny hair, possessing the brilliance of a blazing fire, with a face formidable with fangs and a terrifying appearance due to his furrowed brows. (32.64)
He shone with hair standing erect like a mass of lightning,
and was radiant with a crown adorned with various jewels, rubies, and pearls that bestowed manifold bliss.
Adorned with jeweled earrings resembling the full moon,
the Lord is endowed with eight arms and wears garments of precious gems.
Endowed with the supreme weapons—the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the pestle—along with the noose, the goad, the lotus, and other most formidable [implements]. (32.67)
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine sandalwood paste,
and adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, waist-bands, and anklets.
Adorned with various other diverse ornaments,
he sits upon a lotus throne, bestowing fearlessness upon all his devotees.
Meditating in this way, one is liberated; being freed from all sins,
one attains that very state of meditative concentration (samādhi) which arises through the progressive intensification of the continuous flow of mindfulness.
Yogins know that samādhi to be the manifestation of the mere object;
thereafter, having established himself in samādhi and attained identity with it, the greatness of one steadfast in samādhi is described. (32.71)
He enjoys the entire power of that potent one;
all the qualities beginning with *aṇiman* belong to this great-souled one.
Though without an ally, he destroys even the vast armies of his rivals,
just as the discus [of Viṣṇu] destroys the hosts of Daityas and Rākṣasas.
Indeed, all his desires come to him spontaneously;
the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Yakṣas perform service for him.
All the gods, the sages, the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, as well as the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—all were obedient to his command. (32.75)
The sole cause of the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the entire universe, he is the knower of all, the seer of all, and the possessor of all powers;
assuming his many desired forms, he slays the Daityas and Rākṣasas.
His desires fulfilled, he dwells with his retinue withdrawn.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification of the Channels, the Conquest of the Vital Airs, and the Yoga-limbs such as Prāṇāyāma," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret treatise of the *Pāñcarātra*.
From the beginning, verse 1948.
The thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Maṇiśekhara.
Merely meditated upon once, it swiftly destroys a multitude of sins numbering many tens of millions.
We meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
Nārada repeated the meaning of what had been said: "O Blessed One, you have described everything— the essential nature as well as the qualities."
Likewise, the retinues, the mantras, and the deities with their weapons and missiles [are described]. || 33-1 ||
Distinguished by powers (śaktis), variegated mandalas, and many kinds of lotuses—
this unsurpassed form of the yantra has been thus described.
O Supreme Lord, this yantra has been proclaimed for the protection of all living beings and castes, and especially for that of the Kṣatriya.
There are three questions concerning the power and scope of the Sudarśana: "The greatness of this king of yantras was described previously;
is this [greatness] considered to be the power of the Lord in the form of the Cakra? (33–4).
Is he Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha himself, or is he born of his retinue?
O Lord, please sever this doubt, for you are omniscient.
(p. 300) The commencement of the detailed explanation following that:
Ahirbudhnya says—This power of the Sudarśana has been described by me in brief.
O divine sage, listen to this account of its extent as it is being told.
For the most part, the state of being an attendant belongs to great beings with respect to a superior ground;
if there were no such superior ground for him, the possibility of his being an attendant would not exist at all. (33.7)
Everything is of the nature of the Sudarśana;
therefore, this entire world, both moving and stationary, consists of the Cakra.
Indeed, the Sudarśana itself is the nature of the Kālacakra.
First, hear about Time, whose nature is the wheel and which is without beginning or end.
The description of the true nature of Kālacakra:
That which consists of the year—a wheel endowed with three naves, six rims, and five spokes, and which is imperishable—is known as Kālacakra. (33.9)

Everything is subject to the power of Kālacakra; the entire universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, exists under its control. The Supreme Self is the one who sets the wheel of time in motion.
The Lord, assuming the form of the wheel, causes this to revolve.
The description of the wheel of the world:

it is encircled by spokes consisting of the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the Particularized (viśeṣa), numbering twenty-four, and is joined with the Self (puruṣa) as its hub. (33.11)
The Supreme Self is the impeller of that which is known as the wheel of the universe, and He impels it Himself;
this is the Supreme Self’s role as the impeller of the navel-wheel.
The embodied being abides by means of the twelve-spoked wheel at the navel.
And that body is impelled by Him alone, who exists in the form of the wheel;
therefore, this is the conclusion regarding the Supreme Self’s role as the impeller of all: "The Lord Janārdana is the impeller of everything. (33.13)
Possessing a beautiful form, glorious, and without beginning, origin, or dissolution—He alone is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the universe;
the Lord is the very nature of knowledge, His body composed of the six perfect attributes. (33.14)
He alone is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of all beings.
That very Lord, assuming the form of Śiva, is worshipped by the Śaivas; indeed, that Lord is worshipped by the Śaivas in the form of Śiva. (33–15)
He alone, in the form of Brahman, is the creator of the world;
he alone, in the form of Brahman, creates this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings. He alone, through his own partial manifestations, is the protector of the world.
He himself, having become Viṣṇu, the agitator of men, protects this [universe].
His very nature as the destroyer in the form of Rudra:
he alone, in the form of Rudra, withdraws the entire universe.
His very nature as the Buddha:
And by means of the Buddha-nature, that very same one abides in the world for the sake of the Buddhas.
He alone possesses the form of the Digambara;
he alone assumes the unclad form of the Śāmbaryas;
he alone possesses the form of the Jina.
And he alone, in the view of the Cārvākas, assumes the form of Jineśvara.
He alone possesses the form of the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa);
he alone is designated as the Sacrificial Person by the ritualists, and he alone is enjoined as the object of worship by the Mīmāṃsakas. (33.19)
In the system of the followers of Kapila, that very [principle] possesses the nature of Puruṣa;
by the Kāpilas, that all-pervading one is designated as Puruṣa.
Because it is the essence of all things, it alone is the bestower of all fruits.
Whomever they declare as the object of worship, He assumes that very form.
He alone swiftly grants all their desires;
moreover, among assuming the forms of deities and others, the Lord’s assumption of the form of the Discus is most beloved.
Janārdana [is the source] of these very gods, who are his own bodies. (33.21)
The Blessed Lord Hari, assuming the form of the discus, brings supreme delight; the reason for this is His protection of those who have taken refuge in Him and the destruction of His enemies. (33.22)
Hari assumes this very body consisting of the Sudarśana;
this secret has been told to you because you are a devotee, O one whose wealth is austerity.
In this regard, O divine sage, listen as I relate to you an ancient historical account:
there was a righteous royal sage named Durdharṣa, firm in his valor. (33.24)
The illustrious son of Pramaganda, residing in the city of Naicāśākha,
ruled righteously over the earth consisting of seven continents.
He had a queen of excellent complexion named Vatsalā;
she gave birth to him a son, Maṇiśekhara.
Having transcended that stage as well, Maṇiśekhara—handsome in form, heroic, accomplished in learning, and a scorcher of his enemies—[attained the next]. (33.27)
When he had attained youth, the illustrious and invincible Durdhara gave him his eastern wife— this son who was worthy of sovereignty over all the worlds.
Having entrusted the kingdom to him, he went to the forest for asceticism;
[the king] protected the earth, including the ocean-bound lands, just like his father. (33.29)
While that high-souled Maṇiśekhara was protecting the entire earth, seven sons were born to him in the eastern region.
At that time, there appeared a powerful being known as Vikaṭākṣa, who had received a boon from Brahmā and was a source of terror to all living creatures.
The entire earth was oppressed by that very same great Asura;
the earth was filled with his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. (33–32)
Those terrifying Asuras, thousands in number, possessing fearsome forms and commanded by Vikaṭākṣa, began to oppress all living beings.
O best of sages, those powerful ones put some to flight and slew others, thereby obstructing the sacrifices of the twice-born.
The prescribed duties of all the social classes (varṇas) residing in their respective stages of life (āśramas) were performed exactly as ordained.
The great asura Vikaṭākṣa caused all the jewels and abundant wealth that exist upon the earth to be bestowed upon himself.
Then all the subjects, oppressed by that evil-minded one,
reported that matter to King Maṇiśekhara.
Overcome by great wrath, the lotus-eyed king set his mind upon fighting the great asura Vikaṭākṣa. (33-38)
Then, having assembled all the soldiers, he put on his armor;
seeing him thus equipped for battle, his ministers gathered around him.
They said this regarding his invincibility resulting from his military assault:
"In the past, that evil-souled one chose [this boon] from Brahmā, who was not yet satisfied with his ascetic penance."
When he said, "Let it be so," that Vikaṭākṣa, who had become exceedingly arrogant, granted invincibility against those enemies who came before him.
From that time forward, he became invincible by enemies who came against him face-to-face;
therefore, you too should prepare your armor for him.
Then, having heard the words uttered by his ministers,
the lord of the earth desisted from his preparations for battle.
Then the king, having summoned his blameless family priest Kratu,
consulted with that knower of mantras.
Having related the entire account of Vikaṭākṣa exactly as it happened,
[he described] his invincibility by enemies when standing face-to-face in battle.
"O Blessed One, tell us that means by which we may conquer that invincible one;
let all my subjects become secure once more. (33.46)
Having been addressed thus by the king, the domestic priest reflected for a long time and then spoke these words to Maṇiśekhara.
(306) It is true that he, arrogant due to his boon, cannot be conquered in battle except by the Blessed Viṣṇu, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace. (33.48)
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as long as lotuses,
immeasurable, the Lord of the World, the destroyer of the suffering of those who have taken refuge in him.
O Lord of the World, there is no other means in this world equal to that which possesses lofty and auspicious qualities and crushes the host of Daityas. (33-50)
Therefore, O lord of the earth, go for refuge with your whole being to that God who bears the form of the discus and is consecrated to the protection of his devotees.
Durvāsas, the best of sages, knows the means for attaining that [power];
by his grace, he is capable of destroying that entire asura.
"Go now to that sage who terrifies all living beings. Having resolved, "So be it," the most righteous king [departed]. (33–53)
He went forth from that city together with his family priest to see the great sage performing austerities on a delightful peak of the Himalayas.
Wearing bright bark garments and a bright sacred thread,
bearing matted locks and an antelope skin, he was peaceful yet resembled a blazing fire.
The king, accompanied by his domestic priest, went to where he was situated in that manner;
and that best of sages, seeing the two—the king and the priest—[approached them].
Having honored them according to the prescribed rite, he addressed them with a welcome: "For what purpose have you both come to this forest region? (33.57)
I perceive you two as the very personifications of the Brahmin and the Kshatriya classes. O hero, I know you to be Maṇiśekhara, the son of Pramaganda.

We have heard that the earth, consisting of seven islands, is under your control; in all matters of statecraft and dharma, such as the constituent elements of sovereignty, is all well with you? (33.59)
O Lord of the Earth, you protect all your subjects who abide in their own duties;
having obtained me as your priest for the sacrifice, what will not be accomplished for you? (33-60)
A sage who has mastered the Vedas is superior to all ascetics;
he is peaceful, self-controlled, pure, illustrious, truthful, and firm in his vows.

He was a knower of the Dharma, a knower of all scriptures, and skilled in all ritual acts; he was diligent in his duties, endowed with virtuous conduct, a performer of sacrifices, and free from ailment.

Devoted to compassion for all, possessing an even mind, and endowed with meditative concentration; one who is confident in the doctrine of destiny, supremely generous, steadfast, and honored by kings. || 33-63 ||
Always approved by all, he was devoted to Puruṣottama;
he was a knower of the six duties of statecraft and an expert in policy.
Compassionate, well-born, a practitioner, and a knower of all mantras, and endowed with other virtuous qualities—he is remembered as a domestic priest (purohita). || 33-65 ||
"O Maṇiśekhara, this sacrifice is like a second Bṛhaspati in person; perform all your tasks by means of it."
Nevertheless, he has come as if insulted by certain enemies.
Tell us everything, O King: what is the cause of your arrival? (33.67)
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor, whose wealth is asceticism, became silent;
then Kratu, the best of sages, spoke to Durvāsas.
The entirety of the royal business and the reason for their meeting:
his own kingdom was being oppressed by the evil-minded Vikaṭākṣa.
The power of this great asura, his invincibility by enemies,
his attainment of a boon from Prajāpati, and the expansion of his progeny.
Having described his many kinds of world-condemned actions in this way,
he bowed down to him and spoke with humility.
"Tell me the means for his victory; he has come to you for refuge. Protect this king, who is devoted to righteousness, from this calamity."
"By this very [act], O one whose wealth is asceticism, the worlds have been saved.
Having spoken thus to the best of sages, they prostrated and stood before him.
Beholding them with supreme compassion, he bestowed upon them the six-syllable mantra of Sudarśana, which grants the fruits of the four aims of human existence.
"Accomplish your desired goal with this very priest;
for the domestic priest alone is the achiever of both seen and unseen aims for kings. (33.75)
Especially in the case of this deity, regarding its installation, worship, and so forth, whatever deficiency occurs—all that arises from the transgression of the officiating priest. (33.76)
Likewise, O King, the excellence of this very king in his affairs must be ensured by other priests; indeed, that task must be performed by him and by them.
Having spoken thus, the great sage then related this ancient account:
how the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, assuming the form of a boar [acted].
Then, during the Vārāha Kalpa, she lifted the earth from the waters;
at that time, the goddess Vasundharā, being exceedingly delighted, spoke to the Lord.
O Lord of the World, having assumed this beloved body, you must always conduct yourself on the surface of the earth in a manner pleasing to those who are devoted to you. (33.80)
Having been addressed thus by that goddess, from that time forward Keśava dwelt in the sacred region of the earth known as Sālagrāma.
The glorious Lord, whose form is the Sudarśana discus and who is affectionate toward his devotees,
even today [remains there] out of regard for the greatness of the region and out of compassion for his devotees.
By the prayer for Bhuvaḥ, Hari is eternally present there;
whatever austerity is performed here shall become a thousandfold. (33.83)
There, humans, animals, worms, and birds—whosoever dies marked with the conch and the discus, they become [liberated], of this there is no doubt. (33.84)
The Blessed One, the lotus-eyed one, who bears the form of Sudarśana and is an ocean of true auspicious qualities, is ever present there.
At that time, all the mortals dwelling in that region, as well as the gods, animals, trees, and even the mountains, were marked with the seal of the wheel. (33.86)
On the holy bank of the Sarasvatī, at Sālagrāma, one should worship Janārdana in the form of the discus (Cakra) according to the very path previously described.
By his grace, slay your rivals who act with wicked intent;
thereafter, protect this earth free from thorns, just as in the past.
Having spoken thus to the king and his domestic priest, the blessed Durvāsas, the best of sages and foremost among those who practice self-restraint, ceased speaking.
Then, having bowed down to him, the king and the priest departed,
ascending the victorious celestial chariot toward the city of Naicāśākha.
Then, having gone to Sālagrāma and gathered all the necessary materials, he [worshipped] the Blessed Janārdana, the Lord of the World, who exists in the form of the discus.
The king honored him through the officiating priest according to the sacred formulas;
indeed, the lord of the earth honored him with worship, recitation, and meditation.
He propitiated Hari for a month with supreme devotion;
then, O lord of the earth, He appeared before the king in the form of the Discus.
With his eight divine arms, he bore a mace, a club, a conch, a discus, a bow, a noose, a goad, and a lotus; his eyes were tawny.
Abounding with upward-pointing tawny hair, red in color, and of great splendor,
his face is formidable with fangs, and he is seated upon a lotus throne.
Wearing red garments, proud, and adorned with all ornaments, he whose chest bore a divine garland gazed upon him with a smile. (33.96)
Then, from the chest of Hari, there arose [the discus],
which obstructed the vision of all the worlds,
like a circle of lightning flashing from the sky.
Then the supreme wheel of Indra, of exceeding splendor.
First there is one, then ten,
then a hundred, and from the sequence of ten hundreds come a *niyuta* and an *ayuta*; thus it becomes manifold until the entire sky is filled.
The wheel he had seized became exceedingly terrifying.
Having simultaneously struck down the Dānava Vikaṭākṣa along with all his kinsmen,
Sudarśana remained for a moment here in this inaccessible place, and having leaped up, he departed;
he ruled the earth together with its oceans and forests.

Just as Śacī’s husband [Indra] conquered the triple heaven along with its deities and its cities, so too did Maṇiśekhara, whose fame is pure, conquer the entire earth with all its islands and its ports.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Maṇiśekhara," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.

The thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Mantras such as the Brahmāstra."
Meditated upon even once, it swiftly removes the flood of millions of births;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the Lord Sudarśana.
The inquiry regarding the nature of the mantras of the Brahmāstra and others:
Nārada said—
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, honored by all the worlds!"
And it has been said, O Lord, that the multitude of weapons here emerged from the discus.
O Lord, you ought to explain the essential nature of all those mantras;
for without you, I do not see anyone else who knows them.
To explain that which follows, Ahirbudhnya describes its supreme secrecy:
"O Great Sage, that which you have asked is this most secret and supreme [truth]."
It is extremely difficult to obtain, unspeakable to anyone, and the accomplisher of all goals.
Nevertheless, O great sage, because you are my devotee, I shall speak of it to you;
yet this must not be given by you to anyone else, for it is honored by both gods and demons.
1—The Brahmāstra (p. 313):
the letter *pha* joined with fire (*ra*), combined with the void (*ha*) and *hālā*;

"Bhīṣaya" ending with "śiraḥ"—this is declared to be the Triśūla weapon.

Āṣāḍhayuk sa-caṇḍīśo huṃ phaṭ is known as the Brahmaśiras [astra]. Aiṣīkāstra is hā svā pakṣi yava-drāvi nyaṃsai rapa-mareti.

likewise Āṣāḍha joined with Māyā and endowed with Dīrghadaṇḍa. (35–33)
*Krodhī* and *sāmareśaḥ*, *baka* joined with a long vowel, *vālī* joined with a long vowel, and then the word *nivārita*. (35–34)
And one should say, "For splendor"; this great mantra ends with "well-being" (svasti).
It is renowned as Dhṛtimālin and is honored in all the worlds. || 35-35 ||
*Rucirāstra*,
*saṃvartakaḥ*, *sāmareśaḥ*, *mīnaḥ* joined with *bindu*,
and *māyī* followed by *kṣāmayā*; this is the *āvṛtta* mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables.
The weapon-mantra (praharaṇa), repeated twice, followed by the word "śam" and ending with "namaḥ"—this is proclaimed as the beautiful mantra. (35–37)
20–21. Pitṛsaumanasa, Astra, Lohita, Māyāyukta, Āṣāḍha, and Bhārabhūtimat; from here, "Devasāra" should be recited, followed by "Sarvābhayapada. (35–38)

The word "pradā" should be employed for the purpose of bringing about all forms of pacification; this mantra, ending with "śiras," is known as that which brings about the favor of the ancestors. (35–39)
Vidhūtāstra, Tāra, and likewise Hṛdaya; Khaḍgīśa joined with Māyā; Mīna joined with Aṅghrīśa; and Āṣāḍha joined with Dīrgha. (35–40)
Having uttered the words "Caṇḍa," "Māyī," "Pinākī," "Āṣāḍha," "Dīrghasaṃyuta," "Lohita," and "Karāya," [one should proceed]. (35–41)
Then, having first recited "parama," "dhāmne," "ca," "vidhūtam," "idam," "uttamam," "makarāstra," "namaḥ," and "truṭitaśabdau," [he should proceed]. 35-42.
Having uttered the words *śāstra* and *astra*, and immediately after that the word *śaktaye*, one should then say *śaktiśālinaḥ* and subsequently *makarāya*. (35–43)
Then, at the step of *pravṛtta* and likewise at the step of *mahārṇava*, one should say "vibhedinaḥ"; this is the excellent *makara*.
Having uttered "Karavīra," preceded by "Tāra" (Oṃ) and followed by "Namaḥ," then the word "tiraskṛta," and having pronounced the word "gadā," one should then recite "vīryāya. (35–45)
This mantra, ending with "śiraḥ," is remembered as being equal to the Karavīra [flower]. 24–25.
The Dhanāstra [mantra] consists of the Tāra (Oṃ), followed by a synonym for "praṇāma" (namas), then "lohita" joined with fire (ra). 35–46.
Āṣāḍha conjoined with Ananta, Lohita, and Mīna;
Muṇḍa, Śiva, Kurupada—repeated twice—is known as Dhana (Wealth). [This is] Dhānyāstra. (35–25)
"O white horse, go away"—this mantra, pronounced in reverse order and ending with "śiras," is called *dhānya* by the wise. (35–48)
The science of astrology (jyautiṣāstra),
Lohita, Vahni, Saṃyukta, Caṇḍa, Ādi, Anta, and then in sequence Baka, Muṇḍa, Samāyin, and likewise Savahni and Lohita.
"Bako, poison! Then 'Muṇḍo,' 'Māyī,' and 'Prakaṭita.
Then, having uttered 'Viśva' and 'Pada,' one says 'Praśamaya' thereafter. (35–50)
This mantra, repeated twice, is declared to be the Jyautiṣa. 27–kṛśanāstra, krodhī, pinākī, and māyī; thereafter follows āṣāḍha. 35–51.
*Krodhī* together with *ananta*, *bakayuk* with *dīrgha* and *agnimat*, *muṇḍa* and *vālī* ending with *śiras*: this is declared to be *kṛśana*. (35–52)
One should designate [the mantras] as *nairāśyāstra*, *māyī*, *khaḍgī*, *śikhī*, *mahāmāyī*, *pinākavān*,
and the two terms *kṛtacakra* and *cakrāya*. (35.53)
This mantra, ending with *vaṣaṭ*, is proclaimed as "despair" (*nairāśya*).
(Vimalāstra, p. 336): Khaḍgeśa, Prathamamāyī, Cāṣāḍha, and Dīrghavahnimat. (35)
Bhṛgu joined with Māyā, Āṣāḍha joined with Dīrgha, Māyī, Caṇḍa, Pinākī, and thereafter Ananta in sequence. (35–55)
Bhṛgu, Sāṣāḍha, Dīrghāgni, and Vālī immediately following that; having uttered "to Vimala," ending with the word for the head (śiras), it is remembered as Vimala. (35–56)
30–35.57: One should then recite the *Yogandharāstra* mantra: *bhṛgurlāntaḥ savahniśca māyāśabdam*, followed by the words *mayāstrāya* and *tamobarhaṇa*.
Having indicated "to the embodied form" (mūrtaye), one should then recite "and to Yoga";
likewise, the word "to the Earth" (dharāyai) should follow immediately after "to the Great One" (mahate). || 35-58 ||
One should then say "to Bhīṣaṇa," for this is the Heart-mantra that has been practiced.
This weapon, known as Yogaṃdhara, has been proclaimed and is honored by all.
31–36. Then *vinidrāstra*, *muṇḍa*, *māyī*, as well as *ākāśa* and *āṣāḍha*;
thereafter *meṣa* joined with *māyā*, and *atri* together with the long *agni*.
This mantra, ending with "mudrāya" and "śiras," is declared to be "vinidra.
The "naidrāstra" consists of the syllables *vi*, *ṣa*, *ma*, *gni*, *a*, *nila*, joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*) and the nasal bindu (*m*). (32–35–61)
Those who know the weapon-mantra (astra) recognize this as the "lump" (piṇḍa), ending with the head, belonging to Nidra.
First, having uttered the *tāra* (the syllable Om), one should then utter the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) for the Pramathana-weapon. (33–35.62)
Then, having recited the *Viṣa*, the *Daṇḍīśa* together with the *Māyā*, and likewise the *Āṣāḍha* and the *Baka*, immediately thereafter—
Then Krodhin, together with Sāṣāḍha and accompanied by Caṇḍīśa, [uttered] "Be gracious! and then the weapon known as Pramathana was invoked.
34–65: *Sārcis*, *Mālyasra*, joined with *Varuṇa*, joined with *Dīrgha*, and *Caturmukha*;
then *Pinākī*, *Sānanta*, *Lānta*, and after that, *Māyī*.
Jvālānta, joined with Māyā, and then Pinākī; thereafter, one should recite the first letter of the fourth group followed by Mahāsī. (35–66)
"One is capable," "one of great luster," and "forgive me"—repeated twice—this is the mantra of Mārīci, accompanied by rays of light. (35.67)
35–68. *Hā*, *Svā*, *Nañja*, *Bharañca*, *Asarapattavṛpra*, and also *Rasvā*— this is known as the *Kāmarūpa* [mantra], arranged in reverse order.
36—The *Kāmarucyastra* begins with "Oṃ namaḥ"; followed by *muṇḍa* conjoined with *māyā*, joined with the third vowel (*i*), and then *caṇḍa* followed by the letter *ra*. (35–69)
One should utter the word "kabandha" and finally "saṃdhānāya";
this mantra, ending with the *śikhā* [vinyāsa] and pleasing to the heart's desire, has been proclaimed by the ancients. (35–70)
37— One should then recite the Mohanāstra (the deluding weapon), the Bhautika (elemental) mantra joined with the Daṇḍa (staff), and the Aṅkuśa (goad);
and the word "Mohavāriṇī" ending with the head-mantra is called Moha.

The weapon of the covering (āvaraṇāstra) consists of Khaḍgīśa joined with the long vowel [Ī], followed by Vahni conjoined with Māyā; then Āṣāḍha, Mahākāla, and Vyoma conjoined with the long vowel [Ū]. (38–39)
Mahākāla with Ananta, and Vālī conjoined with Caṇḍīśa—this great mantra ending with Śiras is declared by the wise to be the enclosure (āvaraṇa). || 35-73 ||
39— Having sequentially assigned the Jṛmbhakāstra, the two Dviraṇḍas, and the two Daṇḍas, one should utter the four-faced [mantra] and the word "Muṇḍa," and thereafter extract the word "Svasti."
This great mantra, ending with the word *śiras*, is proclaimed as the *Jṛmbhaka*. Then follows the weapon-mantra (*astra*) of Sarvanābha:
Caṇḍa joined with Ananta, followed by Māyī and Astra. (35–75)
One should utter the first [syllable] of the fourth group immediately followed by *senāpada*; this is called *jīvātava*, ending with the head (*śiras*) and containing all the *nābhas*. (35.76)
41— Having uttered the weapons of Bhṛśāśva’s son in order, beginning with Vego and ending with Anta, and then Viśvādya,
followed by Jitaśabda, and also "Vainateyāya," [he should proceed].
This mantra is said to end with "Śiro'nta" and "Bhṛśāśvatanayā.
Then follow, in sequence: Saṃdhānāstra, Bhṛgu, Varuṇa, Sāgni, Muṇḍa, and Māyī. (42–35–78)
*Khaḍgīśaḥ*, *sāgnidīrghaḥ*, *lohitaḥ*, and then *umāpatiḥ*;
the mantra repeated twice as "śaṃ" is called *saṃdhāna*. (35–79)
The Vāruṇa weapon consists of Bhrigu, Lānta (La), and Agni (Ra), joined with Daṇḍa (Na).
Then there is Bhrigu, Vyoma (Ha), and Jīva (Sa), joined with Varuṇa (Va).
This mantra, ending with the word *śiras*, is proclaimed to belong to Varuṇa.
Regarding the inquiry into whether weapons possess form or are formless, Nārada offered praise to Ahirbudhnya:
Nārada said—
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are saluted by all the worlds!
O Supreme Overlord, immeasurable self, whose sphere of knowledge is inconceivable!
Taking refuge in you, all the gods obtain their desired fruit. (35.82)
From you everything has arisen—the entire world, both stationary and moving;
by you alone, O Maheśvara, it is all protected and withdrawn. (35.83)
You are the beginning of all the worlds, yet you are beginningless; you are composed of the world. You are the Puruṣa, you are the unmanifest, and you are the manifest, O creator of the universe.
You are the sacrifice, you are the object of worship, you are the sacrificer, you are the fires, and you are the oblation;
you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the *oṃ* syllable, and likewise, you are the one to be known through the Vedas.
And from you alone, O Maheśvara, all beings proceed;
you are the instrument, the cause, the agent, the effect, the action, and the fruit, O All-pervading Lord. (35.86)
You alone, O Supreme Lord, are the past, the future, and the present;
though devoid of qualities, you assume qualities for the creation of the world. (35.87)
You are the most minute among the minute, and you are the greatest among the great;
O Lord, one who is devoted to you attains the supreme goal.
One who is not colored by passion indeed goes to hell; yet you are not subject to such transformation.
You are Time itself, consisting of parts such as kalās, kāṣṭhās, and muhūrtas, and you are composed of all these divisions.
O Śaṅkara, although you dwell at all times within all beings,
you are not stained by their transformations, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Since you perceive everything at all times as clearly as an amalaka fruit in the palm of your hand,
you have explained the nature of all weapons to me, who inquired about them.

(On the question of whether weapons are corporeal or incorporeal, p. 341): "O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, you ought to dispel this doubt: do these weapons possess forms, or are they indeed formless? (35.92)
Regarding the demonstration of their corporeality, Ahirbudhnya says:
"O Nārada, their limbs are of terrifying form."
Indeed, their mouths were fierce with curved and terrifying fangs, striking fear into all people.
O Nārada, they were indeed possessed of rolling, bloodshot eyes that struck terror, and their hair was as fearsome as a mass of lightning.
Some were smoke-colored, some possessed the brilliance of the sun; some were white in color, and some were like fire.
With their supreme hands, which possessed terrifying forms resembling great iron clubs,
they each held their respective weapons— vast and powerful.
Swift, agitating, and destroyers of the pride of enemies,
they have been constantly worshipped even by the foremost of gods and asuras.
O Nārada, having thus empowered their limbs and weapons,
they roam about at will, free from fear from any quarter.
These foremost of weapons, whose greatness is immeasurable, terrifying, with blazing bodies and uplifted arms,
possess unimpeded movement.
They wander continuously through the worlds. || 35-99 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Weapon of Withdrawal," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine within the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, verse 2252:
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Predominance of the Qualities of Keśava and Others in the Ritual for Worshipping the Sudarśana Machine of Kings."
Meditated upon, it swiftly removes the flood of sins accumulated over millions of existences;
we meditate upon that divine splendor of the god Sudarśana.
A Question Concerning the Method of Meditation and Worship for the Eastern and Western Limbs of the Sudarśana Yantra:
Nārada said—
"O Blessed One, all [the mantras] of the great-splendored universal weapons have been described."
Likewise, mantras are both initiators and likewise terminators. || 36-1 ||
And all this has been previously declared by you, the Omniscient One:
the great yantra of Sudarśana is to be worshipped by the high-souled ones. (36-2)
In the manner already described, those who seek the fruits of the four aims of human life should worship this supreme face of Sudarśana, if they are kings. (36-3)
"One should satisfy both faces of this machine;
how then should one meditate upon its other limbs, or how should one perform [the ritual]? (36–4)

"O Maheśvara, you ought to sever this doubt of mine. To that, Ahirbudhnya replied: p. 344) [The subsequent explanation: "Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which bestows liberation; it is the essence of all scriptures and is difficult for even the gods to attain. He then spoke: "I shall tell you the truth regarding the nature of the Self, as well as the means of its realization, according to the tradition of the Śaiva scriptures. He said: "The Self is pure consciousness, eternal, omnipresent, and free from attributes; it is the witness of all states and is not an object of perception. He continued: "Its realization arises through the grace of the Guru and the purification of the mind by means of yoga and devotion. He said: "One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who is beyond the qualities of nature (guṇātīta), as residing within the heart-lotus, the source of all existence. He said: "By the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, the Self is revealed, like the sun emerging from behind clouds. He said: "This knowledge is the highest goal, the end of all suffering, and the door to the city of liberation. He said: "One who knows this is liberated while living, and upon the dissolution of the body, attains the state of identity with Śiva. Thus he spoke. p. 345) [End of section.]
Having meditated thus, the king should worship this highly resplendent yantra.
Therein, regarding the meditation on Sudarśana in the center of the yantra within the preliminary section:
one should meditate upon the Great Soul, a person with terrifying eyes, endowed with upright, tawny hair, and a face radiant with blazing fangs. (36–6)
He stands endowed with eight most beautiful arms,
positioned in the midst of a wheel and a lotus, grasping a great bow.
The Lord, with majestic limbs and a symmetrical form, wears red garments and holds in his hands the conch,
discus, lotus, mace, noose, and goad.
Having meditated upon this Sudarśana, who is endowed with all ornaments, adorned with flower garlands,
and surrounded by the twelve forms beginning with Keśava, one should then contemplate him on all sides. || 36-9 ||
Whether they were standing or seated, Keśava and the others were seen in embodied form,
endowed with ornaments and weapons in the very manner described.
Then, one should perform the meditation on the sixteen forms beginning with Viṣṇu, which are the supreme primary [deities] established according to one's desire;
then, [one meditates] upon those sixteen deities beginning with Viṣṇu, accompanied by their weapons.
One should meditate upon this unsurpassed king of yantras as being encased by these [deities], who are embodied, diligent, and adorned with all ornaments. (36.12)
One should meditate on the withdrawal-weapons (saṃhārāstra) as having form all around;
one should likewise meditate on all those great withdrawal-weapons as being embodied, wondrous, and with palms joined in reverence.

"O Nārada, one should meditate on the weapons as being fearless from all sides, powerful in every direction, and then as having taken embodied form; thus one should meditate upon the weapons as they are set in motion."
Then, as if to devour all the luminous worlds in bodily form,
one should meditate upon the Nārasiṃha-form; having thus contemplated this according to the sequence of the wheel, one should reflect upon that which is above.
Then, one should meditate on the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa in his lower portion, bearing the body of Narasiṃha, as the supreme root-treasury.
One should contemplate the glorious machine (yantra) in the form of a wheel, endowed with a blazing rim;
one should visualize a great flame emanating from this rim in the four directions. (36.17)
One should visualize, in sequence, those holding the discus, the kaumodakī mace, the śārṅga bow, and the sword in their hands;
thus one should meditate upon this single-faced [deity] of the highly resplendent yantra. (36–18)
The *aparāṅgadhyāna* has the *aparāṅga* as its limb, fully adorned on all sides by great mantras;
it begins with the *tāra* within, or else with the *viṣṇupañjara*. (36.19)
Without that previously mentioned collection of their respective mantras for the form,
one should meditate upon the mere mantras of all the weapons in the other limbs according to their proper places; thereafter, one should contemplate at its conclusion.
It was the sole source of the mantras for all the weapons of destruction,
and immediately thereafter, it was the activator of other weapons as well.
Having meditated upon the web of mantras, which has excellent rims and is worshipped by the gods—
the great machine of great power, in the form of a wheel, unsurpassed— (36.22).
Endowed with the aforementioned attributes and being the sole means for fulfilling all desires,
that Supreme Person who dwells in the center of this wheel— || 36-23 ||
Therefore, it is proclaimed by the wise in the world as "the universal monarch" (cakravartin).
By worshipping this machine, kings attain the status of a universal monarch.
Hence, whatever king is endowed with devotion should worship this. (36-24)
In a very short time, he shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
This worship should also be performed by others who desire the welfare of the king—whether they be the king himself, the king’s servants, the ministers, or others. (36.25)
All those who desire the welfare of kings should worship this supreme [teaching]; others who long for prosperity, as well as other men who desire abundant fortune, should likewise honor it. (36.26)
This, which accomplishes all aims, should be worshipped constantly by them;
indeed, it has been specifically proclaimed for kings. (36.27)
Those men who are designated apart from that king—of them, great prosperity shall certainly be attained through the king. (36.28)
Whoever, having fashioned [an image] with either metal or stone, should worship it, attains abundant prosperity and finds long life. (36.29)
He attains health, and all his descendants become long-lived.
Regarding the worship of the two-faced yantra, the eligibility belongs exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa who has received the instruction of the mantra;
however, it is only that Brāhmaṇa who has been instructed in the mantra who may worship the two-faced [yantra]. (36–37)
O Sage, only he would be able to endure the supreme power of that one who possesses both natures, through knowledge, austerity, and strength.
The non-difference of the Puruṣas residing in such places as the solar orb and the eyes is stated:
"That supreme Puruṣa who is seen situated within the solar disc, who is golden, and who is likewise seen within the eye. (36–32)
This very person who resides in the center of the navel-cakra is indeed the initiator of the Kālacakra and other systems;
he is that imperishable Puruṣa who impels the wheel known as Time (Kāla). (36–37)
The wise know him alone as the leader of the wheel of the ages;
even the great seers call him the one who sets in motion the wheel of the world. (36.34)
Having established him within the celestial chariot,
his worship alone is the means for accomplishing the fruits of both this world and the next—
he who is the sole creator of all worlds and the sole witness of all worlds.
Having established this imperishable universal monarch within the celestial chariot (vimāna), [he departed].
For one who performs worship, this world and the world beyond shall belong to him.
Even the undertaking of constructing a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) yields great fruit;
O Great Sage, he who would begin the construction of the Sudarśana chariot— || 36–36 ||
Having attained all objects of desire here, he shall go to the world of Viṣṇu;
for even the act of plowing for the purpose of constructing a celestial chariot is a means to achieve every prosperity—
he who indeed performs the plowing for the Sudarśana chariot.
His enemies perish and all his prosperities remain;

even for one who has begun but not completed the construction of a temple, there is ultimately the attainment of liberation, provided that the site was properly commenced but then interrupted by obstacles midway. (36–38)
Having enjoyed all pleasures upon the surface of the earth as a sovereign ruler of the whole world, he,
being a devotee of the Discus, shall again bring his remaining duties to completion.

Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, he shall attain union with Viṣṇu. (This concludes) the description of the succession of fruits for one who performs the installation and other rites along with their ancillaries, having constructed and consecrated a supreme celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and the Sudarśana [discus]. (pp. 349) 36–40.
Having established there, according to one's ability, at least twelve Vaiṣṇava Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, and who subsist on the remnants of those offerings.

Having ensured that their livelihoods are sufficient and having granted them land, monasteries, and other such gifts, he who constantly worships this deity endowed with prosperity [attains the same]. (36–42)
His prosperity increases beyond all bounds day by day;
he attains freedom from disease and long life—of this there is no doubt. (36–43)
Having been born as a sovereign ruler of the entire earth in another birth and having enjoyed it for a long time, in the birth immediately following that—
Having become the lord of Triviṣṭapa, he enjoyed the station of Indra for a long time;
thereafter, having attained the status of various world-protectors in succession, he reached that state.
At the end of that, he attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
For one who does not worship the Lord Sudarśana, kingship is difficult to obtain;
indeed, no one becomes a king without worshipping this very God. (36–46)

O Nārada, through the gradations of this very propitiation, there arises a gradation of results; by the specific degree of this propitiation alone, a king certainly attains a corresponding gradation in enjoyments and lifespan. (36–47)

Therefore, for kings and others as well, there is a necessity to propitiate him; thus, with every effort, the king himself should worship him. (p. 350) And those other men on earth who desire [rebirth in] a particular caste, longevity, or enjoyments... || 36-48 ||
By worshipping this [discus] as well, they obtain everything they desire.

[Now follows] the inquiry regarding the nature of the subordinate status, such as being an attendant, of Sudarśana— who is himself a subordinate (śeṣa) to Keśava and others who are the primary objects of service (śeṣin).
Nārada said:
"The Sudarśana of Viṣṇu is perfected; it is known as the remaining weapon."
How are his attendants, Keśava and the others, described?
And how are the various forms, Viṣṇu and the rest, arranged within the cage? (36–50)
Or how, Blessed One, have the mantras come to be your retinue?
O Lord, you ought to sever this doubt now.
The commencement of the subsequent discourse: Ahirbudhnya said—
Listen, O dear one of great wisdom, to this supreme secret.
No one other than you would be able to ask about this matter.

Just as the Blessed One is, so too Sudarśana, who is of the nature of His resolve, possesses beginninglessness and indivisibility; for it is said: "The divine Nārāyaṇa is the Puruṣa, the lotus-eyed one."
O Nārada, this [universe] likewise is beginningless and immeasurable.
To establish that, the power of the Supreme Self is divided twofold:
"Viṣṇu possesses two powers for the accomplishment of all purposes, by which he carries the burden of the world as their primary force. (36.54)
p. 351) One [power] of His consists of will (*icchā*), while the other consists of action (*kriyā*). Among these, the power whose nature is will has the form of Lakṣmī;
she is the first, supreme Lakṣmī, the consort of the Protector of the World. (36–55)
The knowers of reality have declared that the power whose nature is action takes the form of Sudarśana; this is the second Sudarśana here.
Without these two powers, even the Blessed Lord would be incapable of acting.
Therefore, O Lord, Hari is not capable of even forming a resolve without Lakṣmī.
Without this [third power] as well, Keśava is not able to accomplish anything.
These two powers serve as the instruments for creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth;
by this [power], the Lord creates everything, and by this very [power] he protects it. (36–57)
By this, the Lord brings about the dissolution of the universe at its end;
by this, Madhusūdana slays the Dānavas and Daityas.
By means of this [power], all that action is performed by the omnipresent one; thus,
even the two powers are included within the category of the protected, with respect to the Supreme Self who is the protector.
Therefore, one should protect this [mind] with one's entire being through one's own intelligence. || 36-59 ||
Specifically, the demonstration that Lakṣmī herself is included within the category of those to be protected is as follows:
"Just as one's own property is protected by the owner himself, so too does Lakṣmīdhara himself protect Lakṣmī, the mother of all. (36.60)
Having divided himself fourfold, he protects his own constituent elements;
therefore, the conceptualization of Keśava and the others as a retinue is logical—this is the conceptualization of the forms of Keśava and the others as a retinue. (36–61)
And it is appropriate that the forms of Viṣṇu and the others constitute a cage;
furthermore, they now serve as protectors for all mantras. (36–62)
Alternatively, another way of establishing the relationship between the subordinate and the primary is as follows:
"Or rather, the Blessed One himself, assuming the form of the discus, remains present; thus he is called Puruṣottama by the wise. (36–63)
In the Tretā Yuga, Lord Hari himself, for the sake of protecting the virtuous,
appeared in person in the forms of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, Bharata, and others.
In the same way, Hari himself, whose essence is the wheel, is established in four forms;
the relationship of subordinate and principal attributes, however, is appropriate for him just as it is for Rāma and the others.
Thus Janārdana protects himself by means of his very self,
because for the protection of his own form, there can be nothing other than himself.
Even from hearing this secret and so forth, there is the gradual attainment of the supreme human goal;
for that man who here constantly hears this, or inquires about it, or recites it, or remembers it—
Having attained abundant prosperity in this world,
he then goes to the supreme abode of Hari.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Relationship between Keśava and the Others as Primary and Secondary Attributes in the Ritual for the Worship of the Sudarśana Yantra by Kings," in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, a secret doctrine of the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantra*.
From the beginning, 2,319 verses.
